full_judgment:
Righteousness of decisions recorded by learned Trial Judge and Appellate Judge has been put on fire by plaintiffs-petitioners by way of a Civil Revision Petition under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure (For short the Code) before this Court, Civil Revision Petition led to registration of Civil Revision No. 6406 of 2002.

2. First-fourth-petitioners predecessors of fifth petitioner and twelfth-thirteenth-opposite Parties as plaintiffs instituted a Suit being Title Suit No. 63 of 1988 in the Court of Senior Assistant Judge, Munshiganj Sadar for declaration of title in respect of 0.23 acres of property duly described in schedule ka and kha to plaint and, also, for a declaration that Revisional Settlement Khatian No. 1363 described in schedule 'kha' to plaint is wrong and, also, for a decree of partition in respect of the said 0.23 acres of property. First-third defendants of Suit are first-third-opposite parties in Civil Revision Petition.

3. Plaintiffs sought above stated reliefs pressing into service contentions that Ram Nath Mondol had been owner of Suit property. Ram Nath Mondal drew his last breath leaving behind three sons, Mon Mohan Mondal, Ovi-monue Mondal and Kailash Mondal. In Cadastral Survey record-of-right name of Mon Mohan Mondal and Ovimonue Mondal had been recorded in equal share and Kailash Mondal having been a minor during Cadastral Survey Settlement Operation period his name was not recorded in Cadastral Survey record-of-right, Cadastral Survey period of Right was wrong. Ovimonue Mondal breathed his last leaving behind two brohers Mon Mohan Mondal and Kailash Mondal. Kailash Mondal being owner to the extent of 8 annas share of cadastral surevy Khatian died leaving behind two sons, Hemanta Mondal and Neekunja Mondal. Neekunja Mondal died leaving behind first-fifth plaintiffs. Hemanta Mondal died leaving two sons, Deen Nath Mondal and Personath Mondal, Deen Nath Mondal faced death leaving behind fourth-defendant. Parsonath Mondal died leaving three sons, fifth-seventh defendants. Plaintiffs are successors of Neekanja Mondal. Plaintiffs demanded partition from co-sharer defendnats and that demand of partition had been turned down by first-Seventh defendants taking stand that plaintiffs got no title on Suit property. Cloud had been cast upon right and title of plaintiffs over suit property. Plaintiffs, thus, have been constrained to institute suit for declaration as well as for partition.

4. First-third-defendants laid written statements controvert averments made in plaint. Defendants in written statement denied right, title and interest of plaintiffs over suit property. Defendants put forth pedigree contrary to case projected in plaint. It has been asserted that Mon Mohan Mondal died leaving behind only son Tufani Mondal and Tufani Mondal transferred entire inherited property in favour of Taizuddin by a deed of conveyance dated 14-1-1970. Taizuddin died leaving behind three sons first-third defendants and three daughters nineth-eleventh defendants and they have been exercising acts of possession on Suit property. First-third Defendants put up their ownership in respect of entire 'ka' and 'kha' schedule property.

5. Over pleadings, learned Senior Assistant Judge, framed following issues:

i. Suit as framed can proceed?

ii. Is the suit barred by limitation?

iii. Is the suit bad for defect of parties?

iv. Have plaintiffs got title, interest and possession on Suit Property?

v. Are plaintiffs entitled to relief as sought for?

6. Suit was taken up for preemptory hearing. Plaintiffs in support of their case examined three witnesses. First-third defendants, though, laid written-statement did not contest plaintiff's claim during trial and did not place on witness box any witness in support of contentions pressed into service in Written statement.

7. Learned Senior Assistant Judge, Munshiganj by Judgment and decree dated 14-1-1999 dismissed Plaintiff's suit.

8. Plaintiffs could not accept Judicial verdict pronounced by learned Senior Assistant Judge and sought setting same through a medium of appeal being Title Appeal No. 29 of 1999 before learned District Judge, Mutishiganj. Learned Joint District Judge, Second Court, Munshiganj heard the appeal and by Judgment and decree dated 2-9-2002 dismissed appeal and maintained Judgment and decree recorded in Title Suit No. 63 of 1998.

9. Plaintiffs, having been resentful of Judgment and Decree recorded in Title Appeal, knocked at the door of .this Court on presentation of a Civil Revision Petition under section 115 of the Code.

10. Core question that outlasts for determination in this Civil Revision case is, whether Judgments and Decrees under challenge in Civil Revision Petition can be sustained on pleadings, evidences, materials on record and, also, legal aspect involved in case.

11. Question posed is now approached and answered.

12. Plaintiffs in support of their case placed on witness box three witnesses. Fourth plaintiff Bharat Mondal as plaintiff witness No. 1 furnished following evidence:

রাম মোহন মন্ডল ৩ পুত্র মনমোহন, অভিমনু ও কৈলাস মন্ডলকে রেখে মারা যায়। অভিমনু (অভিমোহন) নিঃসন্তান অবস্থায় ২ ভাই কৈলাশ ও মহমোহনকে রেখে মারা যায় উভয়ে আট আনা অংশে মালিক থাকে। কৈলাস মন্ডল আট আনা অংশে মালিক দখলদার থেকে ২ পুত্র নিকুঞ্জ ও হেমন্তকে ওয়ারিশ রেখে মারা যায়। উক্ত জমিতে আমরা স্বত্ব দখলকার আছি। নিকুঞ্জ বাদীগণকে পাঁচপুত্র রেখে মারা যায়। এস,এ ১১৯৯ ও আর,এস ১৩৬৩ খতিয়ান ভ্রমাত্নক। নালিশি জমিতে আমাদের ২টি ঘর আছে। সত্য নয় যে, রাম নাথ মন্ডলের ২ টি পুত্র ছিল। কৈলাস নামে কোন পুত্র ছিল না। সত্য নহে যে বিবাদীগণ নালিশি জমি ভোগ দখল করে।

Anil Mondal, PW 2 is an old man of 80 years. He provided following version:

উভয় পক্ষগণ ও নালিশি জমি চিনি। কৈলাস মসমোহন রামনাথ নালিশি জমির মালিক ছিল। কৈলাসের ছেলে নিকুঞ্জ মন্ডল ছিল। নিকুঞ্জের ছেলেরা হচ্ছে বাদীগণ। বাদীরা ঘর বাড়ি করে নাল জমি দখল করছে ১০/১৫ বছর যাবৎ এরা নাল জমিতে বসত ঘর নির্মান ভোগ দখল করছে। ইহাতে বিবাদীদের কোন দখল ছিল না।

13. Paresh Chandra Mondal PW 3 is aged about 65 years. He blurted out following account:

উভয় পক্ষ ও নালিশি জমি চিনি। বাদীগণ নালিশি জমি দখল করে। নিকুঞ্জের পিতার নাম কৈলাস মন্ডল। ৩৫ বছর যাবত এরা নাল জমিতে বসত ঘর নির্মান করে ভোগ দখল করছে। ইহাতে বিবাদীদের কোন দখল ছিল না।

<u>14. Cross-examination of a witness is the greatest legal engine for discovery of truth. Cross-examination is directed to bring to light truth by clarifying matters which a witness may desire to keep concealed. Failure of plaintiff or defendant to cross-examine witnesses of other side will raise a presumption and legal inference that evidence provided by witnesses in examination-in-chief has been accepted. Support for the proposition of law is sought to be drawn from Nur Mohammad and another vs Sultan Ahmed and another, 40 DLR 369 wherein it has been held:</u>

<u>It is well settled principle of law regarding cross-examination that on failure of a party to cross-examine the witness of his adversary appearing against him on material evidence it will be presumed by Court that testimony given by that witness-in-chief has been accepted as it cannot be suggested that his statement on a particular fact is untrue unless he is cross-examined drawing his attention to that fact and thereby giving him an opportunity to explain the same. This rule of cross-examination is not merely "a technical rule of evidence" but it is as well "a rule of essential Justice" because it is essential to fair play and fair dealing with witnesses. In the said case the authoritative observation of Lord Chancellor Herschell in the case of Browne vs Dunn (1983) 6. R 67 has been quoted which is in the following language :</u>

<u>"Now, my Lords, I cannot help saying that it seems to me to be absolutely essential to the proper conduct of a cause where it is intended to suggest that a witness is not speaking the truth on a particular point, to direct his attention to the fact, by some questions put in cross-examination showing that imputation is intended to be made, and not to take his evidence and pass it by as matter altogether unchallenged and then, when it is possible for him to explain, as perhaps he might have been able to do if such questions had been put to him, the circumstances which it is suggested indicate that the story he tells ought not to be believed, to argue that he is a witness unworthy of credit. My Lords, I have always understood that if you intend to impeach a witness you are bound, whilst he is in the box, to give him an opportunity of making any explanation which is open to him, and as it seems to me, that is not only a rule of professional practice in the conduct of a case, but is essential to fair play and fair dealing with witness."</u>

<u>Following the aforesaid principle of law PB Mukharji, J (as his Lordship then was) in AEG Carapiet. vs AY Derderain 1961 Calcutta (DB) 359 speaking for the Court observed:</u>

<u>"Wherever the opponent has declined to avail himself of the opportunity to put his essential and material case in cross-examination, it must follow that he believed that the testimony given could not be disputed at all. It is wrong to think that this is merely a technical rule of evidence. It is a rule of essential Justice."</u>

<u>First-third defendants did not cross-examine Plaintiff witness Nos. 1, 2 and 3 and versions supplied by Plaintiff's witnesses remained unimpeached and unsoiled and testimonies stand admitted by first-third defendants.</u>

15. True it is that plaintiff-petitioners could not produce any documentary evidence in support of their contention in respect of heir ship of their predecessor Kailash Mondal from Ram Nath Mondal but it is, also, true that fourth-plaintiff through his testimony as PW 1 and, also, through testimony of PW 2 who is aged 79-80 years as well as PW 3 who is aged 65 years could substantially prove heirship of Kailash visional from his father Ram Nath Mondal. Learned Trial Judge failed to assess and construe testimonies of PWs 1, 2 and 3 and committed a substantial error in holding that plaintiffs failed to prove that Kailash Mondal was son of Ram Nath Mondal.

<u>16. Learned Appellate Judge as last and final Judge of fact, though, was required to discuss and consider evidence of PWs 1, 2 and 3 in true perspective in the matter of coming to a just decision did not discuss and consider accounts supplied by PWs 1, 2 and 3 in right direction and, thus, committed a serious error in finding that statement of PW 1 was not supported by PWs 2 and 3 and by this error a failure of justice has been occasioned to plaintiffs-petitioners.</u>

17. First-third defendants did not substantiate their case set out in written statement by examining themselves and other witnesses and their case was not at all required to be taken into consideration. Learned Appellate Judge positively held that defendants who filed written statement ultimately refrained from contesting the suit and defendants neither cross-examined PWs nor produced any independent evidence in support of defence contention. Learned Appellate Judge again held that defendants did not contest the suit and defendants, though, filed written statement did not substantiate it before Trial Judge. Learned Appellate Judge, thereafter, came to finding that learned Trial Judge committed serious illegality in considering defendant's case in his impugned judgment. In the face of positive findings arrived at by Learned Appellate Judge, he was required to reverse the decisions of Trial Judge and Learned Appellate Judge, thus, committed a grave error whereby a failure of justice has been occasioned.

18. Learned Appellate Judge was absolutely wrong when he held that "It is admitted that Tufani Mondal got entire property and he sold out the said property to predecessor of defendant Nos. 1-3 and there remained nothing residue to claim." Learned Appellate Judge failed to construe true import of "Admission." It was never admitted by plaintiff, neither in plaint nor in evidences adduced by PW1, PWs 2 and 3 that Tufani Mondal got entire property and he sold out entire property to predecessor of defendant Nos. 1-3. Finding of learned Appellate Judge perilously borders on perversity.

19. Learned Appellate Judge found that learned Trial Judge decided the case on contest against defendants. Sentence is in the following term :

In spite of that learned Trial Judge decided case on contest against defendants. Learned Trial Judge did not decide case against defendants and this is a manifestation of non-application of mind on the part of learned Appellate Judge.

<u>20. Learned Trial Judge exhibited two deeds of conveyance dated 13-1-1970 and 14-1-1970 in favour of Taizuddin, predecessor of first-Third defendants and the two documents had been exhibited as Exhibits I and II. These two documents are not original deeds but simply photocopies of deeds. These two deeds, Exhibits I and II had not been at all admitted in evidence and exhibited in accordance with provisions of Evidence Act. None of defendants nor any witness came forward to stand on witness box in proof of the said two documents. Learned Trial Judge out of his own initiative and sun motu exhibited the said two deeds of conveyances as Exhibits I and II. Documents which are not copies of Judicial record should not be received in evidence without proof of signatures and hand writing of persons alleged to have signed or written them, even if such documents are brought on record and exhibited without objection. Soya Rani Guha alias Soya Rani Gupta vs Abdul Awal Mia and others, 47 DLR (AD) 45 orginal Kabala deed was not produced before Court and only certified copy of deed had been produced and the said deed was not proved in accordance with provisions of Evidence Act. It has been laid down that production of a certified copy of a sale deed does not, however, warrant presumption of due execution of original document and a party producing secondary evidence of a document is not relieved of the duty of proving execution of orginal. It has been further stated that even in a case where a document is exhibited without objection Court is to be satisfied as to execution of the document. In Atul Gomez and others vs Julian Rozario and others 6 MLR (AD) 46 original kabala deed was not produced in Court and certified copy of deed was admitted in evidence and marked as Exhibit. It has been held that unless a document is proved in accordance with law such document cannot be admitted in evidence and mere filing of the document is not sufficient to satisfy the requirement of law. In the case in hand, neither the original deed nor certified copy of two documents had been produced and only photocopies of the deeds had been in the record. Having given my anxious thought and consideration in respect of admissibility of the two documents, exhibited as Exhibit I and II and taking stock of Judicial authorities I am of this considered view that two deeds had been illegally exhibited by learned Trial Judge and decision reached by learned Trial Judge on the basis of Exhibits I and II are liable to be quashed and Exhibit I and II are left out of consideration in adjudicating claim of first-Third defendants.</u>

<u>21. Learned Trial Judge found plaintiff's suit to be barred by limitation adopting view that plaintiffs became aware of sale deeds of 1970 in the name of predecessors of first-third defendants and cloud had been cast on title over suit property during that period. Plaintiff laid suit for declaration of title on suit property and as well as for decree of partition. In paragraph No. 13 of plaint it has been stated that cause of action accrued on 25-4-1995 when first-seventh defendants denied title of plaintiff on suit property and, also, refused to effect partition. Paragraph No. 13 is extracted hereunder.</u>

<u>নালিশের কারণ বিগত ২৫-৪-৯৫ ইং তারিখে ১-৭নং বিবাদীগণ বাদীগণকে তপছিলভুক্ত নালিশী দাগের সম্পত্তিতে বাদীগণের স্বত্ব অস্বীকার করায় এবং নালিশি দাগের সম্পত্তি ভাগ বাটোয়ারা করিয়া দিবে না বলিয়া প্রকাশ করার সময় হইতে অত্র নালিশের কারণ অত্রাদালতের এলাকায় উদ্ভব হইয়াছে।</u>

<u>Suit had been filed on 30-5-1995 i.e. within one month of accrual of cause of action of Suit. Suit was laid very much within the period of limitation prescribed by law and Suit cannot be said to be barred by limitation. Knowledge of sale deeds in name of predecessor of first-Third defendants cannot be the starting point of limitation in laying a suit for declaration of title and for partition. It is settled law that plaintiff is to institute a Suit for declaration of title within six years of the date when the right of plaintiff is invaded by other side i.e. defendants. Article 120 of Limitation Act can profitably be pressed into service in this regard. Finding reached by learned Trial Judge that suit stood barred by limitation is based upon total misconception of law and said decision is liable to be turned down.</u>

22. Learned Trial Judge found the suit to be bad for defect of parties for non-impleading Sudir Chandra Dutta and Krishna Mohan Dutta, recorded owners of Revisional Settlement Khatian No. 1363, Exhibit 2(ka). Learned Appellate Judge, also, held that plaintiffs did not imp lead recorded tenants of Revisional Settlement Khatian No. 1363.

23. Learned Counsel for plaintiffs-petitioners and defendant-opposite parties candidly submitted that Revisional Settlement Khatian No. 1363 is in no way connected with suit property and Revisional Settlement Kha-tian No. 1363 had been wrongly and illegally brought in 'Ka' schedule property. Recorded owners of Revisional Settlement Khatian No. 1363 were not at all required to be impleaded as defendants in the suit. It can profitably be stated here that plaint had been drafted by a Muffosil Lawyer. Revisional Settlement Khatian No. 1363 had been inserted in 'Ka' schedule property by way of mistake and this mistake was committed by drafting Lawyer. It was been well settled through catena of Judicial autorities of Apex Courts that Muffosil Court's pleadings should be construed liberally and for confused pleadings, parties should not suffer. Md Zahoor Ali Khan 11 MIA (PC) 468 (Manng) Kyi Oh and another vs Ma Thet Pon AIR 1926(PC) 29, Manmatha Nath Kuri vs Moulavi Muhammad Muklesur Rahman and others PLD SC 565, Brindaban Chandra Chowdhury and another vs Musammat Rezia Begum and another 16 DLR 77, Managing Committee NMC Model High. School and others vs Obaidur Rahman Chowdhury and others 31 DLR (AD) 133 (134)are referred to in this regard.

24. Learned Appellate Judge in discarding claim of heir ship of predecessor of plaintiff’s Kailash Chandra Mondal from Ram Nath Mondal relied upon Cadastral Survey Khatian No. 1142. This Cadastral Survey Khatian had been exhibited as Exhibit A by learned Appellate Judge during appellate stage. Cadastral Survey Khatian No. 1142 was not exhibited in accordance with law and it was not admitted by Appellate Judge as an additional evidence under Order XLI, rule 27 of the Code. Defendants-opposite parties did not at all make endeavor to have this Cadastral Survey Khatian No. 1142 exhibited as an additional evidence by way of a Petition under Order XLI, rule 27 of the Code. None from defendants-opposite parties stood on witness box in Appellate Court in proof of the said Cadastral Survey Khatian. Learned Appellate Judge, thus, committed a serious error in exhibiting Cadastral Survey Khatian No. 1142 as Exhibit-A. Moreover, no evidence had been led in support of recording in Cadastral Survey Khatian that Ramprashad Mondal was father of Kailash Chandra Mondal and Ram Nath Mondal was not father of Kailash Chandra Mondal. Learned Appellate Judge, thus, committed a substantial error in discarding the claim and heirship of Kailash Chandra Mondal from his father Ram Nath Mondal putting reliance upon Cadastral Survey Khatian No. 1142. It is posited here that learned Appellate Judge wrongly noted Exhibit-A as Exhibit 1 and this is, also, a demonstration of non-application of mind on the part of learned Appellate Judge. Learned Appellate Judge misread and misconstrued remarks column "jote Mono Mohan Mondal Raiyat Sthithiban জোত মনমোহন মন্ডল রায়ত স্থিতিবান in Cadastral Survey Khatian Nos. 1142 and by this misreading and misconstruction the merit of decision of appeal in respect of acquisition of interest on the part of Kailash Chandra Mondal on suit property had been materially affected causing thereby a grave injustice to plaintiffs-petitioners.

25. Burden of proof is an obligation to adduce evidence to satisfaction of Court in order to establish existence or non-existence of a fact contended by a party. The provision as to burden of proof is founded on Rule incumbent probation qui deceit non-qui negate =burden for proving a fact rested on the party who substantially asserts the affirmative for the issue and not upon the party who denies it; for a negative is usually incapable of proof. This Rule is derived from Roman Law and is supportable not only on the ground of fairness but,  also upon that of greater practical difficulty  which is involved in proving a negative than in  proving an affirmative Halsburg’s Laws of England Vol. 13 Para 605. It is an ancient Rule  founded on consideration of good sense and  should not be departed from without strong reasons. Per Lord Maugham in Constantine Line vs IS Corporation, 1941 2 ALL ER 165,179.

<u>26. Plaintiff could prove by legal evidence that Kailash Chandra Mondal, predecessor-father of plaintiffs-petitioners is heir son of Ram Nath Mondal and on death of Kailash Chandra Mondal his sons, plaintiffs-petitioners had been and have been in possession of suit property and plaintiffs-petitioners, thus, discharged the burden that lay on them. Defendants-opposite parties, on the other hand, signally failed of discharge the burden of proof through legal evidence that Mon Mohon Mondal was sixteen annas owner of property recorded in cadastral survey Khatian No. 1313 and 1314 and Tufani Mondal inherited the said sixteen annas share from his father Mon Mohan Mondal and Tufani Mondal being owner of sixteen annas share of Cadastral Survey Khatians transferred the same to Taizuddin, predecessor-father of first-third defendants.</u>

<u>27. Cadastral survey record-of-right, though, is the oldest record-of-right prepared under section 103 of The Bengal Tenancy Act State Acquisition record-of-right being a latter record-of-right got presumptive value as to its correctness as enjoined under section 144A of The State Acquisition and Tenancy Act which enjoins that every entry in a record-of-right prepared or revised under section 144 shall be evidence of the matter referred to in such entry, and shall be presumed to be correct until it is proved by evidence to be incorrect. State Acquisition Record-of Right stands in the name of Kailash Chandra Mondal and Record-of-Right prepared in the name of Kailash Chandra Mondal, predecessor-father of plaintiffs-petitioners got presumptive value as to its correctness, of course, the presumption is rebut table one. Presumption of correctness in respect of Record-of-Right prepared in the name of Kailash Chandra Mondal, predecessor father of plaintiffs-petitioners had not been at all rebutted by first-Third defendants-opposite parties on producing reputable evidence. In the event of conflict between old record-of-right and recent record-of-right, recent record-of-right would prevail, inasmuch as presumption of record-of-right loses its weight with passage of time and entry in subsequent record-of-right would be more acceptable than earlier record-of-right. Support for the proposition is sought to be drawn from Bhupendra Krishna Ghose vs Abdur Rahman and others 61 CLL 18 and Abdul Hamid and others vs Abul Hossain Mir being dead his heirs Abdus Sobhan Mir and others 35 DLR 295.</u>

<u>28. Learned appellate Judge as well as learned Trial Judge misdirected themselves in their approach in resolving the controversy involved in the case. Decision reached by Judges do not at all claim any justification from evidence and materials on record and those decisions suffer from gross illegality, legal infirmity and grave error of law and those decisions cannot have any leg to stand and those demand an overthrow. I am of this conviction that since the decisions arrived at by both Trial Judge and Appellate Judge have been vitiated by error of law, those cannot claim any immunity from being attacked in exercise of Revisional Jurisdiction envisaged under section 115 of the Code. Interference is, therefore, warranted.</u>

29. In the discourse made above, the invitable conclusion that legitimately may be drawn is that Rule arising out of Civil Revision Petition under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure got merit and it succeeds. Rule is made absolute, Judgments recorded by learned Senior Assistant Judge, Louhajang, Munshiganj in Title Suit No. 63 of 1998 as well as Judgment and Decree dated 2-9-2002 awarded by learned Joint District Judge, Second Court, Munshiganj in Title Appeal No. 29 of 1999 stand set aside. Suit is decreed. Plaintiffs title on 0.06½ acres of property from plot Nos. 1404 and 1406 recorded in Cadastral Survey Khatian No. 1313 and 0.16½ acres of property from plot Nos. 1402 and 1409 in Cadastrial Survey Khatian No. 1314 = 0.23 acres of property is declared and a preliminary decree of partition in respect of the said 0.06½ + 0.16½ = 0.23 acres of property is granted.

30. Regard being had to the fact and circumstances of the case I direct the parties to bear their respective costs.

Lower Courts Records are sent down.

End.

No one appears---For the Opposite Parties.

full_judgment:
The Rule at the instance of the added respondent was issued calling upon the opposite party Nos. 1 and 2 to show cases as to why the judgment and decree dated 9-7-2001 (decree signed on 19-7-2001) passed by the Sub-ordinate Judge, 2nd Court, Barisal in Title Appeal No. 140 of 1999 allowing the appeal reversing the judgment and decree dated 21-4-1999 (decree signed on 28-4-1999) passed by the Senior Assistant Judge, Incharge, Barisal Sadar in Title Suit No. 305 of 1998 should not be set aside and/or such other or further order of orders passed as to this court may seem fit and proper.

2. The facts relevant for the purpose of disposal of the Rule, in brief, are that the opposite parties Nos. 1-2 as plaintiff filed suit being TS No. 305 of 1998 in the Court of Senior Assist-ant Judge, Barisal Sadar for partition of suit property described in schedule of the plaint.

3. The plaintiff's case, in a nutshell, is that Sarajini was the owner of suit land measuring 5 decimal in Mouza Kawnia SA khatian No. 677 plot No. 690 and her name was correctly recorded; that Sabitra Sundari was the recorded owner 8 decimal of land in SA khatian No. 689 plot No. 714 and it was correctly in her name in revisional survey. On 31-3-1955 the land in SA khatian No. 689 was sold by auction in Rent Execution Case No. 754 of 1954 of Munsif, 2nd Court, Barisal. The plaintiff and defendant No. 2 auction purchased and were delivered possession in the land on 2-4-57. On 5-8-61 land in SA khatian No. 677 was sold on auction in Rent Execution Case No. 4 of 1960 of Munsif, 2nd Court, Barisal and the same was purchased by plaintiff and defendant No. 1 and possession was handed over on 21-2-62. In this way while owning and possessing the land plaintiff wanted to develop the land but quarrel ensued with defendant at different times, when plaintiff proposed amicable partition defendant denied on 15th Ashar, 1405 BS Hence the suit.

4. Defendant Nos. 1 and 2 contested the suit by filing written statement contending, inter alia, that suit is bad for defect of parties and barred in the present form. The suit land claimed by the plaintiff by auction purchase is correct but statement on possession is not correct that the plaintiffs and the defendants possessed the suit land by an amicable compromise for long time but the same was not partitioned through court, that the defendant No. 1 has been in possession of 2½  decimal in plot No. 690/1224 and defendant No. 2 has been possessing 2½ decimal in plot No. 714 by constructing house thereon. Accordingly, they prayed for separate saham.

5. The learned trial Court in the light of pleadings framed issues as follows:-

1. Is the suit maintainable in its present form?

2. Is the suit barred by defect of parties?

3. Is the entire land brought hotchpotch in the schedule?

4. Have the plaintiffs right and title in the suit land.

5. Are the plaintiffs entitled to get decree for partition in separate saham and are defendant entitled to get separate saham.

6. To what relief if any plaintiffs are entitled?

6. The defendants having prayed for separate saham did not press the issues Nos. 1-3 at the time of hearing.

7. The trial Court on consideration of evidence dismissed the suit by judgment and decree dated 21-4-99.

8. Being aggrieved by the aforesaid judgment and decree of the trial Court plaintiffs preferred an appeal being Title Appeal No. 140 of 1999 before the District Judges, Barisal and on transfer the said appeal was heard and disposed of by the Subordinate Judge, 2nd Court, Barisal.

9. In the appeal, the plaintiffs and the defendants filed solenama and petitioner who did not contest the suit by filing statement did not file any cross appeal was impleaded as respondent No. 3. The deposition of the petitioner was recorded and was allowed to cross examine plaintiff and the defendant after their depositions were recorded by the appellate Court in support of solenama.

10. The appellant No. 1 on behalf of the plaintiff-appellants in his deposition stated that they compromised with defendant-respondent Nos. 1 and 2 by solenama. The suit will be decreed in terms of solenama which will be treated as part of the decree. In cross he admitted that they lost in the court below and he is not aware whether trial Court by the judgment and decree discarded and found the papers used by the plaintiffs as complainant filed Criminal Case No. 108/99 and the papers filed in the suit were forged and fabricated. He admitted that the petitioner (respondent No. 3) was in permissive possession on the suit land for 5/6 years. He denied that the petitioner had been residing for 30 years.

11. Defendant-respondent No.1 in his deposition corroborated the plaintiff-appellant on compromise for decree in terms of solenama. He stated that he did not reside on the land: The claim in the suit was for 05 stakes in respect of khatian No.677 and no land for any other khatian. He could not say the number of the suit and name of learned Advocate who conducted his case. He denied that the suit was filed to grab the land of Anowara (petitioner) which she got by gift from Sarajini.

12. The petitioner in her deposition stated that she resided on the land of plot No.690/ 1240 khatian No.677 with her son and daughter. She had house on the land, she used to serve in the residence of Sarajini as domestic aid being pleased she gifted the land to her. She was not impleaded as party and if she was aware about the suit she would have contested.

13. On consideration of certified copies of Bainama, writ of delivery of possession and the service return on the delivery of possession of the Rent Decree Execution Case Nos.754/54 and 4/69 filed by the plaintiff in the suit marked Exhibits 2-2/Ga, the learned trial Court held that in Rent Decree Execution Case No.4 of 1960 the name of decree holder. Bank of Calcutta, represented by the Manager and in the Rent Decree Execution Case No.754 of 1954 the name of decree holder Thakur Estate, represented by Sree Babu Usha Ranjan Ganguly are mentioned. As the auction is for arrear rent of land in SA plot No. and SA Khatian the rent fallen arrear must be on account of the Government and, as such, naturally after the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act Part V came into force Government should have been decree holder of the rent decree Execution case or any person duly authorised by the Government. Since the matter is otherwise, it aroused suspicion. It is further held on careful observation of the papers (Exhibits 2-2ga) it reveals that the stamp papers used in the certified copies have been fraudulently manufactured by using some old used stamp paper and washing out the writings thereon with the help of chemical substances heat of fire by using rubbish in artificial manner and writing and putting seal and signature thereon subsequently. For, although those certified copies were issued about 40 years back the seals used appear crystal clear of most recent origin. The first page of Exhibit 2 is seen burnt out at one place due to heat of fire and in the last page of Exhibit 2/KA Rent Decree Execution Case No.754 of 1954 some previous writing were distinctly visible, on the 1st page of Exhibit 2/Kha on left hand corner over the stamp of the writ of deli-very the specimen mark of previously affixed seal was still found visible distinctly and over the same the figure "4" of the year 1954 and figure "3" in between the date 31-3-55 was found written up after rubbing. In the same way, the specimen of the seal previously used on the left corner of Exhibit 2/ga was almost distinctly visible. Moreover, in the round seal of Munsif Court the word 'Monsif' is wrongly spelt and word 'Bakaganj' is spelt instead of Munsif and Bakerganj causing suspicion about the seal. The learned trial Court further held since papers filed have been created falsely and fraudulently in support of the title claimed by the plaintiff for the purpose of the suit and though alleged auction purchase is admitted by the defendant in order to enjoy the advantage of the suit it does not establish the claim of the plaintiff, rather it appears to the learned trial Court that suit has been instituted to grab the property of the members of Hindu community. Moreover, had the property been purchased in 1961. or before the plaintiffs should have proved payment of rent by filing rent receipt and steps for alleged mutation and separation of Jama in the name of plaintiffs and defendants in due course and this being not done, the manufactured papers filed do not establish any right title of the plaintiffs and dependents over the suit land and they are not entitled to get decree for partition in respect of separate saham. The learned trial Court in dismissing the suit directed not to issue certified copies of the Exhibits-2-2ka /ga and return of the Exhibits and initiate criminal proceeding under Section 476 of the Code of Criminal Proceeding.

14. The learned Subordinate Judge in allowing appeal in terms of solenama filed by the plaintiff-appellants and the defendants-respondents and setting aside the impugned judgment and decree passed by the learned lower Court holding inter alia that as suspicion arose that bainamas were fraudulently manufactured by removing the original writings the trial Court should have got the papers examined by an expert, inasmuch as no specific evidence is adduced to prove the bainanamas as forged, spurious, concocted and fraudulently manufactured and all such finding of the Court is based upon surmise and conjecture, trial Court erred in dismissing the suit on surmise and conjecture. The Appellants and the respondent Nos. 1/2 filed solenama in appeal and their depositions have been recorded. The appellants and respondents were cross-examined by the respondent No. 3 wherein no comment regarding forgery of document was revealed.

15. We have perused the petition, impugned judgment and decree and the judgment and decree passed by the trial Court and heard Mr Khurshid Alam Khan, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner.

<u>16. Ongoing through the judgment and decree passed by the trial Court and the relevant certified copies, it appears that the certified copies of bainama, writ of delivery and service return, Exhibits 2-2/ga are the papers whereby both plaintiffs and the defendants claimed their title and possession on the suit land by virtue of auction purchase in the aforesaid Rent Decree Execution Case Nos. 754 of 1954 and 4 of 1960 of the Court of 2nd Munsif. The case of the plaintiffs in the plaint is that Surajini held title and possession in the land of SA khatian No.677 and Sabitri Sundari was the recorded owner and possessor of the land in SA Khatian No.689 which is admitted in the written statement filed by the defendant but plaintiffs filed certified copy of SA Khatian No.689 in the name of Sabitri Sundari marked Exhibit 1 No certified copy of SA Khatian No.677 in the name Sorajini was filed by the plaintiff at the trial. The trial Court held that right title of said Sarojini cannot be presumed only because of admission by the defendant, inasmuch as defendant is an interested party. As auction sale land of SA khatian land took place in 1954 and 1960 for arrear rent after State Acquisition and Tenancy Act came into force and Part V was finally published, Government or any person duly authorised should have been decree holder giving rise to suspicion. The discussion and finding that Exhibits 2-2ga were written on previously used stamps and signed and sealed and fraudulently manufactured after washing and removing the previous-writings with help of chemical substances by giving hit of fire and spraying dirt superficially, that though the certified copies were issued 40 years before seal used appeared clear and fresh of recent origin with clear distinct and visible marks of subsequent overwriting, manipulation and interpolation on 2ka, 2kha and 2ga in execution case of 1954, figure 4 and figure 3 of the date 31-3-55 after rubbing marks of previous seal, the term 'Munsif' misspelt as 'Monsif' and 'Bakagonj' written in the seal in Exhibits 2, 2ka leading the trial Court to hold that only to grab the property left by the member of Hindu community plaintiffs and the defendant jointly brought the suit and that had the property been acquired by auction purchase in 1961 or before they would naturally take active step for mutation and separation of jama to obtain mutated khatian and rent receipt but no such step was taken, are, in my view, cogent and consistent with materials and evidence and the above findings of fact arrived at by the trial Court on consideration of the evidence on record and the learned Subordinate Judge as last court of fact without adverting to the fact, and circumstances and setting aside the same on consideration of evidence, acted illegally with material irregularity in decreeing the suit occasioning failure of justice and, as such, the impugned judgment and decree passed by the learned Subordinate Judge is not sustainable and liable to be set aside. I further hold that the trial Court requires no expert opinion in support of such finding on the basis of evidence. The finding of the Court of appeal below that no evidence was adduced for discarding the Exhibits 2-2ka /ga as fraudulently manufactured is unwarranted and is without any legal basis. The Exhibits 2- 2/ ga filed apparently show that it is a collusive suit filed on the basis of fraudulently manufactured papers and in view of the findings of the trial Court the depositions of the plaintiff, appellant and respondents 1-2 recorded by the appellate Court which is contradictory to each other, the preliminary decree passed by the learned Subordinate Judge on the basis of sole-nama is not maintainable.</u>

<u>17. The court in an expertise of all experts.</u>

<u>18. The law is well settled that expert opinion is not substantive piece of evidence and in view of sections 45, 57 and 73 of the Evidence Act, 1872 court is competent to decide whether particular paper used and seal and signature thereon is genuine or not in the light of evidence on record.</u>

19. For the reason and discussion above I find merit in this rule.

20. Accordingly, the Rule is made absolute without any order as to cost. The impugned judgment and decree passed by the learned Subordinate Judge dated 9-7-2001 is hereby set aside and those of the Senior Assistant Judge dated 21-4-1999 restored. The ad interim order of stay in the Rule is vacated.

Send down the LCR at once.

End.

caseno: Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 3 of 2004
lawyer:
Kh. Mahbubuddin Ahmed, Senior Advocate, (Osman Gani, Advocate with him), instructed by Sofia Khatun, Advocate-on-Record-For the Petitioners. 
Bivash Chandra Biswas, Advocate-on-Record- For respondent Nos. 3-6. 
Not represented-Respondent Nos.1-2 & 7-10.
parties:
Kulsum Bibi & others ----- Petitioners
Vs.
Deputy Commissioner, Magura and others ----- Respondents
case_source: (From the judgment and order dated 15-4-2003 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision Nos. 330 and 329 of 1996)
full_judgment:
Md. Tafazzul Islam J: This civil petition for leave to appeal has arisen out of judgment and order dated 15-4-2003 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 330 of 1996 discharging the Rule which was obtained against the judgment and decree dated 19-7-1995 passed by the learned District Judge, Magura in Title Appeal No. 76 of 1993 reversing those dated 27-5-1993 passed by the learned Assistant Judge, Mohammadpur, Magura in Title Suit No. 35 of 1987 decreeing the suit.

2. Brief facts leading to the filing of this civil petition are that the petitioners, as plaintiffs, instituted the above suit seeking declaration that (a) the order dated 15-1-1987 passed by the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue), Magura is illegal, void, without jurisdiction and not binding upon them (b) the suit land measuring 11.89 acres appertaining to DS Khatian No. 1260, present Khatian Nos. 3025, 3032 and 3039, Plot No. 6752, is not at all Jalmohal (c) for declaration of their title in the suit land and also for confirmation of their possession in the suit land and also (d) for a decree for permanent injunction so that the Government cannot lease out the suit land to others and cannot interfere with their peaceful possession therein, stating, inter alia, that the suit land measuring 18.14 acres was recorded in the name of Endu Bhuson Bashu as rayot and possessor in the DS record and from him the father of plaintiff No. 4 took settlement of 1.80 acres of land in the year 1302 BS and the father of plaintiff Nos. 1 and 2 took settlement of 4.95 acres of land in the year 1330 BS and the father of the plaintiff Nos. 4 and 5 also took settlement of 11.89 acres of land on 28-3-1912 and they have been possessing the same amicably by paying rents to the ex-landlords and that during SA operation the suit land being wrongly recorded in the name of the Government the predecessors of the plaintiffs filed Title Suit No. 48 of 1965, Title Suit No. 18 of 1974 and Title Suit No. 567 of 1980 for correction of the record of rights and the said suits were decreed and in terms of said decree the predecessors of the plaintiffs mutated their names opening 3 Khatians in their names in the year 1966, 1975 and 1981 and had been paying rents to the Government and after the deaths of their predecessors the plaintiffs had been possessing the suit land by growing paddy and also by rearing fishes in 5 ponds excavated by their predecessors and the ADC (Revenue) by an Administrative Order dated 15-1-1987 cancelled the above mutation Khatians which were opened on the basis of the decrees of civil Court and thus cloud has been created on the title of the plaintiffs in the suit land and hence the suit. The Deputy Commissioner, Magura, the defendant No. 1, contested the suit by filing a written statement contending, inter alia, that the suit land is Beel Class of land which vested to the Government under section 20(2) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act 1950, hereinafter referred to as the Act, and the plaintiffs by obtaining ex parte decree mutated their names in collusion with the officials of the government and so the suit land has been rightly recorded in the name of the Government and the Government had been possessing the suit land through the lessees since 1993. The defendant Nos. 5 and 6 contested the suit by filing joint written statement contending that as co-sharer they have title over 1.65 acres of the suit land. The defendant Nos. 7-10 also contested the suit by filing joint written statement contending that they are the lessees from the Government and have been possessing the suit land which is a fishery. The trial Court, after hearing, decreed the suit. Then the defendant No.1 preferred Title Appeal No. 76 of 1993 and the defendant Nos. 5 and 6 also preferred Title Appeal No. 64 of 1993. The learned District Judge, Magura, after hearing, allowed both the appeals. Then the plaintiffs filed Civil Revision Nos. 329 and 330 of 1996 and obtained Rules as well as orders of status quo order in respect of possession of the suit land. The High Court Division, after hearing, discharged both the Rules. As it appears during the pendency of the above revisions in the High Court Division the plaintiff/petitioners compromised the dispute with the defendant Nos. 5 and 6 and so the petitioners did not file any leave petition against the order dated 15-4-2003 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 329 of 1996 in which the above defendant Nos. 5 and 6 were the opposite parties.

3. The learned Counsel for the plaintiff-petitioners submits that the predecessors of the plaintiffs took settlement of the suit land from the ex-landlord before State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 came into force and they paid rents to the ex-landlord and thereafter the suit land having been wrongly recorded in the name of the Government during SA operation, the said predecessors separately filed Title Suit No. 48 of 1965, Title Suit No. 18 of 1974 and Title Suit No. 567 of 1980 for correction of the wrong recording of rights and got decrees against the Government and then the Government, on the basis of said decrees, corrected the wrong recording of rights and mutated their names and they also paid rents and so the ADC (Revenue) had no authority to cancel the said corrected records by a mere Administrative Order dated 15-1-1987 without taking any steps for setting aside the aforesaid decrees; the issue, nature, cause of action and the parties in the three suits as stated above and the present suit i.e. Title Suit No. 35 of 1987 are completely different but yet the High Court Division wrongly found that the present suit is hit by section 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure; both the appellate Court and the High Court Division failed to consider that section 20(2)(a) of the SAT Act 1950 is not applicable in the present case because the predecessors of the plaintiffs took settlement of the suit land from the owner of the suit land long before SA operation and when the SAT Act 1950 came into force the suit land was the private land of the plaintiffs and not the khas land of the Zaminder and so the same cannot vest in the Government; the appellate Court as well as the High Court Division failed to consider that the plaintiffs by examining 5 witnesses and by adducing documentary evidence, Exhibits 1-39 in respect of which no objection was raised, proved their right title, interest and possession in the suit land for 100 years by growing paddy and by rearing fishes in the ponds excavated by them and, on the other hand, the government miserably failed to prove their case by adducing oral and/or documentary evidence and they filed the present suit when the Government leased out the suit land to others and then they obtained order of temporary injunction from the trial Court against the Government as well as the lessees and ultimately, got decree of permanent injunction in the trial court and the said decree was not stayed by the lower appellate Court and they also obtained status quo order Horn the High Court Division and, as such, always there was an injunction against the defendants till disposal of the civil revision and so the finding of the appellate Court as well as the High Court Division to the effect that the lessees were in possession of the suit land is highly illegal; the predecessors of the plaintiffs having been in possession of the suit land and the plaintiffs, as heirs, having been possessing the suit land, even if by invalid documents, for last 100 years, they acquired valid, title in the suit land by adverse possession against the Government and the suit land cannot be snatched away after 100 years; the appellate Court as well as the High Court Division misread and misconstrued the oral and documentary evidences as adduced by the parties and moreover, none having ever raised any objection against the documentary evidence of the plaintiffs that is Exhibits 1-39, which prove 100 years' possession of the plain-tiffs on the suit land, the adverse comment passed by the High Court Division over those documents are without jurisdiction; the schedule of the suit land along with sketch map and the Advocate Commissioner's report and the Mutation Khatians prove that the suit land is identical, specific and the plaintiffs have been able to prove the amicable partition of the suit land between the co-sharers and, as such, the finding of the appellate Court about schedule of the land and amicable partition is illegal.

4. As it appears the High Court Division found that the lower appellate Court having found that Teta Doa Beel, which is the suit land, is in possession of the fishermen who have taken lease of the same from the government on yearly basis and PW 4 admitted that the fishermen are in possession of the suit property reversed the finding of the trial Court. The High Court Division also found that the records of CS Khatian, SA Khatian and Exhibit 2 the RoR, show that the suit land is a Beel and further exhibit 'Cha' filed by the defendants also shows that Plot No. 6752 is a Beel and that Digha Matshajibi Samabaya Samity got the lease of Plot No. 6752. It also appears that the appellate Court found that the decrees obtained by the plaintiffs in Title Suit No. 48 of 1965, Title Suit No. 18 of 1974 and Title Suit No. 567 of 1980 are not in any specific schedule or portion of land and upon perusal of the decree passed in Title Suit No. 48 of 1965 itself, the High Court Division also found that in the schedule of the decree there is no name of the Mouja, Khatian number or plots or any other description of the property and in respect of Title Suit No. 18 of 1974 the High Court Division found that only the ordering portion of the ex parte judgment has been filed which has been marked as Ext. II and no decree has been filed and consequently the schedule of the property of the above suit could not be gone through and scrutinized and regarding Title Suit No. 567 of 1980 the High Court Division found that the plaintiff only filed the Photostat copy of the ordering portion of the decree of the above suit but the same not being admissible in evidence was not marked as an exhibit and consequently the schedule of the suit properties of that suit could not be ascertained.

<u>5. As it appears the High Court Division further held that the findings arrived at by the lower appellate Court being rested upon consideration of the oral and documentary evidences and there being no instance of misreading or non-reading of evidence and/or non-consideration of the materials on record the said findings as to the facts are not liable to be disturbed by the High Court Division. Regarding the contention that the parties as well as the subject matter of the present suit and that of the previous suits i.e. Title Suit No. 48 of 1965, 18 of 1974 and 567 of 1980 being same, the present suit for declaration of title is barred by res judicata under section 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure, the High Court Division relying on the case of Kala Meah vs Faiz Ahmed reported in 2 MLR (AD) 218 held that the present suit is hit by the principle of res judicata.</u>

6. We are of the view that the High Court Division, on proper consideration of the materials on record and applying the correct principle of law as applicable in the present suit, arrived at a correct decision and there is no cogent reason to interfere with the same.

The petition is dismissed.

End.

lawyer:
Syed Ishtiaq Ahmed with Sayyed Shahid Hossain, Advocates—For the Appellant. 
MI Faruqui with M Saleemullah, Advocates—For the Respondents.
parties:
Kazi Musharraf Hossain ------ Plaintiff-Appellant
vs
Al-haj Aziz Ahmed and others ------ Respondents
full_judgment:
Md Abdul Karim J: This appeal at the instance of the plaintiff is directed against the Judgment and decree dated 19-8-1992 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, Second Court, Dhaka, in Title Suit No. 502 of 1985 dismissing the suit for specific performance of contract.

2. Shortly stated the case of plaintiff Kazi Mosharraf Hossain is that he, the defendant No. 1, is the sole owner of the property described in Schedule 'A' to the plaint and that the property described in Schedule 'B' to the plaint belongs to defendant No. 7 Sambros (Bangladesh) Ltd of which defendant No. 1 is the Managing Director and to defendant Nos. 2 to 6. Defendant No. 1 for self and on behalf of the other defendants with their consent proposed to sell the suit property comprising schedules 'A' and 'B' to the plaintiff at a consideration of Taka 8,000.00 out of which Taka one lac was paid as earnest money on the date of execution of the baina patra dated 20th day of January, 1997. Clauses 7 and 9 of the agreement provide that the vendor 1st party will complete the registration of the property as mentioned in Schedule ''A'' and will induce his full brothers and sons (other defendants) to register the sale deed in respect of the property of Schedule ''B'' within six months of execution of the agreement and that if the vendor 1st party fails to induce his brothers and sons to sell and register the sale deed in respect of schedule ''B'' the purchaser-2nd party will have his option to either refund of the earnest money with 50% compensation or purchase the property of Schedule ''A'' at a discount of 25% of the price settled. It is the case of the plaintiff that he offered the balance amount to the defendants for execution and registration of the sale deed, but the latter did not comply with the request. Hence, the suit for specific performance of contract with a prayer for delivery of possession of the suit property to the plaintiff through process of the Court after removing all obstacles and obstructions of the defendants.

3. The suit was contested by defendant No. 1, defendants 2 to 6 and defendant No. 7 Sambros (Bangladesh) Ltd by filing separate written statements. The case of defendant No. 1 S Aziz Ahamed is that he is not Managing Director of Sambros (Bangladesh) Ltd and that he did not enter into any agreement with the plaintiff on behalf of the said defendant or defendant Nos. 2 to 6 as alleged in the plaint. It is further stated that the property of schedule ''B'' belongs to several owners including defendant No. 7 and that CS Plot No. 220 measuring 1.88 acre as described in Schedule ''A'' and Schedule ''B'' to the plaint is owned by all other defendants in separate shares. It is further stated in the written statement of defendant No. 1 that he tried to induce the owners of the property of Schedule ''B'' to enter into an agreement with the plaintiff for sale of the property, even though the agreement to induce others is void under law, but they refused to enter into any such agreement. CS Plot No. 219 measuring 0.89 acre belongs to defendant No. 1 and his brother, defendant No. 4 Masud Siddique, in equal shares even though it is mentioned in the plaint that defendant No. 1 is the sole owner of Plot No. 219 measuring 0.89 acre and that they were under a mistake as to a matter of fact essential to the agreement rendering it void under section 20 of the Contract Act.

4. The case of defendant Nos. 2-6 is that, there was no privity of contract between these defendants on the one hand and the plaintiff on the other to convey and transfer the property of Schedule ''B'' or any part thereof and that these defendants never received any consideration for any such sale and they never empowered defendant No. 1 to enter into any agreement to sell the property of schedule ''B'' to anybody and that defendant No. 1 is not their attorney

5. The case of defendant No. 7 Sambros (Bangladesh) Ltd is that, it is a body corporate registered under the Companies Act and that the company never entered into any agreement to sell the suit property to the plaintiff. Defendant No. 1 S Aziz Ahmed is not the Managing Director of the defendant company and that the company never appointed defendant No. 1 as its attorney for the purpose of transfer of the company's property to anybody.

6. Before the trial Court evidence, both oral and documentary, was adduced on behalf of both sides. The trial Court was of the opinion that the plaintiff could not prove that the defendant No. 1 had any authority to enter into any agreement for sale of the suit property on behalf of the other defendants, and defendant No. 1 was not sole owner of the property as described in schedule ''A'' and schedule ''B'' to the plaint. The plaintiff defendant No.1 not being the sole owner of the property of schedule ''A'' and schedule ''B'' the parties were under a mistake as to a matter of fact essential to the agreement. The Court also observed that the plaintiff having failed to pray for recession of the contract in his suit for specific performance of contract under section 37 of the Specific Relief Act is not entitled to any compensation under section 38 of the said Act or return of the earnest money. With this finding the learned Subordinate Judge dismissed the suit. Aggrieved by this Judgment and decree the plaintiff has preferred this appeal.

7. Mr Syed Ishtiaq Ahmed, learned Counsel appearing for the plaintiff-appellant, has submitted that the trial Court ought to have decreed the suit in view of the admitted fact that the defendant-respondent No. 1 S. Aziz Ahmed entered into the agreement for sale of suit properties. He submits that the trial Court ought to have decreed the suit particularly with regard to schedule ''A'' to the plaint inasmuch as the contract, so far as it relates to this schedule, stands on a separate and independent footing from the other part of the contract relating to the property of schedule ''B'' and, as such, the trial Court has committed an error of law in not directing specific performance of the property of schedule ''A''. He has further submitted that the trial Court misconceived the provisions of sections 13, 14 and 20 of the Contract Act with regard to a mistake as to a matter of fact essential to the agreement.

8. Mr MI Farooqui, learned Advocate for the defendant-respondents, in upholding the impugned Judgment and decree has submitted that the trial Court was absolutely right in refusing specific performance in view of the failure of the plaintiff to prove that defendant No. 1 entered into an agreement to sell the properties on behalf of other defendant and this is clear from the position taken by the defendants in their written statement that they never empowered defendant No. 1 to enter into an agreement on their behalf and that defendant No. 1 is not Managing Director of defendant No. 7 Sambros (Bangladesh) Ltd. The learned Advocate further submits that defendants Nos. 1 to 7 are owners of the property of schedule ''B'' and that defendant No. 1 is not the sole owner of the property of schedule ''A'' and that the contract so far as it relates to schedule ''A'' does not stand on a separate and independent footing from the other part of the contract and, as such, the trial Court rightly dismissed the suit for specific performance of contract.

9. Admittedly defendant No. 1 entered into an agreement to sell the suit properties to the plaintiff and an agreement (Exhibit 1) was executed on 20-1-1997 for sale of the properties at Taka eight lac and earnest money of Taka one lac was paid on that date. The agreement mentions that the 1st party vendor is the sole owner of the property of Schedule ''A'' and that the property of Schedule ''B'' stands in the names of six owners including Sambros (Bangladesh) Ltd, of which defendant No. 1 is mentioned as the Managing Director. Of the five other co-owners, two are brothers and two sons of defendant No. 1. The other owners is M Co Engineering & Electric Works represented by its proprietor, Mr Nasim Ahmed. They are all defendants in the instant suit.

10. The common defence is that, defendant No. 1 did not enter into an agreement with the plaintiff on behalf of defendant No. 7 (Sambros (Bangladesh) Ltd, a body corporate registered under the Companies Act, and that defendant No. 1 was not the Managing Director of the Company. Defendant Nos. 2-6 also challenge the authority of defendant No. 1 to enter into an agreement to sell the suit property on their behalf.

11. Admittedly defendant No. 1 is not the sole owner of the property of Schedule 'B' comprising as many as 9/10 items. The agreement (Exhibit 1) mentions that the property of schedule 'B' stands in the names of six owners including Sambros (Bangladesh) Ltd, of which defendant No. 1 has been mentioned as Managing Director and of the five other co-owners two are brothers and two are sons of defendant No. 1, the other being M Co Engineering & Electrical Works represented by its proprietor, Mr Nasim Ahmed. They are all defendants, in the present suit. These defendants never accepted the position of defendant No. 1 as being empowered by them to enter into an agreement to sell the suit properties. Defendant No. 7 Sambros (Bangladesh) Ltd in their written statement specifically mentions that defendant No. 1 is not Managing Director of the Company. This makes it clear that defendant No. 1 had no authority to enter into an agreement with the plaintiff to sell the suit property or any part of it on behalf of the other defendants.

<u>12. The plaintiff has filed a Power of Attorney (Exhibit 2) dated 22-8-77 executed by defendant Nos. 3 and 4 empowering defendant No. 1 to manage their properties on their behalf including sale of the same. This Power of Attorney was executed several months after the execution of the agreement Exhibit 1 dated 20-1-1977. Exhibit 2 dated 22-8-1977 does not show that defendant No. 1 had any authority on 20-1-1977 to enter into an agreement for sale of the suit property on behalf of the executants, nor does it approve the act of execution of Exhibit 1 dated 20-1-1977. DW 3 Idris Ali, General Manager of Sambros (Bangladesh) Ltd, states that the Company did not enter into any agreement with anyone to sell the suit property, nor did it authorize anybody to do any such thing on its behalf. This witness in his cross-examination denies that defendant No. 1 was the Managing Director of the company. In his evidence DW 1 S Aziz Ahmed (defendant No. 1) expresses his failure to induce the other defendants to sell the property of Schedule ''B''. Confronted with the situation, Mr Syed Ishtiaq Ahmed learned Counsel appearing for the plaintiff-appellant, in the last part of his argument has abandoned his claim to the property of schedule ''B''. Relying on section 16 of the Specific Relief Act. Mr Syed Ishtiaq Ahmed has argued that the contract so far as it relates to the property of Schedule ''A'' can and ought to be specifically performed and it stands on a separate and independent footing from the part of the contract relating to the property of Schedule ''B''. We may quote section 16 of the Specific Relief Act, which runs as follows:</u>

<u>"Section 16. When a part of a contract which, taken by itself, can and ought to be specifically performed, stands on a separate and independent footing from another part of the same contract which cannot or ought not to be specifically performed, the Court may direct specific performance of the former part."</u>

<u>13. Mr Syed Ishtiaq Ahmed has referred to the decision in the case of Archana Prosad Nandi vs Chilia Randolph & others, 1982 BLD (AD) 90. In this reported case for specific performance of contract, the defendants entered into an agreement to sell certain immovable property. The contract was signed by the mother for herself and for her minor daughter and defendant No. 3 step-son of defendant No. 1 signed the contract on his own behalf. Defendant Nos. 1 and 3 signed the contract. The contract is void for defendant No. 2, the minor. It was held by their Lordships that the part of the contract to the extent of two-thirds share of defendant Nos. 1 and 3 stands on a separate and independent footing and taken by itself can and ought to be specifically performed and so the suit was decreed to that extent on payment of the full purchase money and the Judgments of the Court below were set aside.</u>

14. Mr MI Farooqui, learned Advocate appearing for the defendant-respondents, has referred to the decision in the case of Koleppa Seshaya vs Vedumada Hammayamma and others 1927 AIR Madras 1109. In this case the property (house) was jointly owned by defendant No. 1 and his wife defendant No. 1 had no authority to contract to sell on behalf of his wife. It was held by the learned Single Judge that before section 16 of the Specific Relief Act applies, there must be a contract, which stands on a separate and independent footing and it cannot be said that the contract for the purchase for half of the house stands on separate and independent footing from the contract to purchase the whole house. The facts of the instant case are distinguishable in that it is not a contract for sale of a house jointly owned by two persons.

15. Mr MI Farooqui has referred to another decision in the case of Abdul Aziz Sahib vs M Abdul Sammad Sahib and another AIR 1937 Madras 596. Here the facts of the case are distinguishable from those of the present case.

16. It appears that the property of Schedule ''A'' contains three items as follows:

SL No. 		Plot No 		Area

1.			220. 		0.181/2 decimal

2. 			220			0.461/2 decimal

3. 			219			0.89 decimal

In his evidence as DW 1 defendant No. 1 S Aziz Ahmed states that he is the owner of 0.18½ acre and 0.46½ acre in item Nos. 1 and 2 respectively in schedule ''A'' and in item No. 3 of the same schedule he has ejmali interest with his brother, defendant No. 2. In his written statement defendant No. 1 states that in plot No. 219 he has transferable interest for 0.44½ acre.

17. Admittedly CS Plot No. 220 as described in schedule ''A'' and schedule ''B'' is a large plot measuring 1.88 acre owned and possessed by six persons and the plot falls in two lots in Schedule ''A'' and four lots in schedule ''B'' and CS Plot No. 219 measures 0.89 acre as described in schedule ''A''. The share of defendant No. 1 is only half (0.44½ acre) in Plot No. 219. Mr MI Farooqui, learned Advocate appearing for the defendants-respondents, submits that section 16 of the Specific Relief Act does not come into play in respect of schedule ''A'' inasmuch as here a part of the contract, taken by itself, does not stand on a separate and independent footing from another part thereof, nor is it such a part of the contract, as can and ought to be specifically performed. In the case of 1982 BLD (AD) 90 (Archana Prosad Nandi vs Chilia Randolph & others), their Lordships laid down two tests to be satisfied before the Court can direct specific performance under section 16 of the Specific Relief Act, Viz, (1) taken by itself a part of the contract can and ought to be specifically performed and (2) its stands on a separate and independent footing from another part of the same contract. It appears from the prayer portion of the plaint as mentioned in paragraph 9(c) that the plaintiff, in addition to a decree for specific performance of contract, also prays for possession of the suit property to be delivered to him through the process of the Court after removing all obstacles and obstructions of the defendants. We already mentioned the plurality of ownership in plot No. 220. There is ownership of two persons who are in ejmali possession in Plot No. 219 also. It is therefore, clear a lot of complications may result from a decree of specific performance with recovery of possession in schedule ''A''. In the instant case, the two tests as laid down in the decision of 1982 BLD (AD) 90 being absent it does not apply to the facts and circumstances of the present case before us.

<u>18. There is a stipulation in para 9 of the agreement (Exhibit 1) that if the vendor-1st party fails to induce his brothers and sons to sell and register the properties as mentioned in Schedule ''B'' to the purchaser 2nd party at the price settled in the agreement, the purchaser 2nd party shall have his option to either refund of the earnest money of Taka 1,00,000.00 (Taka one lac) with 50% compensation or purchase the properties of schedule ''A'' at a discount of 25% of the price settled.</u>

<u>19. In the Judgment the trial Court has mentioned that the plaintiff could have prayed for rescission of the contract in the suit for specific performance of contract under section 37 of the Specific Relief Act to get the relief under section 38 thereof, and that the plaintiff having not done so, the Court was not in a position to pass a decree for return of the money. The simple answer to this is that, it is the contractual obligation of defendant No. 1 as mentioned in clause 9 of the agreement to pay Taka one lac with compensation of Taka 50,000.00 to the purchaser in the event of his failure to induce his brothers and sons to sell the property of schedule ''B'' to him and this obligation cannot be avoided on any plea whatsoever. We, therefore, hold that the plaintiff is entitled to a refund of the earnest money of Taka one lac with compensation of Taka 50,000.00 from defendant No. 1.</u>

<u>20. In view of this finding, we do not think it necessary to enter into a discussion in respect of sections 13, 14 and 20 of the Contract Act.</u>

In the result, the appeal is allowed in part. The Judgment and decree passed by the Court below is set aside. Defendant No. 1 is directed to pay Taka 1,50,000.00 (Taka one lac and fifty thousand) to the plaintiff or deposit the same to the credit of the plaintiff in the Court below within 60 days, in default, the plaintiff will realize the amount through Court with interest @ 12% from the date of institution of the suit till realization.

End.
