full_judgment:
Both the Rules arise out of the same judgment and decree and are taken up together for analogous disposal as ordered at the time of issuance of the Rule. These Rules are directed against the judgment and decree dated 7-6-1998 passed by the Additional District Judge in charge, 2nd Court, Bogra in Other Appeal No. 47 of 1998 heard analogously with Other Class Title Appeal No. 44 of 1998, affirming the judgment and decree passed in Partition Suit No. 25 of 1984 allotting respective shares among the parties and refusing the prayer for preemption in partition suit and reversing the findings with the point raised in Other Class Suit No. 9 of 1995 and sending the said Other Class Suit No. 9 of 1995 back on remand.

2. For disposal of the Rules, short facts, are that the petitioner Shafiqul Bari, as plaintiff instituted Partition Suit No. 25 of 1984 on 3-4-1984 against the main 3(three) defendant Mahfuzul Bay who are the opposite party Nos. 1, 2 and other proforma defendants. The claim of the plaintiff was that 6½ decimals of land out of 82 decimals of total land. Title Suit No. 9 of 1994 (95 of 1984) was filed by Mrs. Bari for khas possession of 2 decimals of land from the land to be partitioned.

3. In the plaint of partition suit, it was stated that the land measuring an area of 59 decimals appertaining to CS Khatian No. 572, Plot No. 522 of Mouza-Sutrapur and the land of Khatian No. 512, plot No. 523 measuring an area of 23 decimals of land i.e. in total 82 decimals of land was purchased by the plaintiffs father Abdul Bari by kabala deed dated 26-1-28. Thereafter, he started to construct his dwelling house on the land and at the time of said construction of dwelling house he took 1/4th cost of construction from his elder brother, Keramat Ali, the predecessor of the defendant No. 1 and the plaintiffs father himself spent 12 mutes cost incurred towards the construction of the said homestead. Thereafter, both of them began to live in the said homestead. An area of 11 decimals of land of plot No. 522 and area of 23 decimals of land of plot No. 523 belonged to Lal Mohammad. The plaintiff's father got from the southern part of the suit plot No. 523 from Lal Mohammad by way of exchange.

4. At the time of construction of the house Keramat Ali had no issue and he took the defendant No. 1 to be his adopted son and began to live in the said homestead in ejmali with the plaintiffs father Keramat Ali was given amicably an area of 17-3/4 decimals of land from western side of plot No. 522 and the rest land was amicably got by the plaintiffs father. For the purpose of use of Keramat Ali, a kitchen, bathroom, bedroom and storeroom were constructed and also a passage was there for exit and entry into the said homestead. Amicably the plaintiffs father got the other structures of those plots along with kitchen MOM, storeroom, bedroom, etc. In this way Keramat Ali and the plaintiffs father were possessing the homestead amicably. There was a partition deed dated 29-3-45 in between Keramat Ali and the plaintiffs father Abdul Bari. During possession Keramat Ali took second wife and out of their wedlock one son and one daughter were born. After second marriage of Keramat Ali, he wanted to use one of the rooms of the plaintiff’s father and permission was accorded to him. Thereafter, he began to live in one of the room of the plaintiff’s father. Keramat Ali died leaving behind defendant No. 1 as his only son and the defendant Nos. 2 and 3 as his daughters. At that time the plaintiffs father Abdul Bari was in Dhaka under treatment. The defendant No. 1 was the caretaker and taking advantage of the absence of the plaintiff and other inmates of the house the defendant No. 1 erected boundary wall almost at the middle of the dwelling house covering an area more than that of his share without any consultation with other shareholders.

5. Thereafter, the plaintiff’s father died leaving behind one widow, 6 sons including the plaintiff and 2 daughters. The heirs of the plaintiff’s father requested the defendant Nos. 4-10 and that the plaintiff Nos. 11 and 12, with a view to get the plaintiffs share through partition by metes and bound. He demanded partition on 15-3-1984. The same demand was refused by the defendant No. 1 and, as such, the instant partition suit.

6. In the said suit, the defendant Nos. 13 and 14 were added claiming to be the stranger purchasers from the defendant Nos. 1-3 by the deed as mentioned above.

7. The defendant No. 1 contested the suit by filing written statements contending, inter-alia, that the property of Plot Nos. 522 and 523 were acquired jointly by the plaintiffs father and by his father Keramat Ali also claimed that the cost incurred towards the construction upon those 2 plots, were spent equally by the plaintiffs father and his father Keramat Ali. The defendant's father and mother were living in 2 rooms and rests were being possessed by the plaintiffs father. Both the brothers were living separately with separate Mess. There are two separate exits to enter into the said homestead being used by those two brothers. Keramat Ali purchased an area of 11 decimals of land from plot No. 523 by kabala deed dated 7-12-45 from Lal Mohammad and constructed his homestead on the said portion of land. The plaintiff’s father and the defendant's father Keramat Ali Jointly constructed the homestead on those two plots. Both the brothers by partition deed dated 29-3-45 got the suit land amicably partitioned amongst themselves. As per the said partition deed, the defendant's father got 4 annas share and the plaintiffs father got 12 annas share and began to live accordingly, as per the said partition deed. The defendant's father got 3 decimals of land from plot No. 523 and got 14-1/4 decimals of land from plot No. 522, here are two exits and that one exit situated towards the south of the homestead, was being used by the defendant's father and other exit was being used by the plaintiff’s father. The plaintiff’s father and the defendant's father were in ejmali possession in some portion of the homestead and were in separate possession in other portion of the homestead. The defendant No. 1 got his share separated by a boundary wall in presence of the plaintiffs father covering some are of plot No. 518, about 35 years back. The plaintiff’s father disclosed that he purchased the land of plot No. 518 by his own fund. For convenience of possession the defendant got some land out of plot No. 518 by way of verbally exchange. Previously there was only one exit to enter into the homestead and that for facilitating the plaintiff of the said exit and for the cause of parda the boundary was constructed and that thereafter both the brothers were being possessed their homestead amicably Keramat Ali died in the year 1971. The plaintiffs mother never acquired the land of plot No. 518. The defendant No. 1 and his sister the defendant Nos. 2 and 3, transferred 8V4 decimals of land by kabala deed dated 23-9-82 in favour of Bilkis Begum and her husband, the defendant Nos. 13 and 14 who are stranger purchasers.

8. The defendant Nos. 13 and 14 also filed written statement disclosing that they have purchased the land by as many as 4 kabalas deeds dated 22-3-1983, 14-3-1983, 15-3-1983 comprising and 16-3-1983 an area of 8-1/4 decimals of land from the defendant No. 1 and his sisters, the defendant Nos. 2 and 3.

9. Thereafter, the plaintiff filed an application for amendment of the plaint of the Partition Suit on 28-1-1990 seeking for a further relief for getting preempted land transferred to the defendant Nos. 1-3 under the provision of section 4 of the Partition Act and by an order dated 24-1-1991 the said prayer was rejected.

10. The said order dated 22-2-1983 was then challenged up to the Appellate Division and the same was upheld. However, the Appellate Division in dismissing the appeal and upholding that section 4 of the Partition Act is applicable in partition suit and held that:

"Upon perusal of the matters however we find that even though the High Court Division was not justified in its reasoning in interfering with the order of the learned Subordinate Judge, yet taking over all view of the whole litigation we do not find it to be a fit case for interference, because all said and done the plaintiff at the last part of paragraph 3 of the original plaint clearly asserted that in respect of 'Bontonnama' dated 29-3-45 the parties are enjoying the partible partition as before or, in other words it was not acted upon. The allegation of 'Bontonnama' not being acted upon and being already in the original deed, it will work injustice to the defendant petitioners, if paragraph 3 is sought to be amended so as to make the assertions of the plaintiff with regard to the 'Bantonnama' clearer and louder."

11. It appears that on 12-4-1984 the opposite party No. 4 and others predecessor Sufia Bari being dead instituted other Suit No. 95 of 1984 (Other Class Suit No. 9 of 1995) in the court of learned 2nd Munsif, Bogra impleading Mahfuzul Ban to be the sole defendant praying for a decree for khas possession after demolition of structure from the suit land measuring an area of 2(two) decimals as shown in a sketch map in the plaint and this Other Class Suit No. 9 of 1995 (95/96) was tried along with Partition Suit filed by the petitioner and dismissed by the trial Court praying for khas possession.

12. On 31-5-1998 both the suits for recovery of khas possession of 2 decimals and suit for partition were heard together. The decree has been signed on 7-6-1998 by a different judge.

13. The Partition Suit No. 25 of 1984 filed by the petitioner was allowed but the application for pre-emption under section 4 of partition Act was rejected on the ground that the homestead was not undivided in the suit property.

14. Thereupon the petitioner filed one Title Appeal No. 47 of 1998 against the aforesaid only order rejecting prayer for pre-emption under section 4 of the Partition Act as both the courts below allowed partition. The defendants also filed appeal No. 44 of 1998 against judgment and decree passed by the trial court dismissing the suit for khas possession of 2 (two) decimals of land filed by the predecessor of the petitioner and decreed the suit for khas possession & eviction.

15. Both the aforesaid appeals one arising out of Other Class Suit No. 9 of 1995 and one arising out of partition Suit No. 25 of 1984 only under section 4 of the Partition Act as aforesaid were heard together. The learned lower Appellate Court uphold the judgment and order allowing the prayer for partition as prayed in the Partition Suit but disallowed the prayer for preemption of the petitioner under section 4 of the Preemption Act. The appellate court remanded the Title Suit No. 9/95 holding that suit No. 9/95 cannot be heard with partition suit and trial of the two suits is illegal and sent the other suit No. 9 of 1995 for fresh trial to the relevant proper trial Court. Both the appeals were heard together. By the impugned judgment the appeals were disposed of holding that the partition as decreed in the Partition Suit No. 25 of 1984 is upheld but disallowed the prayer of pre-emption and sent the Title Suit No. 9 of 1995 disposal by the appropriate Court.

16. Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the said order of rejection of the prayer for pre-emption under section 4 of the Partition Act in Preemption Case No. 25 of 1984 and sending the Title Suit No. 9 of 1995 on remand for fresh trial the petitioner preferred the above Revision and obtained the Rules.

17. Mr. Md Fazlul Karim with Mr Khandakar Aminul Huq appeared for the petitioners in both the Rules. Mr Md Aminul Ehsan with Mr Md Nurul Amin appeared for the opposite party Nos. 122 in CR No. 4496 of 2006 arising out of Title Suit No. 9 of 1995 and opposite party Nos. 13 and 14 strangers purchasers in Partition Suit No. 25 of 1984.

18. Mr Md Fazlul Karim, the senior Counsel appearing for the petitioners submits that the petitioner as plaintiff filed the suit for partition for his shares of 6½, decimals and then amended for 8-1/4, decimals from defendant No. 1-3 out of 82 decimals of land. He submits that the trial court allowed the prayer for partition of 6½, decimals and decreed in part but illegally rejected the application under section 4 of the Partition Act for pre-emption on the ground that the homestead was dividable. The appellate court though affirmed the decree of partition but misdirected itself in not considering the application under section 4 of the partition Act. He seriously argued that the trial court decreed the suit for recovery of khas possession of 20 decimals. But the appellate court without giving any proper reasoning and controversy the finding of the decreetal court set aside the decree, allowed the appeal and sent the case back the case on remand.

19. He further submits that on 31-5-1998 both the suits were heard together but the decree has been signed on 7-6-1998 by a different judge. The Partition Suit No. 25 of 1984 filed by the petitioner was allowed so far partition of property in concerned but his application for pre-emption was rejected in the same suit on the ground that the homestead was undivided in the suit property.

20. It is stated that both the appeals as aforesaid were heard together, that the learned lower Appellate Court uphold the judgment and order of the trial Court passed in Title Suit No. 25 of 1984 about partition and refused the prayer for pre-emption. The prayer for khas possession after eviction holding the analogous trial of the suits was held illegal and sent the Other Suit No. 9 of 1995 for recovery of khas possession of 2 decimals of land for fresh trial to the relevant lower court.

21. Mr Md Nurul Amin, learned senior Advocate appearing for the opposite party submits that he has no objection about the concurrent findings of the court below wherein the prayer for partition of the properties was allowed. Because it is admitted that by a 'Bantannama' dated 29-3-1945 there was partition between the parties who exclusively possessed their respective shares earmarking in the 'Bantannama' as such he has no objection to that decision about allowing partition. But he submits that the courts below rightly decided that the prayer for pre-emption under section 4 of the Partition Act is not allowable and rightly rejected the prayer giving reasons that the homestead on the partible plot being not undivided the petitioner is not entitled for preemption. The learned Advocate for the petitioners submits in reply submits that the property in question is undivided and homestead. Both the learned Advocates after argument in CR No. 4496 of 2006 arising out of Title Suit No. 9 of 1995 honestly agreed that the appellate Court by impugned judgment rightly sent the case back on remand for trial by an appropriate and proper court having jurisdiction. But the they sought an order for early hearing of the said suit which for recovery of khas possession of 2 decimals of land of original owner of the property.

22. The learned Advocate for the opposite party submits that in the said suit the defendant Nos. 13 and 14 were added claiming to be stranger purchasers from the defendant Nos. 1-3 by the deed as mentioned above dated 22-3-1983, 14-3-1983, 15-3-1983 and 16-3-1983 the property of Plot No. 522 and 523 were acquired jointly by the plaintiffs father and by his father Keramat Ali and also claimed that the cost incurred towards the construction upon those two plots, were spent equally by the plaintiffs father and his father Keramat Ali. He also submits that the defendant's father and mother were living in two moms and rest were being possessed by the plaintiff's father. He also submits that both the brothers were living separately with separate Mess and both the brothers by partition deed dated 29-3-45 got the suit land partition among themselves amicably. He further submits that as per the said partition deed the defendant's father got 4 arenas share and the plaintiffs father and the defendant's father were in ejmali possession in some portion of the homestead and were in separate possession in other possession in other portion of the homestead. He also submits that for convenience of possession the defendant got some land out of Plot No. 518 by way of verbally exchange and previously there was only one exit to enter into the homestead and that for facilitating the plaintiff of the said exit and for the cause of parda the boundary wall was constructed and that thereafter both the brothers were being possessed their homestead amicably and that Keramat Ali died in the year 1971 and that plaintiffs mother never acquired the land of plot No. 518 that the defendant No. 1 and his sister the defendant Nos. 2 and 3, transferred 8-1/4 decimals of land by kabala deed dated 23-9-1982 in favour of Bilkis Begum and her husband, the defendant Nos. 13 and 14. They have purchase by as many as 4 kabala deeds dated 22-3-83, 14-3-83, 15-3-83 and 16-3-83 an area of 8-1/4 decimals of land from the defendant No. 1 and his sister the defendant Nos. 2 and 3.

23. The plaintiff filed an application for getting pre-empted the land transferred to the defendant Nos. 13 and 14 by the defendant No. 1-3 under the provision of section 4 of the partition Act and that by order dated 24-1-1991 the said prayer was rejected by the impugned judgment and decree which is not liable to be interfered with and may kindly be upheld.

24. Under such situation as there is no objection of the impugned judgment and decree about allowing partition of the parties in Title Suit No. 25 of 1984 and sending the Title Suit No. 9 of 1995 for remand. Now only question is to be decided in this Revision whether the prayer for pre-emption is allowable or not?

25. It appears that both the courts below affirmed and allowed the shaham in the preliminary form passed in partition suit No. 25 of 1984 and no objection was raised by the opposite party in the Court. On scrutiny of the materials on record and evidence this court is of the view that there is nothing to interfere with the impugned judgment preliminary decree passed in partition suit allowing the prayer for partition in both the courts below.

26. But both the courts below made observation and finding that the prayer of the plaintiff under section 4 of the partition Ad which need to be taken into consideration. But surprisingly none of the courts below considered the prayer made under section 4 of the Partition Act. The trial Court and appellate Court found that:

“অত্র মোকদ্দমায় দেখা যায় যে, আঃ বারী মাত্র একজন ওয়ারিশ অত্র বাদী ৬৫ শতক জমি বাবদ বন্টনের প্রার্থনা করিয়াছেন। এহেন অবস্থায় আদালত মনে করে যে, বাদীপক্ষের আনীত পার্টিশন এ্যাকট এর সেকশন ৪ রক্ষণীয় নয়। কারণ এখানে আনডিভাইডেট ডুইলিং হাউস নাই এবং সেপারেট এনটিটি এবং সেপারেট বসবাস দেখা যায়।”

“২৫/৮৪ বণ্টন মোকদ্দমাটি দোতরফা সূত্রে আংশিকভাবে প্রতিদ্বন্দ্বী বিবাদীর বিরুদ্ধে এবং অন্যান্য বিবাদীর বিরুদ্ধে একতরফাসূত্রে বিনা খরচায় বিভাগ বণ্টনের প্রাথমিক ডিক্রি হইল। এতদ্বারা বাদীকে ২৯-৩-৪৫ সালের বণ্টননামা দলিলের শর্তমতে ৫৩.৭৫ শতকের মধ্যে নিজ অংশে বাদী জমি প্রাপ্ত হইবে। বাদীর অংশ উক্ত বণ্টন নামা দলিল দস্টে অ্যাডভোকেট কমিশনার দ্বারা নির্ধারিত হইবে। অন্যথায় আবেদক্রমে আদালতযোগে বিভাগ বণ্টন করিয়া নিবেন।”

The appellate Court also only observed that—

“বিজ্ঞ সাবজজ বাটওয়ারা ডিক্রী প্রদান করেন...... কিন্তু বাদীর আনীত পার্টিশন অ্যাক্ট এর ৪ ধারার দরখাস্তটি না মঞ্জুর করেন।“

and in order portion the appellate court only ordered that—

“৪৫/৯৮ নং বাটোয়ারা আপীল মোকদ্দমটি আপীল্যান্ট ১, ১৬-১৭ নং রেসপনডেন্টের মধ্যে দোতরফাসূত্রে ও অন্যান্য রেসপনডেন্টের বিরুদ্বে একতরফাসূত্রে শুনানি অন্তে বিনা খরচায় না-মঞ্জুর হয়। ৯/৯৫ অন্য নং মোকদ্দমার তর্কিত রায় ও ডিক্রি  রদ রহিত করা হইল। অন্য ৯/৯৫ নং মোকাদ্দমাটি পুনরায় বিচারের জন্য পর্যবেক্ষন মোতাবেক অন্য ৯/৯৫ নং মোকদ্দমায় নতুন করিয়া সিদ্বান্ত দিবার জন্য নির্দেশ দেওয়া গেল।”

27. I have gone through the application of the plaintiff pending hearing of the partition suit for amendment of plaint on 28-1-1990 praying for amendment for getting pre-empted land transferred to the stranger defendant Nos. 13 and 14 by the defendant Nos. 1-3 under section 4 of the Partition Act. Also seen the application of the plaintiff made on 16-2-1993, filed an application claiming pre-emption of the land transferred by the defendant No. 1 to the strangers-defendant Nos. 1-3 stating, inter alia, that the homestead being a ejmali homestead of the plaintiff and of the defendant Nos. 1-3 and that the defendant Nos. 13 and 14 being admittedly stranger, the transfer made to them by the defendant No. 1-3 are liable to be pre-empted under section 4 of the partition Act. But the said prayer was also not considered in the impugned judgment and decree.

28. This order was challenged up to the Appellate Division of the Supreme Court and it was held up to the Apex court that the plaintiff is entitled to pray for pre-emption in the partition suit as the property is ejmali and dwelling house in undivided.

<u>29. I have carefully gone through the findings of the judgments of the Appellate Division and the High Court Division in this regard and perused the materials on record and the findings of the courts below but the courts below showed no respect or regard to consider the judgments of the High Court Division as well as the Appellate Division and disregarded the findings of the Appellate Division in which it was held that the amendment to prayer for pre-emption under section 4 of the Partition Act is allowable and on legal basis and in the plaint the matter was amended and application under section 4 was entertained but the courts below found the application under section 4 of Partition Act is not maintainable and acted illegally and showed disregard to the Higher Courts of the Country. If the courts below considered the prayer under section 4 of Partition Act they ought to allow the prayer as it appears from the materials on record and findings of the Court below. Moreso, there are clean observation are there in the judgment of the Appellate Division above the maintainability of the pre-emption prayer.</u>

30. From the material on record it appears to this court that the plaintiffs, the defendants No. 1-3 are enjoying the undivided partition of the homestead and the defendant Nos. 13 and 14 are stranger purchaser and the courts below failed to exercise jurisdiction by not allowing the prayer of pre-emption under section 4 of Partition Act. In the light of the facts and the evidence and circumstances in the case the impugned judgment and preliminary decree so far it relates to the rejection of pre-emption is liable to be set aside and prayer for pre-emption may be allowed.

31. The plaintiff petitioner as it appears not only owners of the family dwelling house but also resides there so be being a member of the family had locus standi to claim purchase of the share of the stranger purchaser defendant Nos. 13 and 14 under section 4 of the partition claim of the plaintiff, the matter went up to appellate Division and both the Appellate Division and the High Court Division were of the views that the plaintiff is entitled to pray for the pre-emption of 8½ decimals of land. Both the courts below failed to consider the facts and circumstances of the case and failed to consider the points raised by the plaintiff petitioner to its legal perspective. Although both the courts below allowed the prayer of partition as prayed for preemption in favour of the plaintiff as prayed for but no reason whatsoever was given why refused the application made under section 4 of the Partition Act.

<u>32. The facts and circumstances of the case has not been considered so far it relates to the prayer under section 4 of partition Suit Act, wherein both the courts below allowed the prayer for partition on such facts. Admittedly defendant Nos. 13 and 14 who are the stranger purchases. On looking to the materials on record, 2 reports about the dwelling house given by two responsible government officials and on looking into the plaint and prayer as it is stood upon amendment by an application by pre-emption to assert the claim, for 84 decimals of land, for purchases under section 4 of the partition Act it clearly appears that the plaintiff petitioner's prayer for allowing him to purchase the stranger defendants share only in the dwelling house that stood on the suit land claimed for pre-emption. But both the courts below acted illegally in not allowing or even considering the prayer giving no reason. This was illegal being contrary to the provisions of law and was also without jurisdiction under such circumstances the judgment and decree of the courts below, so far it relates to the prayer for pre-emption cannot be sustained and are liable to be set aside.</u>

<u>33. The plaintiff in order to get benefit of section 4 of partition Act, proved that he is a co-shares i.e. suit was decreed in his favour up to appellate court and proved that property is a dwelling house which belonged to an undivided-family and the same was transferred to strangers who are not a member of the undivided family and I am of the view that the courts below ought to allow the prayer for pre-emption.</u>

34. Section 4 of the Partition Act, 1993 was enacted to afford protection to the members of an undivided family against a stranger purchases and it is not necessary that a person must live in the family of dwelling house and undivided family must be taken to be means house has not been divided. It is not the residence but the ownership of the dwelling house that entails a person to apply under section 4 of the partition Act. Thus the application under section 4 of the partition Act is allowed.

35. Since the prayer for partition have decided concurrently by both the courts below in favour of the plaintiffs so far ends of justice also the prayer for pre-emption under section 4 of the Partition Act is liable to be allowed with a direction to the trial court, to appoint a suitable pleader Commissioner at the cost of the plaintiff physically to assess and ascertain the actual position of the property and suit land and assess the value thereof and upon the report the learned trial court shall determine the area of the dwelling house and its value either on the basis of the said report or on taking evidence about the local price in presence of both parties to that effect if necessary, and thereafter to pass a final decree in favour of the plaintiff accordingly to law and in the light of the above observation.

36. In the light of above findings, observation and direction both the Rules are absolute in part. The judgment of affirmance of the courts below allowing the partition is upheld. The prayer of the petitioner under section 4 of the Partition Act praying for allowing the pre-emption is allowed.

37. The trial Court will appoint a pleader commissioner to ascertain the value of the pre-empted property and after assessment pass a final decree to hand over the possession of the pre-empted homestead to the petitioner.

38. The order for remand of Title Suit No. 9 of 1995 passed by the appellate court below is upheld. The trial court is directed to dispose of Title Suit No. 9 of 1995 expeditiously.

Send down the LCR at once.

End.
