M Moniruzzaman Khan with Morshed Ahmed Khan, Advocates  --- For the Defendant No. 6.
parties:
Giasuddin (Md) ------ Plaintiff
Vs
M V Forum Power and others ------ Defendants
full_judgment:
Mr Md Giasuddin, Proprietor of Sobhan Marine Syndicate as plaintiff instituted this Admiralty Suit against the defendants claiming therein, inter alia, for a decree for realization of Taka 9,50,535.60.

2. The plaintiff is a bonafide businessman. He has been caning on business of general ship repairer and Shipchandler Watchmen, Chipping and painting, Engine store and Bunker suppliers, Marine Contractors for considerable time with reputation and goodwill under his proprietary firm namely, Sobhan Marine Syndicate.

3. The defendant No. 1 is a merchant vessel, MV Forum Power carrying on Cyprus Flag. The defendant No. 2 is the Master and the defendant No 3 is the Chief Officer of the said vessel, The defendant No.4 is the foreign agent and/or owner of the vessel MV Forum Power. The defendant No. 5 is the owner and the parties interested in the said vessel. The defendant No. 6 is the local agent of the vessel. The defendant Nos. 7-9 are the proforma defendants in this suit.

4. The case of the plaintiff, in short, is that, the defendant No. 4 wanted to have supply of (1) Vertical centrifugal Main Cooling Sea Water Pump complete with motor, VDK 440E, (2) Fire/General Service Pump complete with motor, type VSK 95J, (3) Bearing Unit complete, blower side, VTR 200, (4) Bearing Unit complete, Turbine Side, VTR 200, and (5) Lubricating Disc for VTR 200 for the defendant No 1 vessel which was lying at the relevant time in a distressed condition at the port of Mongla, Khulna for want of those items and the vessel was unable to discharge her cargo without those main parts of the vessel. Accordingly, the defendant No. 4 by their Fax Message dated 1-10-1996 asked for quotation for supply of those items to the defendant No. 1 from the plaintiff and the plaintiff by his Telex Message dated 3-10-1996 quoted price including installation cost, and on 22-10-1996 specifications thereof were supplied to the plaintiff by another Telex Message. The plaintiff on 20-10-1996 on the request of the defendant No. 4, by a Fax Message gave his terms on supply ie minimum 30 days credit, advance 50%. By Fax message dated 23-10-1996 the defendant No. 4 confirmed that the vessel at Mongla Port, should be supplied with the following items:

(1) Main Cooling Sea Water Pump complete with motor, type VDK 440E, 1 Piece.

(2) Fire/General Service Pump complete with Motor, type VSK 95J, 1 Piece.

(3) Bearing Unit complete, Blower side, VTR 200, 1 Piece.

(4) Bearing Unit complete, Turbine side, VTR 200, 1 Piece.

(5) Lubricating Disc for VTR 200, 1 Piece at the rate, terms and conditions of the plaintiff.

The defendant No. 4 gave supply orders to the plaintiff as agent of the defendant No. 1 vessel to be delivered and installed on board the defendant No. 1 vessel. Cost for installation, transportation and labour shall be borne by the defendant Nos. 1 and 4, and by fax message dated 24-10-1996, the plaintiff also informed the defendant No. 4 about the actual cost for such works.

5. The plaintiff as per terms and conditions aforesaid supplied those items to the defendant No. 1 vessel. On 29-10-1996 the defendant Nos. 2 and 3 under their joint signatures acknowledged receipt of those items on board the vessel, at Mongla Port in accordance with their type and specifications, and issued a certificate therefor and the said defendant Nos. 2 and 3 issued another certificate acknowledging and certifying that those items have been installed by the plaintiff on board the vessel, the defendant No. 1. Accordingly, the plaintiff submitted a bill for those supply and works according to quotation and confirmation amounting to US $ 14,851.00 only.

6. The plaintiff has further stated that the defendant No. 2 in the meantime sent a list of spare parts to the plaintiff for the defendant No. 1 vessel numbering 17 items with a request to supply those as soon as possible and the plaintiff by his Telex dated 27-10-1994 informed the same to the defendant No 4 stating the items, their numbers and quoting rate therefor and by Fax Message dated 1-11-1996 the defendant No. 4 requested the plaintiff by way of confirmation to supply those 17 items of spare parts at the rate given by the plaintiff. The plaintiff, also, supplied those 17 items of spare parts of the defendant Nos. 2 and 3. The defendant Nos. 2 and 3 acknowledged receipt of those 17 items by issuing a certificate dated 18-11-1996. The plaintiff submitted a bill to the defendant No. 4 for supplying of those 17 items of spare parts amounting to US $ 4289.67 only in accordance with quotation and confirmation.

7. The further case of the plaintiff is that the defendant No. 2 requested the plaintiff for supply of food (provisions) and laundry service. The plaintiff informed the defendant No. 2 by Fax Message dated 22-10-1996. The defendant No. 4 by his Fax Message dated 22-10-1996 and 14-11-1996 requested the plaintiff to supply provision to the defendant No. 1 vessel and also to arrange laundry service as per Master''s request. Accordingly, the plaintiff supplied provisions and provided laundry service to the officers/crews of the defendant No. 1 vessel. The bill for provisions amounting to US $ 2,138.52 and bill for laundry service amounting to US $ 536.61 respectively were also submitted. The defendant No. 2 along with the steward of the defendant No 1 vessel acknowledged receipt of those provisions and laundry service by issuing certificates. The plaintiff sent those bills to the defendant. On the request of the defendant Nos. 2 and 3 the plaintiff also supplied stationery and sent bill amounting to US $ 134.00 only.

8. On completing of supply and installation of pumps and motors the plaintiff requested the defendant No. 4 for 50% advance against supply of pumps, motors and spares and full payment of bills for provisions and laundry service etc. The defendant No. 4 by Fax Message dated 6-11-1996 informed the plaintiff that in a few days time remittance for an advance will be effected. But no remittance as promised was made by the defendant No. 4. The defendant No. 4 by his Fax Message dated 14-11-1996 informed the plaintiff that they will do their best for remittance of US $ 8000.00 at the beginning of the next week but they did nothing to pay the dues of the plaintiff. Rather on 18-11-1996 the defendant No. 4 asked for breakdown of the total bills. The, plaintiff sent it immediately. The defendant No. 4 then promised to the plaintiff over telephone that he will remit 10000 US $ within 21-11-1996 but did not do so. The plaintiff repeatedly requested the defendants to make payment but the defendants with malafide motive started playing foul with the plaintiff. The defendants did not pay any advance to the plaintiff and, in fact, avoided payment of entire dues even after expiry of credit period. The plaintiff has stated that he is entitled to net US $ 22,631.80 on account of supply of main parts, spare parts, provisions, laundry service and stationery as confirmed by the defendant No. 4. In fact, the plaintiff has prayed for a decree of Taka 9,50,533.60 in this case against the principal defendant Nos. 1-5.

9. The defendant No. 6 namely, United Sea Transport Co Ltd, has contested the suit by filing written statement. The defendant No. 6 has stated that the suit is not maintainable in its present form and the plaintiff has no cause of action. The plaintiff has filed this present suit with a malafide and on vexatious pleas to harass the defendants the suit is also bad for mis-joinder and non-joinder of parties. Moreover, the defendant No. 6 has contended that the suit is not maintainable under the Admiralty Jurisdiction and is barred under the principle of waiver, acquiescence and estoppel. This defendant has categorically denied that the plaintiff had or has ever supplied any spare parts and/or provision as contended by the plaintiff. The defendant No. 6 has stated that since the plaintiff did not supply any spare parts, provisions and render laundry service etc, they are not at all entitled to US $ 22,631.80. Further, the defendant No. 6 has stated that they are the shipping agent of the defendant No. 1 vessel. They never forwarded any requisition for the said items to be supplied on board the vessel by the plaintiff. The plaintiff is required to obtain endorsement on the shipping export bill from the Customs Authority against the supply of those requisitioned items. Further, the defendant No. 6 has stated that no supply was made in presence of Customs Boarding Officer and no shipping bill/export bill was endorsed/sealed and signed by the Master of the vessel, and the Customs Boarding Officer. The plaintiff presented no Customs shipping bill/export bill along with supporting documents to the defendant No. 6, the shipping agent. The plaintiff was as required under law to present those shipping bill/export bill to this defendant for verification, if any supply was made on board the vessel. Mainly on the aforesaid pleas the defendant No. 6 fully denied the claim of the plaintiff.

10. On the aforesaid pleadings made by the parties this Court framed the issues which are as follows:

1. It the suit maintainable under the Admiralty Jurisdiction?

2. Is there any cause of action to file the suit?

3. Was the defendant No. 4 asked for quotation from the plaintiff for supply of any item mentioned in the plaint to the defendant No. 1?

4. Did the plaintiff supply the items mentioned in the plaint to the defendant No. 1?

5. Did the plaintiff present any shipping bill/export bill to the shipping agent for verification?

6. Is the plaintiff entitled to the reliefs claimed for?

11. Let me discuss all the issues together for the sake of convenience. In this case the plaintiff filed certain documents in support of his case and these documents have been proved by PW 1. Ext.1 is the photo copy of Fax message sent by Forum Maritime SA as agent to Sobhan Marine Syndicate, the proprietary concern of the plaintiff for sending quotation for one vertical centrifugal pump complete with electric reconditioned in good working orders. Ext 1(a) is a photo copy of Fax Message sent by Forum Maritime SA to Sobhan Marine Syndicate cancelling the previous Fax dated 1-10-96 and requested for technical details for vertical centrifugal pump with motor and also requested for further quotation for certain other parts of the vessel. Ext 1(b) is the Fax Message regarding price quotation sent by Sobhan Marine Syndicate to Forum Maritime SA. Ext 1(c) is the price quotation for certain spare parts of the vessel sent by Fax Message to Forum Maritime SA by Sobhan Marine Syndicate Ext 1(d) is also a Fax Message sent by Sobhan Marine Syndicate to Forum Maritime SA regarding certain spare parts. Ext 2 is a Fax Message confirming to supply the vessel certain spare parts at Mongla Port. This confirmation for supply was subject to change. This Fax Message was sent by Forum Maritime SA to Sobhan Maritime Syndicate. Ext 2(a) is the Fax Message sent by the proprietor of Sobhan Marine Syndicate to Forum Maritime SA informing that they are trying to proceed towards Mongla on 26-10-96, evening with main Cooling Sea Water Pump/Fire GS Pump and Turbocharger Spares. It was also stated in the said Fax Message that after receiving of sample of spares Sobhan Marine Syndicate will confirm the cost. Ext. 3 is a certificate issued by Chief Engineer of MV Forum Power at Mongla Port and Master of the said vessel at Mongla Port indicating that they received certain spare parts and pumps. Ext. 3(a) is also a certificate issued by the Chief Engineer as well as Master of the vessel of MV Forum Power confirming Sobhan Marine Syndicate that they completed the installation works of pumps and Fire & GS pump complete with Motor. Ext 4 is the bill sent by Sobhan Maritime SA for payment of an amount of US 14,851.00. Ext, 5 is a Telefax transmission to Forum Maritime SA by Sobhan Marine Syndicate informing that they received a requirement of 17 items as spare parts from Master of the vessel and the said Sobhan Marine Syndicate quoted price for the aforesaid spare parts. Ext. 5 is a photo copy of Fax Message sent by Forum Maritime SA to Sobhan Marine Syndicate confirming to proceed with fabrication and supply of spare parts for the ballast pump only. It was also stated in the Fax Message not to supply the Pneumatic Engine cleaning gun. Ext 7 is the certificate issued by the Chief Engineer as well as Master of the vessel MV Forum Power indicating that they received 17 items of spare parts. Ext.8 is the bill sent by Sobhan Maine Syndicate to Forum Maritime SA for payment of US 4289.67 in respect of the aforesaid supply of spare parts. Ext. 9 is a photo copy of Fax Message requesting Sovhan Marine Syndicate for supply with provisions to the subject vessel and also arrange laundry service as per Master''s request. Ext. 10 series are the indents for supply of certain provisions for Master as well as Chief Steward of the vessel MV FORUM POWER, subject to owners approval. Exts 11, 11(a) are the bills for supply of necessary to the subject vessel. Ext. 12 and 12(a) are also on indents for providing laundry service issued by Chief Steward and Master of the vessel subject to owners approval. Ext. 13 is the bill for laundry service provided by the said Sobhan Marine Syndicate amounting to US 536.61. Ext.15 is the photo copy of Fax Message sent by Forum Maritime SA to Sobhan Marine Syndicate indicating that they received Fax Message regarding payment. It was also stated in the said Message to deliver ballast parts and with provisions ordered by supply department. Ext. 16 is also a photo copy of fax message sent by Sobhan Marine Syndicate in respect of supply of provisions. Ext. 17 is a Fax Message sent by Forum Maritime SA to Sobhan Marine Syndicate requiring him to send breakdown of supply bill amounting to US 22,540. Ext 17(a) is photo copy of Fax Message sent by Sobhan Marine Syndicate to Forum Maritime SA showing breakdown of bills. Ext. 17(b) is the photo copy of Fax Message sent by Forum Maritime SA to Sobhan Marine Syndicate wherein it is stated that the bills have been sent to the Accounts Department for checking. Ext 18 is also a bill in respect of Fax Message sent by Sobhan Marine Syndicate to Forum Maritime SA during the relevant time.

12. The plaintiff has himself deposed as PW 1 in this suit. PW 1 has stated that dues of the plaintiff have not yet been satisfied by the defendants and as such, the plaintiff prayed for a decree for realization of Taka 9,50,535.60 against the principal defendants No. 1-5.

13. In cross-examination PW 1 has stated that he does not know when the vessel arrived at Chittagong Port but he said that the vessel left Chittagong Port on 3-10-96 for Mongla Port and the vessel left the Mongla Port in the month of April, 1997. PW 1 has stated that the agent of this vessel is United Sea Transport, and it has been added as defendant No. 7 in this suit. PW 1 has stated that agent has no roll to play in respect of supply of goods to the vessel. PW 1 has stated with regard to supply of machinery that the owner first sent him a Fax Message asking him for quotations. PW 1 has stated that he supplied all the items as per Exts 3-3(a) and he said that he received the Fax from Greece and he delivered these spare parts at Mongla Port through his agent. PW 1 has stated that Nazma Enterprise was his agent at the relevant time. However he has stated that he did not make Nazma Enterprise a party in this suit. PW 1 has denied that the certificate issued by the Master and the Chief Engineer. Ext 3 is not genuine. PW 1 has admitted that the goods are supplied with the approval of the Chief Engineer. PW 1 has admitted that the Fax Message dated 1-11-96 (Ext.6) relates to confirmation to proceed with the fabrication and supply of spare parts. PW 1 denied the suggestion that the certificate dated 18-11-96 (Ext 7) is not genuine. PW 1 has admitted that according to certificate spare parts were sent to Mongla Port by mini truck but he has not filed the truck receipt to prove the said fact. He has stated that the spare parts were not available at Mongla or Khulna. PW 1 has stated that he paid Taka 6,000.00 as transportation cost. He has further stated that his men supplied the provisions at Mongla Port and he first supplied the provisions on 24th October, 1996. In Ext. 10 the Master wrote in his own handwriting "subject owners approval" and he has admitted that in Ext. 10 series there is a condition at the bottom "Subject owners approval". PW 1 has stated that he knows the agent of the vessel. Mr Abul Hossain is one of the owners of the Sea Transport. PW 1 has stated that since he obtained-approval of the owner he did not think it necessary to take permission of the local agent. PW 1 has admitted that for the liability of the owners agent is also liable. PW 1 has stated that although the goods were supplied during October, 1996 and the vessel left Bangladesh in April, 1997 but he did not make/submit any claim of payment to the defendant No. 6. PW 1 has denied that the agent requested him to submit the bills for scrutiny before payment. PW 1 has stated that he knows that bank guarantee has been filed in this suit but he does not know if the bank guarantee was filed by the agent, then he said that it has been filed on behalf of the owner. PW 1 has denied to have obtained certificate from the Master without supplying spare parts. He has denied that he did not supply the provisions to the subject vessel at Mongla having office at Chittagong. He said that his agent supplied those provisions. PW 1 has stated that he does not remember the name of other vessels to which he supplied the provisions but he has said that he had been doing business for 7/8 years. However, later on he said that he supplied provisions to MV Hallbard and the vessel called at Chittagong Port in 1996. He also said that he supplied provisions to Al-Atiar at Mongla Port.

14. In this suit the principal defendants did not appear and contest the suit. Only the added defendant No 6 has filed a written statement denying the claim of the plaintiff. This added defendant acted/acts as local agent for foreign vessel. The defendant No. 6 was a local agent for defendant No. 1 vessel for both Mongla and Chittagong Port. Other than defendant No. 6 there was no other local agent for the defendant No. 1 vessel. Defendant No 6 has also examined in this suit one Mr Ashok Kumar Saha as DW 1, who is an employee of defendant No. 6. DW 1 has stated that defendant No. 6 was the local agent for defendant No. 1 vessel both at Mongla and Chittagong Port and they furnished bank guarantee covering the plaintiffs claim. DW 1 has stated that upon arrival of any foreign vessel within the territorial waters of Bangladesh the authorized officer of the Customs Department boards the vessel and remains there till departure. DW 1 has further stated in his examination-in-chief that no goods, provisions, machinery can be supplied to a foreign vessel without the approval of Customs Authority. For supplying goods to foreign vessel there is a requirement of bill of entry. DW 1 has said that the plaintiff did not take any approval from the local agent for alleged supply of necessary goods and provisions to the defendant No. 1 vessel. DW 1 has stated that they are not aware of such supply DW 1 has said that the claim of the plaintiff is baseless and he is not entitled to get the claim as prayed for. In cross-examination DW 1 has stated that in normal course of business of shipping Customs Act is the guiding law. DW 1 has further stated that he has come to depose on behalf of defendant Nos. 1 and 4. DW 1 has stated that acts of principal or owner are binding on the agent. DW 1 has stated that agency is created and functions are regulated by the Customs Act. He said that it is within his knowledge that there are provisions in the Customs Act that a supplier must take permission from the local shipping agent for any kind of supply to the vessel. He has further stated that if the supplier is appointed by the owner or principal directly still approval must be taken from the local agent. DW 1 has stated that the money that was deposited with the bank was furnished by the owner of the vessel. He has stated that he does not know if there is any paper in their office from the defendant No.1 to show that the defendants Nos. 1 and 4 ever denied or disputed the claim of the plaintiff. He has stated that he does not know whether the plaintiff supplied the goods in question from the order of the owner by observing all formalities and he is entitled to suit amount. He has further stated that he does not know if the plaintiff was under a duty to maintain communication since he was not appointed by the local agent. DW 1 has stated that he does not know whether there are factories at Chittagong for making spare parts of ship in Chittagong. DW 1 has denied that the owner has given the claim amount to them to give it to the plaintiff and they are not making payment to the plaintiff. Further, DW 1 has stated that he is also deposing on behalf of the defendant No. 6 but he could not bring any paper to show that he was authorized to depose in the matter but later on he said that defendant No. 6 has sent him to depose for him in this suit. DW 1 has stated that he does not know whether the defendant No. 6 has admitted the claim of the plaintiff by way of reply to the legal notice. DW 1 has categorically stated that he could not say if the vessel was lying in a distressed condition in Mongla Port. He has further stated that he even did not hear that the vessel needed spare parts at Mongla Port. On re-call DW 1 has stated that in case of foreign vessel coming in any part in Bangladesh an officer of Customs Department boards the vessel and continues to remain there till departure of the vessel. DW 1 has formally proved certain documents and the same have been marked as Exts 4, wherein generator was supplied to a foreign vessel and bill of export was submitted. That is a requirement of law.

15. In cross-examination DW 1 has stated that the Exts 1-4 which he has filed are the documents of October, 1995 and he was not in the service of the defendant No 6 at that time Exts. 1-4 are not the related papers of the suit vessel. However, DW 1 categorically denied that for supply of goods in the vessel seal and signature of the customs officer are not mandatory. DW 1 has stated that they did not receive any objection from the Customs that the supply was made without permission. DW 1 has stated that they did not receive any objection from the Customs Authority for no supply was made. He has stated that one Mr Abul Hossain is the Chairman of the defendant No. 6, DW 1 has stated that he does not know if Mr Qashim is a partner. He has stated that he has not filed any letter of authority from the defendant No. 6 authorizing him to depose in the suit. DW 1 has volunteered that he has not filed the letter of authority to the Court but if required he may file the same during the court hour. DW 1 has denied that the plaintiff has ever supplied the spare parts in question observing all rules and formalities to that effect.

<u>16. The plaintiff has filed certain documents and the same has been formally proved by PW 1. Ext 5 shows that this was a list of requirement from the Master. Ext 7 shows that the plaintiff has supplied on 18-11-96 as many as 17 items of spare parts to the defendant No. 1 vessel. It is the definite case of the plaintiff that they fabricated the spare parts of the ship in question in workshop in Chittagong but the plaintiff has not filed any vouchers and receipts showing that they received the spare parts from the workshop located at Chittagong in order to effect supply to the defendant No. 1 vessel. On perusal of the plaint it appears that neither the plaintiff has stated that the plaintiff fabricated those spare parts in their workshop in Chittagong and/or fabricated those spare parts in any other workshop in Chittagong. PW 1 has tried to support his own suit in material particulars that he has supplied the said spare parts to the defendant No. 1 vessel and Ext. 8 is a bill dated 18-11-96 for supply of those spare parts including transportation/customs gratuity/ shipping/labour cost etc. Be that as it may, the plaintiff has neither filed any papers showing that he did not manufacture those spare parts of ships in his own workshop nor he has filed any papers/vouchers/receipts showing that he purchased the said spare parts from the local market.</u>

17. The defendant No 6 has filed certain papers and the same has been formally proved by DW 1 and those papers have been marked as Exts 1-4. The defendant No. 6 has filed those papers in order to show that the Customs Authority''s approval is necessary before any local agent can effect supply of spare parts and/or generator to the vessel. Perusal of Exts. 1, 2 and 3 filed by the defendant No 6 will show that there are clear endorsement made by the Customs Authority in respect of the supply of goods to the vessel in question (the name of the vessel was DAE JIN) and if supply is made to the vessel, then question of submission of bill or payment will arise. Ext. 4 is also a document namely, bill of entry, showing that the vessels DAE JIN was supplied with a generator. In view of the above I am of the opinion that if any supply of spare parts, pumps, generators, etc is made to a foreign vessel then it has to go through the Customs Authority, Without Customs concurrence no supply could be effected to the foreign vessel. In the present suit although the plaintiff has asserted that they supplied 17 items of spare parts including pump but they have failed to file any papers showing that they obtained any approval from the Customs Authority and/or they failed to file any bill of entry showing that they had supplied those 17 items of spare parts to the defendant No 1 vessel after observing the customs formalities.

<u>18. The plaintiff has however, argued that these spare parts are related to pump to keep supply of ballast in the vessel and therefore no Customs permission is necessary as contemplated in the Customs Act. Ballast means, in fact, either water or to any other substance having weight to keep the vessel at a balance. Perusal of Ext 4 filed by the plaintiff shows that the plaintiff not only supplied the aforesaid 17 items of spare parts, he also supplied 5 numbers of other spare parts namely, (i) Main Cool SW pump complete with motor type: VDK 440E, (2) Fire & GS pump complete with motor type: VD 95, (3) Bearing unit complete blower side VTR 200, (4) Bearing unit complete turbine side VTR 200, (5) Lubricating disc for VTR 200. It appears that these are Machineries and spare parts and it cannot be termed as machinery for pump for supply of ballast. These are spare parts of a vessel and can only be effected after obtaining the proper permission through bill of export for free goods for vessel. In that view of the matter I find substance in the submission of the learned Advocate for the defendants that the plaintiff, in fact, did not supply the aforesaid machinery to the vessel in question. I further hold that the certificates that have been given by the Master and the Chief Engineer are all false and fabricated documents procured by the plaintiff for his personal gain.</u>

19. With regard to supply of certain provisions like tomatoes, fish, potatoes, onion, cucumber, vitki fish, pineapples, etc the same should also be supplied with necessary permission from the customs authority. No provisions can be supplied to foreign vessel without the sanction from customs authority. In fact, sanction is not necessary for passenger, passenger bag and for ballast. In this particular case Ext. 11(c) is the bill dated 15-11-96 for supply of provisions like tomato, vitki fish, mango juice, pineapple juice etc, but it appears that these provisions were supplied without any prior permission from the customs authority. Accordingly, customs authorities'' endorsement in the said Ext 11(c) is lacking.

20. In view of the above I am of the opinion that the bills submitted by the plaintiff for supply of provisions to the defendant No. 1 vessel also appears to be false and fabricated and the plaintiff is not entitled to the payment of supply of provisions as stated herein above.

21. With regard to providing laundry service to the seamen and other officers of the defendant No. 1 vessel, the plaintiff has submitted a bill for an amount of US 536.61 but there is no endorsement whatsoever on the said bill by the customs authority.

22. Perusal of section 24 of the Customs Act, 1969 appears that provisions and stores may be exported free of duty. Further section 50 of the Customs Act provides that no goods other than passengers baggage and mail bags shall be loaded on a conveyance unless certain conditions are fulfilled.

<u>23. It further appears that section 24 of the Customs Act, 1969 that goods should not be loaded or unloaded or water-borne except in presence of officer, save where general permission is given under section 67 or with permission in writing of the appropriate officer, no goods other than passengers, baggage or ballast urgently required to be loaded for the vessel''s safety, shall be shipped or water-borne to be shipped or discharged from any vessel in any customs-port, nor any goods except passenger, baggage shall be loaded in or unloaded from any conveyance other than a vessel at any land customs station or customs airport except in the presence of an officer of customs. It appears from the record of this case that no general exemption was recorded from the application under sections 64 and 66 of the Customs Act as contemplated under section 67 of the Customs Act. In view of the aforesaid provisions of law, I am of the opinion that the goods, necessaries and services which are alleged to have been supplied by the plaintiff are not at all evidenced as contemplated under section 67 and/or section 66 of the Customs Act. On the contrary, the documents that have been filed by the defendant No. 6 shows that any goods to be supplied to a foreign vessel has to go through the formalities that is, through the Customs Authority. In other words, supply of spare parts, provisions and laundry service should be effected through the customs authority. It appears from the documents filed by the plaintiff that the alleged supply of spare parts, provisions and laundry services were not effected through the approval from the customs authority. Over and above, the plaintiff has also failed to file any papers showing that those spare parts were fabricated in his own workshop and/or he purchased from the local market. In view of the aforesaid position of evidence on record it is hard to believe that the plaintiff had fabricated/ manufactured those spare parts in his own workshops. Moreover, there is no iota of such assertion in the plaint that the plaintiff had himself manufactured or fabricated these spare parts in his workshop. Further, it is not understood as to how the plaintiff supplied those spare parts and provisions to a foreign vessel without the prior sanction of the Customs Authority. The learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the plaintiff has argued that these are machinery and spare parts for pump in respect of ballast. I have also gone through the plaint and I do not find any such averments that he supplied the necessary spare parts in connection with pump for ballast.</u>

<u>24. Considering the facts and circumstances of the case and the evidence on record I am of the view that plaintiff has not, in fact, supplied these spare parts, provisions and provided laundry service in accordance with law and I very much doubt that if the plaintiff had himself fabricated and/or manufactured those spare parts in his own workshop and supplied the same to the defendant No. 1 vessel. Therefore I find that the plaintiff has failed to discharge its onus of proving that he had supplied spare parts, provisions and provided laundry service to the defendant No. 1 vessel. In fact, the plaintiff has failed to prove this case by adducing sufficient and reliable'' proper evidence. Accordingly, I am of the opinion that the plaintiff is not entitled to a decree as prayed for.</u>

25. In the result the suit is dismissed on contest against the defendant No. 6 and ex parte against the other defendants.

In view of the aforesaid facts and circumstances of the case there shall be no order as to cost.

End.

lawyer:
Syed Mokaddas Ali, Advocate — For the Petitioner. 
Md Harun-ar-Rashid, Advocate — For the Opposite Parties.
parties:
Fakhruddin Ahmed ------ Petitioner
vs
Kutubuddin Ahmed and another ------ Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
Mahmudul Amin Chowdhury J: This Rule was issued calling upon the opposite parties to show cause why order dated 3-5-98 passed in Title Suit No. 289 of 1992 by the learned Subordinate Judge, Additional Court, Dhaka accepting the report of the Advocate Commissioner and rejecting the written objection of defendant No.1 filed against the said report and also rejecting the application for allowing the witness to depose on behalf of the defendant No.1 in Title Suit No. 289 of 1992 should not be set aside.

2. The short fact leading to this Rule is that, the petitioner and two opposite parties are full-brothers and they constructed a tin-shed house at 28 Shantibagh Road, Dhaka and when the plaintiff requested his two other brothers for partition of all of their properties it was refused which resulted in the filing of the suit for partition. In that suit the defendants entered appearance and the parties compromised the suit and the same was decreed in terms of a solenama and for effecting sole-decree an Advocate Commissioner was appointed who after executing the commission submitted a report against which the petitioner filed an objection which was on hearing rejected by the learned Subordinate Judge, Additional Court, Dhaka and he accepted the report. The petitioner on being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the Commissioner''s report moved this Court and obtained the present Rule.

3. Mr Syed Mokaddas Ali, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioner, submits that the original suit for partition was decreed on compromise and the solenama filed was made a part of the decree and a commissioner was deputed from the Court to effect partition by metes and bounds. But while distributing the saham the Advocate Commissioner admittedly left certain properties and also has not taken proper measurement of the lands is question. He also admittedly kept out a pond and its banks out of partition and also has not partitioned the village properties. The learned Advocate contends that such partition cannot be piecemeal. He also submits that the Commissioner has given more Dhaka lands to opposite parties 1 and 2 which is inconsistent with the decree passed and no explanation has been given by the Commissioner why he has given more land than the due lands to the opposite parties. The learned Advocate contends that the measurement of Dhaka properties given by the Commissioner is also vague and indefinite and the Commissioner''s report is not at all satisfactory by which the partition cannot be effected. Against this the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the opposite parties submits that the report of the Advocate Commissioner indicates that he has given more Dhaka land to the opposite parties and this may be due to effecting partition.

<u>4. We have gone through the available materials, particularly the sole-decree and the Commissioner''s report as well as the maps and it appears that the Commissioner''s report is not in conformity with the sole-decree as admittedly it kept out certain properties while distributing the saham and those are village properties. A decree for partition cannot be executed in piecemeal as has been done by the Advocate Commissioner. Here it appears a pond in the village which was to be partitioned but the same was not done. All those have affected the report of the Commissioner which has escaped the notice of the trial Court. When a Commissioner is deputed to effect partition he is to effect the saham by metes and bounds taking all the properties in suit. But here in the present case this has not been done by the Advocate Commissioner and this definitely affected the report as well as the partition. It appears that the trial Court has not considered the decree, Commissioner''s report and his evidence while rejecting the objection. While deposing in Court the Commissioner himself admitted that he has not effected partition in the pond in the village and when such is the evidence the Commissioner''s report ought not to have been accepted.</u>

<u>5. Thus, after consideration of the materials on record and after hearing the learned Advocates of both the sides we hold that this is a fit case where this Court should interfere and set aside the order dated 3-5-1998 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, Additional Court, Dhaka in Title Suit No.289 of 1992 and make the Rule absolute.</u>

<u>6. Court-fees paid are correct.</u>

<u>7. The Rule is accordingly, made absolute without any order as to costs. The order dated 3-5-1998 passed in Title Suit No. 289 of 1992 is hereby set aside. The objection raised by the petitioner is hereby accepted and the Commissioner''s report submitted by the Commissioner is rejected;</u>

The parties in litigation are hereby directed to approach the trial Court for appointment of a fresh Advocate Commissioner so that the sole-decree passed may be effected legally and properly.

End.

lawyer:
Akhter Imam with Sheikh Hasan Arif, Advocates—For the Petitioners. 
Md Asadullah with Khaleda Sultana Nur, Advocates—For Respondent No.1. 
Zafarullah Chowdhury, Advocate—For Respondent No. 3.
parties:
Sultana Jute Mills Ltd and another ------ Petitioners
VS
Bangladesh Bank and others ------ Respondents
full_judgment:
Farid Ahmed J: This Rule Nisi was issued calling upon the respondent Nos. 1-3 to show cause as to why inclusion of the names of the petitioners in the CIB Report of Bangladesh Bank under the Borrower Code No. 4999 as mentioned in Annexure-A should not be declared to have been passed without lawful authority and is of no legal effect and why the respondents should not be directed to delete the name of the petitioner from the CIB Report and/or pass such other or further order or orders as to this Court may seem fit and proper.

2. The facts of the case as stated in the petition are that the petitioner No. 1 is a company engaged in jute mills business and petitioner No. 2 is its Managing Director. Petitioner No. 1 has been enjoying various loan, overdraft and banking facilities from its banker, respondent No. 3, for the purpose of its business; that the respondent No. 1 has been enjoying various loan, overdraft and banking facilities from its banker, respondent No. 3, for the purpose of its business; that the respondent No. 1 Bangladesh Bank included the names of the petitioners in the Credit Information Bureau Report (CIB Report) as defaulting borrowers for the alleged loan liabilities of respondent No. 3 Agrani Bank under Borrower Code No. 4999. The petitioners by reason of the said CIB report are unable to obtain and renew various facilities from various banks, which is causing a total disruption and stoppage in the business of the petitioners. The CIB Report has been published by the respondent No. 1 periodically without any notice to the petitioners and it has been also circulated to all banks behind the back and Knowledge of the petitioners. The respondent No. 3 bank instituted Mortgage Suit No. 21 of 1990 in the Court of Subordinate Judge and Artha Rin Adalat No. 1, Chittagong, claiming an amount Taka 8,89,94,800.22 against the petitioners and others. The petitioners duly appeared and filed written statements in the suit denying the claim of the respondent No. 3. While the suit was pending, there were negotiations for an amicable settlement of the dispute between the petitioners and respondent No. 3 by rescheduling the loan liabilities of the petitioners. As a result, the Board of Directors of the respondent No. 3 approved the terms and conditions for the settlement of the petitioners' liabilities and respondent No. 3 vide letter dated 25-2-1995 communicated the terms and conditions of the compromise. The petitioner by a letter dated 19-3-1995 addressed to the respondent No. 3 suggested some modifications in the terms and conditions. The respondent No. 3, however, vide its letter dated 14-6-1995 informed the petitioners that its Board of Directors did not accept the modifications suggested by the petitioner and the Board kept its earlier decision and asked the petitioners to take steps according to its letter dated 25-2-1995. The petitioners by their letter dated 25-6-1995 immediately wrote back to the respondent No. 3 communicating the unconditional acceptance of the offer contained in the letter dated 25-2-1995, of respondent No. 3. Accordingly, the petitioners filed an application on 27-10-1996 before the Court of Subordinate Judge and Artha Rin Adalat No. 1, Chittagong under Order XXIII, rule 3 of the Civil Procedure Code for a compromise decree in terms of the Board resolution of respondent No. 3 as contained in its letter dated 25-2-1995.

3. The respondent No. 3 submitted a written objection refusing to accept compromise earlier agreed by the parties on some flimsy and untenable grounds. Upon hearing the parties the learned Court passed an order dated 15-3-1997 rejecting the application for compromise decree holding that respondent No. 3 had not agreed to the compromise and that there was no signature of respondent No. 2 on the deed of compromise.

4. The petitioners then filed a writ petition being Writ Petition No. 1862 of 1997 before the High Court Division whereupon a Rule Nisi was issued and all further proceeding in the said suit was stayed by an order dated 7-4-1997. The respondent No. 1 has now started publishing the name of the petitioners in the CIB Report as mentioned above at the instance of respondent No. 3 instead of regularising the loan account. The CIB Report has been prepared arbitrarily and without any basis at the back of the petitioners and without their knowledge, and the same has been distributed to various banks to the great detriment of the petitioners and their business. Such CIB Report arbitrarily prepared at the back of the petitioners and also distributed without their knowledge, does not have sanction and support of any law as it has the effect of interfering with, jeopardising, stifling, causing detriment and adversely affecting the business of the petitioners. The respondent No. 1 has acted absolutely arbitrary, malafide, without lawful authority and for collateral purpose in including the names of the petitioners in the CIB Report for the liabilities of respondent No. 3 without any basis at all and without considering the question whether they are at all liable for the same or not.

5. Being aggrieved by the inclusion of the names of the petitioners in the CIB Report, they have filed this writ petition and obtained the present Rule.

6. The respondent Nos. 2 and 3 have contested the writ petition by filing 2 separate affidavit-in-oppositions denying all the material allegations made in the petition. The case of respondent Nos. 1 and 2 are that the Bangladesh Bank collects credit information from all financial institutions and banks including respondent No. 3, Agrani Bank. The respondents further stated that respondent No. 1 did not disclose such credit information to anyone except banks and financial institutions. There was no settlement/compromise between the petitioners and respondent No. 3. The petitioners owe the respondent No. 3 a huge amount of money which he has defaulted to repay and therefore his name has been rightly included in the CIB Report. That the CIB Report was prepared in accordance with paragraph-43 (Chapter IV) of the Bangladesh Bank Order, 1972 and the Bangladesh Bank legally included the names of the petitioners in the CIB Report and, as such, the Rule is liable to be discharged.

7. The respondent No. 3 has stated in their affidavit-in-opposition that the names of the petitioners have been included in the CIB Report as defaulting borrower for loan liabilities of respondent No. 3. That the instant writ petition is intended to delay the realisation of rightful claim of the bank. The petitioners' liabilities were classified by the respondent No 3 as defaulting borrower. The name of the petitioner was forwarded to the Bangladesh Bank for inclusion as defaulting borrower in the CIB Report and no illegality was done in inclusion of the petitioners' name in the CIB Report. The writ petition is misconceived and the same is liable to be discharged.

8. Mr Akhter Imam, the teamed Senior Counsel with Mr SK Hasan Arif, appearing on behalf of the petitioners, submitted that the respondent No. 3 approved the terms and conditions for the settlement of the loan liabilities of the petitioners and the petitioners having. unconditionally accepted the said offer thereafter refusal of the respondent No. 3 to give consent on the application for recording compromise decree and sending the name of the petitioners for inclusion in the CIB Report is malafide, arbitrary and without lawful authority. Mr Akhter Imam thereafter submitted that the petitioners have deposited an installment and now ready and willing to pay the rest installments as per terms and conditions of the offer of compromise and, as such, the inclusion of the names of the petitioners in the CIB Report is liable to be declared to have been made without lawful authority and of no legal effect

9. Mr Md Asadullah and Mr Zafarullah Chowdhury, the learned Advocates appearing on behalf of the respondents, submitted that the petitioners though accepted the terms and conditions of the offer of compromise but they did not deposit a single installment as per terms of compromise against their loan liabilities. They further submitted that before issuance of compromise letter dated 25-2-1995 by the respondent No. 3 rescheduling the loan liabilities, the petitioners, defaulted in payment of installments and, as such, their names are rightly included in the CIB Report. They also submitted that after issuance of the compromise letter the petitioners on this and that plea refrained from payment of installments and after passing the decree by the civil Court on 12-12-2006 they have paid Take 11,84,598 as installment while the civil Court decreed the suit for an amount of Taka 8,89,94,800.

10. The respondent No. 3 offered certain terms and conditions by its letter dated 25-2-1995 to the petitioners for rescheduling its loan liabilities on condition of reopening and running the jute mill at their own cost and expenses and to execute charge documents for rescheduling the loan and depositing shares of the petitioner company to the bank executing a document for transferring the same without intervention of the court and the suit filed by the bank would be compromised as per terms of the bank for protecting its interest for realisation of the bank dues to be drafted and approved by the legal adviser of the Head Office and withdrawal of the suit filed by the petitioner against the bank. The petitioner company was asked to express its consent to the said sanction letter by signing duplicate copy of the letter and filing the same with the bank. On receipt of the aforesaid sanction letter dated 25-2-1995 the respondent No. 3 bank filed written objection against the said application stating that the defendant-petitioners failed to submit undertaking to re-start the mill arranging sufficient fund as working capital and that the petitioner also failed to submit resolution of the Board of Directors of the company along with petition for loan as required under the Jute Reforming Schedule Terms 3.4 (ka)

11. The Artha Rin Adalat by order dated 15-3-1997 rejected the petitioner's application on the ground that plaintiff did not give consent to the application for compromise and prayed for rejection of the same. Challenging the said order of the Artha Rin Adalat, the petitioners preferred writ petition No. 1862 of 1997 before the High Court Division and this Court after hearing by judgment and order dated 29-6-1999 discharged the Rule. Being aggrieved by the said judgment and order the petitioners preferred Civil. Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 973 of 1999 before the Appellate Division and the Appellate Division by judgment and order dated 3-6-2001 disposed of the said Leave Petition observing that the High Court Division on a very technical ground discharged the Rule that whether letter dated 25-2-1995 has been written to the petitioner by the plaintiff bank and whether the same has been accepted by the petitioner are matters of evidence. The points at issue now before us can well be decided at the time of trial of the suit but on a writ jurisdiction this question cannot be decided. Defendants will be at liberty to adduce evidence on this point."

12. Subsequently the suit was renumbered as Artha Rin Suit No. 304 of 2003. The Artha Rin Adalat also framed issue No. 2 on the point whether the suit is Sable to be decreed in terms of compromise under Order XXIII, rule 3 of the Code of Civil Procedure along with other issues. The Artha Rin Adalat after hearing by judgment and decree dated 15-10-2006 decreed the suit in favour of the respondent No.3 bank and against the petitioner for an amount of Taka 8,89,94,800 and decided the issue No.2 against the petitioners upon a finding that the present petitioners did not prepare any solenama as per terms of the sanction letter dated 25-2-1995 and that there was a condition for giving an undertaking by the petitioners to the effect that they will run the mill by arranging working capital.

13. Being aggrieved by the judgment and decree passed by the Artha Rin Adalat, the petitioners filed writ petition No. 10946 of 2006 before the High Court Division and at the time of issuance of the Rule this Court passed an ad-interim order or condition that the petitioners take steps to pay the money as per offer of the Agrani Bank dated 25-2-1995 in the manner indicated in the bank's letter dated 25-2-1995.

14. During hearing of this writ petition the petitioners have filed the Rule issuing order and judgment of Writ Petition No. 1862 of 1997 and judgment of Artha Rin Adalat passed in Artha Rin Case No. 304 of 2003 by a supplementary affidavit. With the said supplementary affidavit the petitioner has annexed a letter dated 5-12-2006 as Annexure-H written by the petitioner to the Bank alleging that as per direction of the High Court Division passed in Writ Petition No. 10946 of 2006 he deposited Taka 11,84,598 as 1st installment in favour of the bank. It has been also stated in the supplementary affidavit that for the sake of continuous good relationship between the petitioners and the bank, the petitioners have withdrawn the said writ petition and informed the bank by letter dated 13-12-2006 and requested the bank to confirm the rescheduled arrangement. Certified copy of the order passed in the aforesaid Writ Petition No. 10946 of 2006 shows that on the prayer of the petitioners the Rule of the said writ petition was discharged for non-prosecution by order dated 13-12-2006.

15. The petitioners in their writ petition has annexed a list of borrowing debtors whose names have been included in the CIB Report. In the said report the name of the petitioners' company has appeared and from the said report it further appears that the petitioner was granted overdraft facilities in the year 1985 which was due for repayment on 30-6-1986. Since then the petitioners did not repay the said overdraft loan. From the Column of date of classification of unsatisfactory advance mentioned in the said report it appears that on 31-12-1992 the loan of the petitioner company was classified. Thereafter the respondent bank filed Artha Rin suit for the realisation of the dues of the bank and at one stage, the respondent bank issued a letter on 25-2-1995 offering certain terms and conditions to the petitioners as proposal for compromise. The petitioners thereafter by a letter dated 25-6-1995 accepted the proposal of the respondent-bank. As per terms of the said sanction letter the petitioners did not prepare the compromise petition and also did not prepare an undertaking to the effect that he is ready to start the Mill arranging sufficient fund as working capital and also failed to submit a resolution of the Board of Directors of the company. The petitioners thereafter on 27-10-1996 filed an application for compromise decree of the suit as per terms of the banks letter dated 25-2-1995 but the bank raised objection against the said letter as the petitioners did not fulfil the terms and conditions of the bank's letter dated 25-2-1995. Not only that since after issuance of the said letter in the year 1995 the petitioners did not pay a single installment against his loan liabilities. The petitioners deposited Taka 1148409 on 12-12-2006 as per direction of the High Court Division passed in Writ Petition No. 10946 of 2006. It appears from the letter dated 25-2-1995 that the bank offered to pay the dues quarterly but after depositing 1st installment on 12-12-2006 the petitioners did not pay any installment in favour of the bank. Already we have found that before issuance of the letter dated 25-2-1995 by the bank, offering some terms and conditions for compromise, the petitioner company had become defaulter and under the provision of Bank Companies Act the petitioner is a defaulting borrower. The respondent-bank filed the suit in the year 1990 for realisation of the dues from the petitioners but upto 12-12-2006 they have paid only Take 1148509 out of total out-standing of Taka 8,89,94,800.

<u>16. The CIB Report was prepared by the Bangladesh Bank under the provisions contained in Chapter IV of the Bangladesh Bank Order, 1972 on the basis of the Credit Information furnished by the respondent Agrani Bank under section 27 kaka of Bank Companies Act 1991. The bank advanced loan to the petitioner company as per certain terms and conditions. The petitioner company violated the loan contract and defaulted in payment of loan. As per credit information furnished by the respondent No. 3, Bank the Bangladesh Bank prepared the impugned credit information report. Since the petitioner company failed to repay the loan, the respondent No.3 legally furnished credit information to the Bangladesh Bank in compliance of section 27 kaka of Bank Companies Act, 1991. The respondent No. 1 did not violate any provisions of law and or acted contrary to any provisions of law in including the name of the petitioners' Company in the CIB report. The respondent No. 3 classified him as defaulter in the year 1992 and the names of the petitioners were included in the CIS Report in 1997.</u>

17. In the facts and circumstances stated above, we find that the respondents legally included the name of the petitioners' company in the CIB report. We find no merit in this writ petition.

In the result, the Rule is discharged without any order as to cost. The order of stay granted at the time of issuance of Rule on 3-12-2000 is hereby vacated.

End.

lawyer:
Md Badruddoza Advocate—For the Petitioners  
Mahbubey Alam with ABM Bayezid—For the Respondents No. 1, 4 & 6.
