As such I find the learned Appellate Judge committed error of law and fact in reversing the judgment and decree of the learned trial Judge when it has been a admitted fact that there was a deed of agreement (Bainapatra) entered into and executants by and between the defendant Nos. 1-3 and the plaintiff and the defendant No. 4 (as purchaser). And the same having not been cancelled or rescinded by the defendant Nos. 1-3 it was very much enforceable as a legal piece of document and by ignoring this the defendant Nos. 1-3 had no authority to transfer the property in favour of the defendant No. 4 ignoring the right and interest of the plaintiff and by ignoring this very vital aspect of the case the learned Appellate Judge has committed an error of law and fact in reversing the judgment of the learned trial Judge for which the impugned judgment is not sustainable in law. In this respect as Mr Saha has submitted that conveyance document Is concluded agreement and the same is binding upon both the parties until and unless it is cancelled and in this respect the citation that has been referred to by Mr Saha being the case reported in 14 DLR (SC) 112 is in agreement with his submission as it is agreed and apparent from the evidences on record that the defendant Nos. 1-3 did not cause any notice to be served on the plaintiff rescinding or canceling the deed of agreement or the Bainapatra and without canceling the same having being remaining in force the transfer of the property in favour of the defendant No. 4 who according to pleadings and statement of the plaintiff side jointly in connivance with each other taking recourse to deceitfully tactic to defraud the plaintiff has created and registered deed of transfer in favour of the defendant No. 4 on 4-3-1989 for whole of the contracted land whereas the plaintiff was still entitled to get saf kabala deed for half portion of the said contracted land. As such the transaction transferring the suit land being 17 decimals of land in favour of the defendant No. 4 one of the baina purchaser together with the plaintiff is an illegal act on the part of the transferor as well as on the part of the transferee as the purchaser and the seller was quite aware of the earlier bainapatra and the purchaser himself being one of the intending purchaser of the said bainapatra was not at all a fair transaction on his part. As such I find that the plaintiff acquired right, and interest in the half portion of the said contracted land i.e. 17 decimals of land as has been purchased by the defendant No. 4 in a single name and the defendant No. 4 is bound to hand over possession of 50% of the A schedule land which has been described in the schedule B of the plaint. On receipt of balance consideration money of Taka 4,500 from the plaintiff.

16. Although Mr Nandi the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the opposite party has submitted that the plaintiff did not comply with the four elements as has been discussed earlier and those having not been complied with by the plaintiff was not entitled to get a decree for Specific Performance of Contract as the defendant No. 4 on payment of enhanced price of Taka 70,000 at a time got the schedule property transferred in his favour as the bainapatra was cancelled by the defendant Nos. 1-3 after expiry of one months of stipulated period. In this connection Mr Nandi has referred to a decision reported in 43 DLR 360 which is not in agreement with the facts and circumstances of the present case before me and it is in no way coming to any aid of Mr Nandi and the other points as has been submitted by Mr Nandi that the plaintiff hopelessly failed to complying with the four elements as deem and decided by our High Court Division in the cited case but after going through the pleadings and evidences on record I do not find any substances in the submission of Mr Nandi in this respect. As such I am unable to accept his submission and contention rather I find substances in the submission of Mr Shaha the learned Advocate for the petitioner and the citation that has been referred to Mr Shaha is in agreement with his submission and contention and on scrutiny I find that the judgment and decree passed by the learned trial Judge is well evaluated and well discussed judgment save and except the learned trial Judge decreed the suit against the defendant No. 4 alone directing him to execute and register the sale deed to the extent of half portion of first schedule land upon accepting the balance consideration money in favour of the plaintiff. This portion of the judgment requires to be modified in view of decision of our Lordships in the Appellate Division reported in 2 BLC (AD) 30 in the case of Ezher Meah vs Shaher Bairn; which runs as follows "Specific Relief Act (1 of 1877) section 27 : In a suit for specific performance of contract where the Courts below directed the subsequent purchasers to execute the kabala in favour of the plaintiff although they were not parties to the contract but the proper form of decree would be to direct specific performance of the contract between the vendor and the plaintiff and direct the subsequent transferee to join in the conveyance so as to pass on the title which resides in him to the plaintiff and this view is being followed in our Courts for a long time which is strengthened by the judgments of the Supreme Court of India" After going through the aforesaid judgment of our lordships in the Appellate Division, I feel that the judgment and decree passed by the learned Assistant Judge needs be modified to this extent that the suit be decreed against defendants No. 1-3 and they be directed to execute and register kabala in favour of the plaintiff for half portion of the first schedule land and the defendant No. 4 shall also join in executing the kabala with defendant Nos. 1-3 for transferring the suit land in favour of the plaintiff who will pay the balance consideration money to the tune of Taka 4,500 to the defendant No. 4 and the judgment and decree passed by the learned Assistant Judge be modified accordingly. I find that the judgment passed by the learned Appellate Judge suffers from misreading and non-reading and non consideration of the evidences on record being very short cut judgment without properly adhering to the provision of Order XLI, rule 31 of the Code of Civil Procedure. As such I do not find any cogent reason to sustain the same rather I find that the impugned judgment is liable to be set aside.

17. In the result the rule is made absolute without any order as to cost. The impugned judgment dated 10-6-1999 and decree dated 20-6-1999 passed by the learned Additional District and Sessions Judge, 10th Court, Dhaka in Title Appeal No. 211 of 1993 is hereby set aside and the judgment and decree dated 28-4-1993 and decree dated 16-5-1993 passed by the learned Senior Assistant Judge, 1st Additional Court, Dhaka in Title Suit No. 45 of 1991 is upheld and maintained with modification tot heat effect that the plaintiff is legally entitled to get 50% of the suit land i.e. 8.50 decimals of land out of 17 decimals (first schedule land) from the defendant Nos. 1-3 through execution and registration of kabala and the defendant No. 4 shall join in executing the kabala with defendant Nos. 1-3 for transferring the suit land in favour of the plaintiff who will pay the balance consideration money Taka 4,500 in the trial Court and the defendant No. 4 would be entitled to the same. Regarding possession the defendant No. 4 shall amicably deliver possession of the 50% of the schedule A property to the plaintiff petitioner otherwise the plaintiff will get possession through the trial Court as pr provision of law.

18. Order of stay granted at the time of issuance of the rule stands vacated.

Send down the lower Court record together with copy of the judgment to the Courts below expeditiously.

End.

lawyer:
Fazlul Haque, Advocate-For the Petitioner 
ASM Abdul Mobin, Advocate-For Opposite-Parties.
parties:
Saydur Rahman Chowdhury Rupa ------ Petitioner
VS.
Rani Begum & others ------Opposite-Parties
full_judgment:
The Rule at the instance of the defendant-petitioner issued calling upon the opposite-party Nos. 1-6 to show cause as to why the impugned judgment and order dated 14-3-2010 passed by the learned Senior Assistant Judge and SCC Judge, Sadar, Sylhet in SCC Suit No. 01 of 2009 should not be set-aside.

2. The facts leading to the issuance of the Rule in a nutshell can be stated thus, the plaintiff-opposite-party Nos. 1-6 instituted the original SCC Suit being No. 01 of 2009 in the Court of learned Senior Assistant Judge and SCC Court, Sadar, Sylhet against the defendant-petitioner and his one brother proforma-opposite party No. 17 for their eviction from the suit shop premises and recovery of khash possession impleading defendant Nos. 3-12 their step brothers and sisters as proforma-defendants contending that the suit shop premises belonged to their father Tara Mia who inducted one Azad Mia Chowdhury as evictable monthly tenant in The suit shop premises, Tara Mia died on 11-12-2003 and thereafter the plaintiff and proforma-defendant got the suit premises with other properties left behind their lather. By way of amicable partition the suit premises fell in the share of the plaintiffs. But the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 are running their business in the shit shop premises of the suit property illegally without any basis. The plaintiffs for their urgent need of the suit shop premises asked the defendants to give up possession, but the defendants without rendering vacant possession of the suit shop premises filed a House Rent case being No. 15 of 2008 for depositing rents in the Court of Controller of House Rent. Sadar, Sylhet claiming that the defendants are not the defaulters and the suit shop premises is required for their personal use to run business. Finding no other alternative the plaintiffs instituted the original suit as the defendants arc defaulters having, no right to retain possession.

3. The contrary case of the defendant-petitioner is such that, knowing about the filing of SCC Suit by the plaintiff-opposite-parties the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 filed an application under section 23 of the Small Causes Courts Act, stating that the father of the plaintiffs Tara Miah entered into a contract with the brothers of the defendants on 10-4-1987 granting right of possession of the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 and their brothers in the suit shop premises for 99 years on receipt of Tk. 75,000 (seventy five thousand) and fixing monthly rent @ Tk. 200 (two hundred) and acknowledged receipt of Tk. 75,000 as consideration money for possessory right and since then the defendants had been paying rents @ Tk. 200 and then as Tk. 300 and had been possessing the suit shop premises. After the death of the Tara Miah Chowdhury his son Shajahan Mia realized rent till June, 2004 without granting receipts. Subsequently while he stopped in realizing rent the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 started to deposit rents with the controller of House Rent in House Rent Case No. 15 of 2008. The further case of the defendant-petitioner is such that they are not ejectable tenants or, illegal trespassers in the suit shop premises and they never violated the terms and condition of the deed executed by Tara Miah in their favour and as such the plaintiffs are not entitled to get any relief. The defendants have acquired a possessory right and permanent tenancy in the suit shop premises and since the matter cannot be decided in SCC jurisdiction they filed the application for returning the plaint under the purview of section 23 of the Small Causes Courts Act.

4. The learned SCC Judge on hearing the application rejected the same and being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the impugned order dated 14-3-2010 the defendant-petitioner preferred this revisional application under seetion 25 of the Small Causes Courts Act.

5. Mr AS Md Abdul Mobin, the learned Advocate appeared on behalf of the defendant-petitioner while Mr Fazlul Haque the learned Advocate appeared on behalf of the plaintiff-opposite-parties.

6. The learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the defendant-petitioner during hearing of this revisional application submits that the learned SCC Judge erred in law in finding that the defendants admitted them as tenants under the plaintiffs by filing rent deposit case. In fact the rent deposit case was filed by the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 against Md Shajahan, son of late Tara Miah who used to realize rents after the demise of his father and subsequently denied to accept rent. The learned Advocate further submits that the learned Court below committed illegality in not taking notice of the defendant-petitioner's case that they purchased the possessory right for 99 years by virtue of the deed dated 10-4-1987 from the father of the plaintiffs and the learned Assistant Judge committed error of law in misreading the positive ease of the present defendant-petitioner that the plaintiffs in tie plaint alleged that the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 are illegal trespassers in the suit premises where the elder brother of the plaintiffs Azad Miah realized rents from the defendants admitting their tenancy right for 99 years on payment of Tk. 75,000 in the year 1987 and as such the defendants are not ejectable tenants as alleged from the side of the plaintiffs. The learned Advocate for the petitioner lastly submits that the defendant paid Tk. 75,000 and acquired promissory right over the premises for 99 years and thereby acquired status of non-evictable tenants.

7. As against the submissions of the learned counsel for the petitioner the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the opposite-parties opposing the Rule submits that the learned SCC Judge in rejecting the application filed under section 23(1) of the Small Causes Courts Act, committed no illegality or irregularity rather rightly opined that in the instant case there is no complicated question of title of the plaintiffs to be determined and it is an admitted position that the predecessor-in-interest of the plaintiffs their father Tara Miah being the owner of the suit premises entered into an agreement with the defendants and in the year 1987 the defendants were inducted into the possession of the suit premises as a monthly tenant under the landlord Tara Miah. It is also an admitted position that the monthly rent was fixed at the rate of Tk. 200 initially and subsequently raised to Tk. 300 per month. The defendants also admitted that after the death of Tara Miah one of his sons namely Shajahan realized rents till the months of June, 2004 and while he stopped in realizing rent from the defendant-petitioner the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 after filing a House Rent Case being No. 15 of 2008 started to deposit rents with the controller of House Rent, Sadar, Sylhet. The learned Advocate further submits that the learned Court below consulting the connected papers on proper appreciation of the provisions of law laid down in section 23(1) of the Small Causes Court Act finding no merit rejected the application for returning of the plaint and, as such, there is nothing to interfere with the impugned & order of the learned SCC Judge, Sadar, Sylhet dated 14-3-2010.

8. Heard the learned Advocates of both sides and perused all the connected papers including the impugned order. On perusal of the relevant papers it appears that the plaintiffs to the suit filed the original suit against the defendants for their eviction from the suit shop premises on the plea that their father Tara Miah Chowdhury was the original owner of the suit premises who entered into a contract with the defendants as a monthly tenants in respect of the suit premises in the year 1987. The defendants were inducted into possession as monthly tenant under the original owner Tara Miah Chowdhury at a rental of Tk. 200 per month which was subsequently raised to Tk. 300. After the demise of the original owner the plaintiffs including their brother Shahjahan Miah inherited the property left behind their father Tara Miah. The defendant-petitioner admitting the ownership and title of the plaintiffs father paid rent and after the death of plaintiffs father they also paid rent in respect of the suit shop premises and it is their specific case that the elder son of Tara Mia one Shahjahan realized rent from them till the month of June, 2004. The further case of the defendant-petitioner as it appears from their contention is such that Shahjahan Miah did not grant any receipt in their favour and subsequently stopped in realizing rents from them and thereafter finding no other alternative the defendant-petitioner instituted a House Rent Case being No. 15 of 2008 in the Court of Rent controller.

9. I have gone through the application filed on behalf of the defendant-petitioner for return of the plaint wherefrom it is noticed that the defendant-petitioner in their application specifically asserted to the effect that they are the monthly tenants under the landlord and on 10.04.1987 a deed of contract was executed by the landlord in their favour for 99 years at a monthly rent of Tk. 200 which was a permanent lease in their favour and thus acquired a possessory right in the suit premises. The learned Court below during passing the impugned judgment and order on perusal of the respective case of the petitioner opined that the provisions laid down in section 32(1) of the Small Cause Courts, Act. 1887 have got no manner of application in the instant case and there is nothing to hold such a view that any complicated question of title is involved here in this case. In this context; on plain reading of the respective provisions of law as contemplated in section 23(1) of the Small Causes Courts Act, 1887 it is very much evident that the learned Court below committed no wrong. The aforesaid provisions of law runs as follows:-

"Notwithstanding anything in the foregoing portion of this Act, when the right of a plaintiff and the relief claimed by him in a Court of Small Causes depend upon the proof or disproof of a title to immoveable properly or other title which such a Court cannot finally determine, the Court may at any stage of the proceedings return the plaint to be presented to a Court having jurisdiction to determine the title."

<u>10. Having regard to the facts, circumstances and the provisions of law I have every reason to constrained such a view that the learned trial Court i.e. the SCC Court committed no illegality in deciding that the title of the plaintiffs is not challenged and no complicated question of title is required to be determined in respect of the suit premises. In the instant case, scope is very limited to entertain such application for return of the plaint. Only when the right of the plaintiff and the relief claimed by him in the Court of Small Causes depend upon the proof and disproof of a title to immoveable property, the said provision can be invoked. Hence, I have nothing to hold that there lies any merit in the application filed on behalf of the defendant-petitioner therein and as such the Rule have got no substance to succeed.</u>

11. In the result, the Rule is discharged.

12. The order of Stay granted earlier by this Court at the time of issuance of the Rule stands vacated.

13. However, there will be no order as to costs.

Communicate the judgment and order at once to the Court concerned for information and necessary action.

End.

caseno: First Miscellaneous Appeal No. 22 of 2007 with Civil Rule No. 412 (FM) of 2006.
lawyer:
M Hafizullah with Md Al-Amin Sarker & Md Ohiullah, Advocates--For the Appellant. 
Md Ismail Mia with Md Solaiman Munshi, Advocates--For Respondent No. 1.
parties:
Canon Kabushiki Kaisha ------ Appellant 
Vs
 Canon Electronics Industries Ltd ------ Respondent.
full_judgment:
Plaintiff Canon Kabushiki Kaisha, having felt saddened by a decision handed over by learned Additional District Judge performing functions of Bankruptcy Court, Dhaka by which its petition for Temporary Injunction stood refused, knocked at the door of this Court as appellant on bestowing a Miscellaneous Appeal being First Miscellaneous Appeal No. 22 of 2007 and craves for quashment of the decision under challenge in the appeal and, also, for a verdict of temporary injunction in its favour.

2. Portrayal of intrinsic datum forming backdrop of Miscellaneous Appeal may conveniently be taken heed of.

3. Plaintiff Canon Kabushiki Kaisha represented in Bangladesh through constituted Attorney Mr DP Mazumder instituted a Suit being Title Suit No. 11 of 2006 in the Court of District Judge, Dhaka seeking following reliefs:

a. Declaration that plaintiff is entitled to exclusive use of Trade Mark "CANON" in respect of Cameras, Cine-cameras, Electro-photographic apparatus, Electronic Calculating Machines, Projectors, Optical apparatus and other goods belonging to International Class 9.

b. Defendant Canon Electronics Industries Ltd was restrained permanently by way of Permanent Injunction from importing, manufacturing, marketing, using, selling their pro-ducts under Trade Mark "CANON" and all other products in Class 9 of Trade Marks Rules, as well as International Class 9 along with device, colour, scheme, design and get-up as shown in schedule "B" or any other get up, packing or trading style confusingly similar to that used by plaintiff or any other word, mark or marks, levels, packaging, etc. which may conflict with plaintiffs aforesaid Trade Mark either visually or phonetically and from using Trade Mark "CANON" in its business name.

c. Mandatory injunction be granted compelling defendant to deliver to plaintiff all spurious goods in its possession and to deliver on oath all infringing designs, tickets, containers, carton boxes, all dices, stamps, blocks, advertisement materials, price lists, shipping forms, payment slips receipts, signboards, name cards, etc. in its possession.

Core averments made in the plaint are:

Plaintiff is a company incorporated and existing under laws of Japan and represented in Bangladesh through its Constituted Attorney. Plaintiff is one of the largest manufacturers and merchants of cameras, cine-cameras, electro-photographic apparatus and all other goods belonging to International Class 9. In order to distinguish their goods from other competitors plaintiff adopted the word "CANON" on its Trade Mark and secured registration thereof in most of countries including Bangladesh under Registration No. 13549 in Class 9 dated 25-5-1999 from the office of Registrar of Trade Marks, Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh. Plaintiff by virtue of long use of all the goods under International Class 9 has acquired exclusive and monopoly right over Trade Mark "CANON". Defendant has been manufacturing and marketing similar goods by adopting "CANON" as Trade Mark on their goods, cartons and packaging’s representing the same colour scheme, writing style, wording and in same particular manner similar to plaintiffs Trade Mark "CANON" as well as by adopting and incorporating a deceptively similar company named "Canon Electronics Industries Ltd" just to create confusion and deception in the market amongst purchasers. Trade Mark used by defendant under Trade Mark "CANON" along with its device, design, get-up and colour scheme together with name of defendant's company is usually and phonetically similar to the Trade Mark "CANON" of plaintiff and defendant has adopted device including design, art get-up, colour scheme as used by plaintiff which is highly objectionable under sections 8(a), 10(1), 20(b), 21 of Trade Marks Act, 1940. Defendant by illegal and wrongful act, as aforesaid stated is crippling and jeopardizing the well-built Trade Mark of plaintiff and plaintiff has been suffering irreparable loss and damage in respect of reputation and goodwill which it has earned.

4. Plaintiff almost upon the same averments as averred in plaint presented a petition for temporary injunction under Order XXXIX, rules 1 and 2 read with section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure for restraining defendant by way of a temporary injunction from manufacturing, marketing, using and selling products of defendant under Trade Mark "CANON" and, also, from using deceptively the similar company named "Canon Electronics Industries Ltd."

5. Learned District Judge issued notices upon defendant to show cause as to why temporary injunction as prayed for by plaintiff would not be granted.

6. Defendant Canon Electronics Industries Ltd contested Temporary injunction matter on laying a Written Objection pressing into service contentions that defendant is a registered Company incorporated under the Companies Act, 1994 and defendant is genuine adopter and user of Trade Mark word "CANON" along with its logo in respect of Television since 2003. Defendant has been producing, assembling, marketing and selling its products in local market of Bangladesh with Trade Mark word "CANON" and other logo as a composite Trade Mark of company. Defendant laid a petition for registration of Copyright in respect of Television on 31-8-2005 before Registrar of Copyright and Registrar of Copyright was pleased to issue a Registration Certificate in favour of defendant on 29-9-2005. Defendant has filed an application for registration of Trade Mark on 3-6-2004 and Registrar, Department of Patent, Design and Trade Mark issued a provisional certified copy in favour of defendant being No. 85977 in Class 9 under provision of section 75 of Trade Marks Act, 1940. On a petition in respect of supplying information whether "CANON" Trade Mark in respect of Television is registered in name of plaintiff, Registrar by letter dated 28-3-2006 informed that no Trade Mark is registered in the name of plaintiff.

7. Learned Additional District Judge who had been, also, performing functions of Bankruptcy Court heard Temporary Injunction matter and by Judgment dated 12-4-2006 rejected plaintiff's petition for temporary injunction.

8. Against the aforesaid Judgment this present action by way of First Miscellaneous Appeal has been resorted to before this Court.

9. Mr M Hafizullah with Mr Md Al-Amin Sarker and Mr Md Ohiullah, learned Counsels, appeared for plaintiff-appellant in the appeal. Defendant-respondent is represented by learned Counsels Mr Md Ismail Mia and Mr Md Solaiman Munshi.

10. Contentions surged forward in support of Appeal are catalogued hereunder:

(i)	Court below erred in law by not allowing plaintiff /appellant's application under Order XXXIX, rules 1 and 2 read with section 151 of The Code of Civil Procedure, although Trade Mark "CANON" is a well reputed international mark duly registered in the name of plaintiff in different countries of the world and the same has, also, been registered in Bangladesh under Registered Trade Mark No. 13549 in Class 9 and, as such, plaintiff is lawful owner of the said International Trade Mark and no one can use this mark in respect of any goods.

(ii)	Court below erred in law in not considering plaintiff/appellant's application under Order XXXIX, rules 1 and 2 read with section 151 of the Code for restraining defendant/respondent from manufacturing, importing, using, selling, marketing their products under the Trade Mark "CANON" along with deceptively packaging, colour scheme, design, get-up, device and all other products in Class 9 confusingly similar to that used by plaintiff/appellant or any other mark or marks or labels which may conflict with plaintiff /appellant's Trade Mark either visually or phonetically and ingredients of application for injunction against defendant-respondent is present and is maintainable.

(iii)	Court below erred in law in holding that no trade mark exists on record in the name of plaintiff/appellant in respect of television without considering extracts/certified copy of plaintiffs registered Trade Mark No. 13549 in Class 9 dated 26-5-1977 relating to Trade Mark "CANON" and those goods under Class 9 of Trade Mark Rules, 1963 covers television, DVD voltage stabilizer but Court below rejected plaintiffs application under Order XXXIX, rules 1 and 2 on assumption that plaintiff has no good prima facie case and, in view of above, impugned order is liable to be set aside.

(iv)	Court below erred in law in misconstruing the provisions of section 15(1) of The Trade Marks Act, 1940 in holding that no conflicting Trade Mark was found in record and accepted Trade Mark of defendant for registration as per provisions of section 15(1) of The Trade Marks Act, 1940 and the said finding is quite wrong in the present case since plaintiff /appellant's Trade Mark has already been registered in plaintiffs name under Registered Trade Mark No. 13549 and plaintiff has acquired proprietary right by registration of Trade Mark "CANON" in plaintiff's name and plaintiffs mark is being infringed by defendant but Court below most illegally held that plaintiff/appellant has no good prima facie case and balance of convenience and inconvenience is not in favour of plaintiff and, in view of above, impugned order is liable to be set aside.

(v)	Court below has failed to apply its judicial mind in adjudicating application under Order XXXIX, rules 1 and 2 of The Code and has failed to consider that plaintiffs Trade Mark "CANON" was registered in Bangladesh on 26-5-1977 being Registered Trade Mark No. 13549 under Class 9 of The Trade Marks Rules, 1963 and, on the contrary, defendant has applied for registration of Trade Mark "CANON" being No. 85977 under Class 9 only on 10-6-2004 showing the date of use of Trade Mark since 2003 and certified copy of the said application clearly shows that the said application is pending for consideration and, in view of above, impugned order, is liable to be set aside.

(vi)	Court below erred in law in not considering that Search Report alleged to have been issued by Registrar of Trade Marks on 28-3-2006 and filed by defendant stating that "CANON" Trade Mark has not been registered is false in view of fact that plaintiff has already proved by submitting certificate issued by Trade Marks Registry that Trade Mark "CANON" has already been registered in favour of plaintiff under Registration No. 13549 in respect of goods in Class 9 and, in view of above, impugned order is liable to be set aside.

In support of contentions some Judicial Authorities such as Shafquat Haider and others vs M Al-Amin and another, 1987 BLD (AD) 130 = 39 DLR (AD) 103, Kabushiki Kaisha Toshiba (also Trading as Toshiba Corporation) vs Ch Muhammad Altaf (Trading as Murad Industries (Regd) and another, PLD 1991 SC 27, Nasir Miah, Malik Nasir Soap Factory vs Md Anwar Hossain, Executive Officer, Commander Soap Factory Ltd., 48 DLR 28, Universal Pharmaceutical Ltd and another vs Social Marketing Company and others, 50 DLR 548, Universal Pharmaceutical Ltd and another vs Social Marketing Company 2 MLR (AD) 201 = 50 DLR (AD) 92, Abdul Mannan Miah vs Md Salaiman Miah, 54 DLR 394, Sunil Kumar Das vs Canon Kabushiki Kaisha & another, 57 DLR 93 and Sunil Kumar Das vs Canon Kabushiki Kaisha & another, 10 BLC (AD) 92 have been referred to.

11. Contentions so raised have been hit back from side of defendant-respondent in putting forth counter-contentions which are as follows:

i.	Plaintiff has no registration in respect of television and defendant's application for registration of Trade Mark under No. 85977 in Class 9, dated 10-6-2004 is not only pending but defendant is, also, user of the Mark since 2003 in respect of television and defendant's application for registration of Trade Mark under the aforesaid number has been provisionally accepted for registration by the Authority.

ii.	Plaintiff-appellant's Trade Mark "CANON" is not registered in Bangladesh in respect of Television under Registration No. 13549 as registration under the aforesaid number is neither in respect of Television nor goods in Class 9 and goods of plaintiff-appellant and defendant-respondent are different and question of using Trade Mark "CANON" of plaintiff by defendant does not arise.

Messers Modi Sugar Mills Limited, through Managing Director and Proprietors, Modi Vanaspati Manufacturing Co vs Tata Oil Mills Co Ltd., Bombay, AIR (30) 1943 Lahore 196, SM Toufiq and others vs National Biscuit Co New York, PLD 1962 Karachi 355, Consolidated Foods Corporation vs Brandon and Co., Private Ltd AIR 1965 Bombay 35, Dhaka Match Factory Ltd vs Bangladesh Match Company Ltd 30 DLR 244 have been relied upon in aid of contentions advanced from side of defendant-respondent.

12. In the fact of pleadings of parties, materials brought on record and rival contentions coming forward from both sides, the prime point boils down in the appeal is, whether plaintiff-appellant can be graced with an order of temporary injunction on over-turning adjudication rendered by learned Additional District Judge by which petition for temporary injunction laid by plaintiff-appellant stood rejected.

13. In broaching and riposting to the point posed, relevant provisions of law engrafted in Trade Marks Act of 1940 and Trade Mark Rules, 1963 are required to be given an eye. Laws and principles regulating grant or refusal of temporary injunction, also, demands meditation.

14. Section 8 of Trade Marks Act, 1940 imposes prohibition of registration of certain matters. Section 8 postulates: No Trade Mark nor part of a trade mark shall be registered which consists of, or contains, any scandalous as designed, or any matter the use of which would:

(a) by reason of its being likely to deceive or to cause confusion or otherwise, be disentitled to protection in a Court of justice; or

(b) …………………..

(c) …………………..

15. Section 10 of Trade Marks Act of 1940 enjoins prohibition of registration of identical or similar trade mark. Section 10 enshrines:

Save as provided in sub-section (2), no trade mark shall be registered in respect of any goods or description of goods which is identical with a trade mark belonging to different proprietors and either already on the register in respect of the same goods or description of goods or which so nearly resembles such trade mark as to be likely to deceive or cause confusion.

(2) …………………….

(3) …………………….

16. Section 21 speaks of right conferred by registration. Section 21 states:

Subject to the provisions of sections 22, 25 and 26, the registration of a person in the register as proprietor of a trade mark in respect of any goods shall give to that person the exclusive right to use of the trade mark in relation to those goods, and, without prejudice to the generality of the foregoing provision, that shall be deemed to be infringed by any person who, not being the proprietor of the trade mark or a registered user thereof using by way of the permitted use, a mark identical with it or so nearly resembling it as to be likely to deceive or cause confusion, in the course of trade, in relation to any goods in respect of which it is registered, and in such manner as to render the use of the mark likely to be taken either:

(a)	as being used as a trade mark; or

(b)	to import a reference to some person having the right either as a proprietor or as registered user to use the trade mark or to goods with which such a person as aforesaid is connected in the course of trade.

17. Classification of goods and names of classes are contained in Fourth Schedule of The Trade Marks Rules, 1963. Class 9 enumerates the following goods:

9. Scientific, nautical, surveying and electrical apparatus and instruments (including wireless), photographic, cinematographic, optical, weighing, measuring, signaling checking (supervision), life-saving and teaching apparatus and instruments: coin or counterfeit apparatus; talking machines; cash-registers; calculating machines; fire-extinguishing apparatus.

18. An Injunction is a Writ framed according to the circumstances of the case commanding an act which the court regards as essential to justice or restraining an act which it esteems contrary to equity and good conscience. The object of Interlocutory Injunction is to protect plaintiff against the injury by reason of violation of his right and relief by way of interlocutory remedy. Injunction is granted to mitigate the risk of injustice to plaintiff during pendency of Civil proceeding.  Generally, interlocutory remedy by way of grant of injunction is intended to preserve and maintain in status quo rights of parties and to protect plaintiff, being the initiator of the action against incursion of his right and for which there is no appropriate compensation being qualified in term of damages. Basic principle of grant of an order of injunction is to assess the right and need of plaintiff as against that of defendant and it is duty incumbent upon Law Courts to determine as to where the balance lies.

Following are certain specific considerations in the matter of grant of interlocutory injunction, the basic being non-expression of opinion as to  the merit of the matter by Court, since the issue of grant of injunction, usually, is at the earliest possible stage so far as the time frame is concerned. The other considerations which ought to weigh with the Court hearing the petition for grant of injunctions are as below:

i.	Protect the plaintiff's interest for violation of his rights, though, however, having regard to the injury that may be suffered by the defendants by reason therefore;

ii.	Court while dealing with injunction matter ought not to ignore the factum of strength of one party's case being stronger than the others.

iii.	The issue is to be looked at from the point of view as to whether on refusal  of injunction plaintiff would suffer irreparable loss and injury keeping in  view the strength of the party's case;

iv.	Balance of convenience or inconvenience ought to be considered as an important requirement even if there is a serious question or prima facie case in  support of the grant;

A good prima facie case means a case where plaintiff has a fair question to raise at the trial and the suit is not likely to fail on a technical flaw.

19. Point formulated is now being approached and answered. On resolving the point Judicial Authorities referred to from Bar shall be, also, taken into consideration.

20. Section 21 of the Act of 1940 enshrines that registration of a Trade Mark in respect of any goods shall give to that person the exclusive right to use trade mark in relation to those goods. From a reading of section 21 it pre-eminently came to light that registration of a Trade Mark in respect of any goods confers the exclusive right to use the Trade Mark in relation to those goods. Plaintiff-appellant on 26-5-1977 registered Trade Mark under Reg No. 13549 in Class 9 in respect of Cameras. Cinecameras, Electro-photographic apparatus, Electronic Calculating machines and all other goods belonging to International Class 9. Defendant-respondent, on the other hand, filed a petition for registration of Trade Mark under No. 85977 in Class 9 on 10-6-2004. In the petition registration was sought in respect of goods in Class 9, Television, VCD. Two-in-one but registration did not reach to its finality. Defendant-respondent asserted that its petition for registration of Trade Mark had been provisionally accepted for registration by Authority. Plaintiff-appellant's Trade Mark is "CANON". Defendant-respondent, also, sought registration of Trade Mark "CANON", of course, with logo. In the teeth of law engrafted in section 21 of The Act of 1940 no right has been conferred upon defendant-respondent for using Trade Mark "CANON" in respect of their goods i.e. Television, VCD and Two-in-one. Defendant-Respondent having not been proprietor of Trade Mark or registered user till today it is not at all entitled to use a Mark identical with the Mark of plaintiff-appellant and by the use of Trade Mark "CANON", by defendant-respondent, Trade Mark of plaintiff-appellant appears to have been infringed. In case of infringement of Trade Mark there will be resemblances and the controversy demands solution by comparing striking resemblances. A careful comparison and examination of Trade Mark "CANON" registered in the year 1977 in favour of plaintiff-appellant and user of Trade Mark "CANON" by defendant-respondent in their goods i.e. Television, VCD and Two-in-one, demonstrates that Trade Mark of defendant-respondent "CANON" got absolute similarity and identity with Trade Mark "CANON" registered in favour of plaintiff-appellant in the year 1977.

21. Strenuous argument has been advanced from the side of defendant-respondent that there had not been any registration certificate from Authority in favour of plaintiff-appellant in respect of Television and latter got no right to file suit against defendant-respondent as per provision of sections 20(1) and 21 of The Act of 1940.

22. Petition presented by defendant-respondent for registration of Trade Mark in Class 9 manifests that Television, VCD and Two-in-one had been subject matters of registration. It has, thus, been admitted by defendant-respondent that Television is, also included in Class 9 under Fourth Schedule of Trade Mark Rules. Since Trade Mark "CANON" in favour of plaintiff-appellant is registered in Class 9, Television, thus, stood included in Class 9. It does not lie in the mouth of defendant-respondent that Television is not registered in Class 9 under Fourth Schedule of Trade Mark Rules, 1963 in favour of plaintiff-appellant.

23. In resolving war of words, Judicial Authorities referred to from the side of plaintiff-appellant may profitably be looked.

24. In Kabushiki Kaisha Toshiba (also trading as Toshiba Corporation) vs Ch Muhammad Altaf (trading as Murad Industries (Regd) and another (Supra), Trade Mark 'TOSHIBA' sought to be registered by applicants is the same as opponent's name and their world famous Trade Mark 'TOSHIBA'. The goods for which applicants sought to obtain registration of 'TOSHIBA' viz Electric fans (all kinds), are same goods or goods of the same description for which opponents have obtained registration of the word 'TOSHIBA' and hence the use and registration by applicants was likely to cause confusion and deception in the Trade. It has been held:

The respondent had shown no reason tenable at law to pick up an invented word of foreign firm enjoying inside the country and outside a reputation for electric goods of various descriptions. It is registered in this, country as such. In this background, the adoption of the said trade mark phonetically in respect of electric fans is, thus, bound to create likelihood of confusion and deception to the consumers of such goods. Hence, it is against public interest to register such a Trade Mark.

25. In Shafquat Haider and others vs M Al-Amin, (Supra) Civil Appeal by Special Leave arose out of a temporary injunction matter in respect of use of a Trade name "Ciproco Computers" by respondent which is similar to Trade name "Ciproco Computers Ltd." by appellant. It was alleged that respondent by practicing deception and creating confusion by close similarity between the two names and also by misrepresentation already enticed away the appellant's company's customers while application for winding-up is pending and in these circumstances, temporary injunction was sought to restrain respondents from using trade name "Ciproco Computers" which is similar to appellant's company's name, "Ciproco Computers; Ltd". High Court Division came to hold that there is a gulf of difference between Ciproco Computers and Ciproco Computers Ltd which is the name of Appellant No. 3, a Company of which respondent No. 1 is Managing Director. Appellate Division held:

Here we find not only the case of close similarity between the two names likely to create confusion in the minds of the customers, both existing and intending, but, also, we find that respondent No. 1 took definite steps to entice away customers from the company to his private business. In the circumstances, respondent No. 1 should be restrained from doing so. In coming to the decision, Appellate Division took into stock a good number of Judicial Authorities of Foreign Jurisdiction such as Hendrils vs Montagu Ch D (17), 638; The National Bank of India vs The National Bank of Insore, AIR 1923 Born 119; Simatul Chemical Industries Ltd vs Cibatul Ltd. AIR 1978 Guj, 216; Exxon Corporation vs Exxon Insurance Consultants International Ltd. All ER (1981) Vol. 2 page 495; Turton vs Turton 42 Ch Division, 128; Office Cleaning Services Ltd vs West Minister Window and General Cleaners Ltd RPC Vol 62-63 page 39; KM Multani vs Paramount Talkies, AIR 1942 Bom 119.

The application for injunction was allowed. Respondent No. 1 was restrained from using the trade name "Ciproco Computers" till disposal of winding-up petition.

26. In Nasir Malik Nasir Soap Factory vs Md Anwar Hossain, Executive Officer, Commander Soap Factory (Supra) respondent as plaintiff laid a suit for perpetual injunction against appellant restraining the defendant and his employees and representatives from using Trade Mark and Copyright similar to that of plaintiff in toilet bath soap produced by defendant. In the suit plaintiff prayed for temporary injunction in the line of relief sought in the suit. It has been laid down:

Plaintiff prima facie being owner and earlier user of Trade Mark is entitled to restrain the defendant by an order of temporary injunction.

Shafquat Haider vs Md Al-Amin (Supra) has been relied upon in the case.

27. In Universal Pharmaceutical Ltd and another vs Social Marketing Company and others (Supra) plaintiff-respondent Social Marketing Company, which is a registered company under The Company's Act of 1913, started marketing life drug with name and Trade Mark "Orsaline" since the year 1983. Appellant Universal Pharmaceutical Ltd which is a Private Limited Company on the basis of provisional registration obtained on 5-8-1993, started marketing and selling life drug with the name and Trade Mark "Oralsaline" from the last part of 1994. High Court Division taking into consideration Shafquat Haider vs M Al-Amin and another (Supra), KM Multani vs Paramount Talkies of India Ltd AIR 1942 Bombay 241, Modi Sugar Mills Limited, through Managing Director & Proprietors Modi Vanaspati Manufac turfing Co vs Tata Oil Mills Co Ltd Bombay, AIR (30) 1943 Lahore 196 (204), Zenith Laboratory vs British Drug Homes, 20 DLR 1171 and Mount Mettur Pharmaceuticals vs Dr A Wander, 'AIR 1977 Madras 105 (107) held:

Phonetically and visually also the marks "Orsaline" and "Oralsaline" invite confusion and deception among the customers and since the products are life drugs, more consideration needs be given.

Appellant cannot be allowed to run business, marketing and selling its product "Oralsaline" as there is impending and continuous chance of deception and confusion, which may occur every time while purchasing the said life-drug by the half educated and not educated people of this country and balance of convenience and inconvenience also is found in favour of the plaintiff-respondent.

High Court Division did not find any illegality committed by Lower Court in granting ad-interim injunction in favour of plaintiff Social Marketing Company and order of ad-interim injunction was maintained. Judgment pronounced by High Court Division was, also, maintained by Appellate Division in Civil Appeal No. 438 of 1997 carried by defendants-petitioners Universal Pharmaceutical Ltd and another vs Social Marketing Company 2 MLR (AD) 201 = 50 DLR (AD) 92.

28. In Abdul Mannan Miah vs Md Salaiman Miah (Supra) Plaintiff, Proprietor of Zakir Shop Factory on laying suit for permanent injunction prayed for an order of temporary injunction restraining defendant from producing and distributing soap containing Trade Mark "Ghari" which was being used by plaintiff since long but defendant with full knowledge of the fact that "Ghari" and clock device has acquired fame and reputation through Bangladesh, with a view to capitalise on such good-will and reputation of plaintiff in respect of plaintiff's Trade Mark "Ghari" and clock device, started producing and distributing soap by using similar Trade Mark "Ghadi" and device which is similar and identical to "Ghari" and clock device of plaintiff thus encroaching upon rights of plaintiff-defendant on presentation of written objection against petition for temporary injunction took stand that defendant applied to Trade Mark Registry for registration of their Trade Mark "Ghadi" and defendant was producing soap with Trade Mark "Ghadi" since 18-7-1999 and if defendant gets registration the same would be effective from 18-7-1999. Learned Judge of High Court Division compared covers of soaps using Trade Mark "Ghari" and "Ghadi" and he could not find any significant differences and held:

Pendency of an application for registration before Registrar of Trade Marks or even granting of a provisional certificate of registration of mark does not debar a civil Court, in a suit for infringement of a trade mark, from passing an order of temporary injunction against use of mark where there is likelihood that mark would deceive or cause confusion in the minds of unwary purchasers.

In pronouncing Judicial verdict learned Judge took into stock Nasir Miah, Malik Nasir Soap Factory vs Md Anwar Hussain, Executive Officer, Commander Soap Factory Ltd (Supra), Shafquat Haider vs M Al-Amin and another (Supra), Universal Pharmaceutical Ltd vs Social Marketing Company and others (Supra), Abdul jabbar vs Ahmed Jan PLD 1973 Karachi 289, Burneys Industrial and Commercial Co Ltd vs Rahman Match Works, PLD 1983 Karachi 357, Flowerdale vs Hale Electric (1949) 66 RPC 33 and AR Gonga Dhara and Co Nirmal vs Firm of Police Mallaih Rajeswar and Co and others, AIR 1962 AP 510.

29. In Sunil Kumar Das vs Canon Kabushiki Kaisha (Supra) appellant Sunil Kumar Das laid an application in Class 25 in respect of hosiery goods for registration of their mark "CANON" against which First-respondent Canon Kabushiki Kaisha laid an opposition stating, inter alia, that since the inception of their business the opponents adopted the word "CANON" and the 'LOGO' and adoption of a deceptively similar Trade Mark by appellant is not honest and appellant has dishonestly adopted the word "CANON" with malafide intention to trade unfairly upon the worldwide reputation of the opponents and they took the stand that the goods bearing the same and similar trade mark, i.e. "CANON", are likely to create confusion and deception in the minds of the people and the products would indicate that such goods originate from none but respondent No. 1 it has been held:

One who had designed or used the trade mark first is entitled to claim proprietorship thereof, unless subsequently he has abandoned the same and some other person has obtained rights to use the same in the manner known to and recognised by law.

It has been further laid down:

The appellant's selection of the mark was made with the intention to deceive and cause confusion, and we should not hesitate to hold that the use of the mark is likely to deceive or cause confusion.

It has been, also, held:

Adoption of the mark by the appellant is dishonest and malafide.

In conclusion it has been laid down:

The interest of the original owner of the mark must be protected and the applicant-appellant must not be allowed to reap the benefit of the world famous mark of the respondent No. 1.

30. Principles emerged from Judicial  Authorities manifestly demonstrate that one who had got registration and used the Trade Mark first is entitled to claim proprietorship  and also got the right to use Trade Mark and use of the said Trade Mark by another which is likely to deceive or cause confusion in the minds of the customers cannot be allowed and the person or company in whose favour a Trade Mark was registered earlier is to be protected with the arms of law, one arm of law being injunction and a person/company is to be graced with an order of injunction.

31. This drives me to the Judicial Authorities referred to from the side of defendant-respondent.

32. In Messrs Modi Sugar Mills Limited through Managing Director and Proprietors, Modi Vanaspati Manufacturing Covs Tata Oil Mills Co Ltd Bombay (Supra) plaintiff alleged that Trade Mark "Cocogem" had been used for 19 years and they had, therefore, acquired a Trade Mark in the name 'Cocogem' but defendants' got Trade Mark 'Kotogem' which was similar to the name and mark of plaintiff's product "Cocogem" and was an ingenious imitation thereof and that not only the illiterate and unwary purchasers but even educated persons were apt to be deceived in purchasing "Kotogem" for "Cocogem."

It has been held by Sale J:

A mere phonetic similarity might deceive the unwary incautious customer, but such a possibility is not sufficient to justify an injunction in a passing off action. The probability of deception in case of average customer exercising ordinary caution is, in my view, practically excluded by the striking dissimilarities between the two products.

33. In the case in hand defendant-respondent's mark "CANON" is exactly like the mark "CANON" of plaintiff-appellant which is being used by plaintiff-appellant for the last many years. Plaintiff got Trade Mark "CANON" registered in the year 1977 and defendant-respondent only processed Trade Mark "CANON" for registration but was not yet registered. This Judicial authority is of no assistance to defendant-respondent.

34. In Dhaka Match Factory Ltd vs Bangladesh Match Company Ltd (Supra), plaintiff Dhaka Match Factory Ltd has been manufacturing and selling safety matches for last twenty years under Trade Mark Horse Brand. Bangladesh Match Company had been alleged to have infringed plaintiffs registered Trade Mark by manufacturing safety matches and using the mark of Horse with the design, appearance and general set-up so nearly resembling plaintiff's Trade Mark that is likely to deceive or cause confusion in course of trade and to unwary consumers. It has been held:

In an action for infringement of a registered Trade Mark the Court must of necessity enquire whether defendant's Trade Mark is identical or deceptively similar to plaintiffs Trade Mark.

It has been further held:

From the pleadings of the parties and Annexures submitted by them and examination of the plaintiffs trade mark as a whole and not merely a particular part of it, namely, the Horse mark the defendant's label does not appear to be identical to the plaintiff's trade mark and there is no confusion at least among the dealers of safety matches, as to the respective identities of the two contending marks.

35. In the case in hand on a careful examination and comparison of the two marks "CANON", it indicates that the two marks of plaintiff-appellant and defendant-respondent are absolutely identical, and, as such, it cannot be at all suggested that there would be no confusion amongst consumers, dealers and customers of goods in Class 9, not to speak of Television, VCD and Two-in-one as is being sought to be registered in Class 9 by defendant-respondent. Cited decision cannot, thus, ensure any benefit to defendant-respondent.

36. In Consolidated Foods Corporation vs Brandon & Co Private Ltd (Supra) respondent Company filed three applications for registration of the mark consisting of the word "Monarch" in Classes 29, 30 and 32 respectively. Petitioner Corporation filed separate notices of opposition to each of these applications. Grounds of opposition set out in the said notices were that by reason of use of the word "Monarch" by petitioners prior to 1951 the use of said word by respondents was likely to deceive or cause confusion, and, therefore, registration would be contrary to provision of section II(a) of Trade and Merchandise Marks Act, 1958. Petition was allowed and order passed by Joint Registrar of Trade Marks on the applications filed by respondent Company for registration of mark "Monarch" stood set aside and applications were dismissed.

This Judicial decision is, also, of no assistance to defendant-respondent.

37. In SM Taufiq vs National Biscuit Co New York (Supra) the dispute between the parties was in respect of registration of "Nabisco" under clause 30 in respect of biscuits, bread, cake and confectionery. Appellants SM Taufiq and Company filed application on 13-8-1951 for registration of Trade Mark "Nabisco" proposed to be used in respect of articles to be manufactured in their factory. Respondent National Biscuit Company on 3-3-1954 filed an application for registration of Trade Mark "Nabisco" in clause 30 of the above mentioned goods and, thereafter, they opposed registration of trade mark "Nabisco" at the instance of appellants on the ground that "Nabisco" was first adapted by them in USA in 1901. Taking into account that respondents' Trade Mark was used in other parts of the world and they got it registered in 1944 in India but they never bothered about Pakistan market and the import of foreign biscuit is now prohibited for a long time and there is no likelihood in its introduction in the near future Learned Judge of Karachi High Court held:,

It is not possible for him to hold that the registration of Trade Mark "Nabisco" will in any way cause prejudice to public interest.

38. In the case in hand, case goods and articles of plaintiff-appellant are being very much marketed in Bangladesh and not that it is not being marketed in Bangladesh. Judicial decision, also, cannot bring any fruit of defendant-respondent.

39. It has already been posited that plaintiff-appellant's Trade Mark "CANON" had been registered as far back as in 1977 and defendant-respondent had only presented a petition for registration of Trade Mark in respect of Television, VCD, Two-in-one in Class 9 of Fourth Schedule to Trade Mark Rules, 1963 only 3-6-2004 and the proposed Trade Mark "CANON" is yet to be registered.

40. It has already been voiced that on a close examination of registered Trade Mark "CANON" of plaintiff-appellant and proposed Trade Mark "CANON" of defendant-respondent it transpires that registered Trade Mark "CANON" of plaintiff-appellant is visually and phonetically similar to the proposed Trade Mark "CANON" of defendant-respondent.

<u>41. Since plaintiff's-appellant's Trade Mark "CANON" had been registered earlier as far back as in the year 1977 and defendant-respondent's proposed Trade Mark "CANON" is just in the process of being registered, plaintiff-appellant is legally entitled to demand proprietorship of the goods in Class 9 which, also, includes Television and, as such, plaintiff-appellant got the legal right to have its Trade Mark "CANON" protected through court of law by way of an injunction.</u>

42. Learned Additional District Judge found that no Trade Mark is registered in the name of plaintiff-appellant in respect of Television and no conflicting Trade Mark was found in the record except the Trade Mark of defendant-respondent. Learned Additional District Judge failed to construe import of documents and papers as well as pleadings of plaintiff-appellant and defendant-respondent. Learned Additional District Judge misdirected himself in his approach in resolving legal battle in respect of grant or refusal of injunction. Learned Additional District Judge did not follow specific considerations regulating grant of injunction in favour of plaintiff-appellant, such as, protection of plaintiff-appellant's right in respect of its Trade Mark "CANON" which is being invaded by defendant-respondent, factum of strength of plaintiff-appellant which is stronger than defendant-respondent, sufferance of irreparable loss by plaintiff-appellant in the event of non-grant of injunction, actuality of strong prima facie case and balance of convenience in favour of plaintiff-appellant and overall fact and circumstances of the whole episode. Findings reached by learned Additional District Judge that plaintiff-appellant got no good prima facie case and balance of convenience and inconvenience is not in favour of plaintiff and plaintiff would not suffer loss if injunction is not granted in its favour and defendant would suffer irreparable loss in the event of grant of temporary injunction against it is vitiated by grave error and those findings are wholly unsustainable and demand overthrow.

<u>43. Taking into stock pleading of parties, documents placed, materials brought on record and legal aspect involved and fact and circumstances of the case, I am of this considered and dispassionate view that plaintiff-appellant would suffer irreparable loss and injury if defendant-respondent is not restrained by way of an injunction in using, applying and administering its proposed Trade Mark "CANON". I am, also, of this conviction that plaintiff-appellant got strong prima facie case in support of being graced with an order of injunction and balance of convenience and inconvenience, also, is in favour of plaintiff-appellant and against defendant-respondent.</u>

44. The prime point formulated stands resolved in the epithet that plaintiff-appellant can be entitled with an order of Temporary Injunction on overturning adjudication handed over by Learned Additional District Judge whereby petition for temporary injunction presented by plaintiff-appellant stood rejected.

<u>45. Corollary thereof is that First Miscellaneous Appeal got merit. It succeeds. Appeal is allowed. Judgment dated 12-4-2006 recorded by learned Additional District Judge who has been, also, functioning as Bankruptcy Court, Dhaka in Title Suit No. 11 of 2006 stands set aside/quashed. Plaintiff's petition for temporary injunction under Order XXXIX, rules 1 and 2 read with section 151 of The Code of Civil Procedure is allowed. Defendant-respondent Canon Electronic Industries Ltd is restrained by an order of Temporary Injunction from directly or indirectly manufacturing, importing, using, selling, marketing their products under Trade Mark "CANON" on their products along with deceptively packaging, colour scheme design, get-up, device as adopted by plaintiff-appellant in respect of goods under Class 9 of Fourth Schedule of Trade Marks Rules, 1963 and International Class 9 as shown in Schedule "B" to the plaint as well as petition for temporary Injunction or any other colour, scheme, get-up, style confusing similar to that used by plaintiff or any other word, mark or marks and packaging which may conflict with plaintiff-appellant's Trade Mark as shown in Schedule "B" to the plaint as well as petition for Temporary injunction and from using deceptively similar company name "Canon Electronics Industries Ltd" till disposal of the Suit.</u>

46. Since destiny of First Miscellaneous Appeal is decided in favor of plaintiff-appellant allowing petition for temporary injunction, connected Civil Rule No. 412 (FM)/2006, also, stands disposed of in favor of plaintiff-appellant.

No costs.

End.

AKM Asiful Haque, Advocate—For the Petitioners.
