full_judgment:
JBM Hassan J: In this Rule Nisi, the petitioners have challenged entertainment of the Artha jari Case No. 170 of 2007 and continuation thereof before the Artha Rin Adalat No. 4, Dhaka arises out of the judgment and decree dated 12-5-2003 (decree draw on 31-8-2003) passed by the High Court Division in First Appeal No. 432 of 1996 decreeing Title Suit No. 106 of 1993 for Taka 3,57,46,721.78 with simple interest @ 14% till realization of the decretal amount.

2. Pertinent facts necessary for disposal of the Rule are as follows:—

The respondents No. 2, Rupali Bank Ltd. Hazaribagh Branch, Dhaka represented by its Branch Manager (shortly, the Bank), as plaintiff, instituted Title Suit No. 106 of 1993 on 28-7-1993 before the Artha Rin Adalat No. 4, Dhaka (shortly, the Adalat) impleading the petitioners as defendants for realization of loan money amounting to Taka 3,57,86,721.79 (inclusive of interest till 24-4-1993) by selling the mortgaged properties as mentioned in the schedule of the plaint. The plaint case, in short, is that the petitioner No. 2 has been maintaining a current account with the plaintiff Bank since 1983 in the name of his proprietary firm, the petitioner No. 1 and was enjoying credit facilities from the Bank. The plaintiff Bank sanctioned loan in favour of the petitioners on various heads within the period from 12-7-1989 to 28-8-1990 for the business purpose, To secure the said loan the Bank took different charge documents, registered deed of mortgage as well as registered power of Attorney in respect of the schedule property. Eventually, the liability stood at Taka 3,57,86,721.79 as on 24-4-1993 and that in spite of repeated demand, the defendants failed to make the payment and hence, the suit.

3. The defendants contested the suit by filing written statement denying plaintiff's claim. Ultimately, the Adalat by judgment and decree dated 12-10-1996 decreed the suit in part for Taka 1,10,00,000 and accordingly preliminary decree was drawn up on 19-10-1996. Against the aforesaid judgment and decree, the plaintiff Bank preferred First Appeal No. 432 of 1996 before the High Court Division. After hearing, the appeal has been allowed by judgment and decree dated 12-5-2003 (decree drawn up on 31-8-2003) for Taka 3,57,46,721.78 with simple interest @ 14% with a direction that the decretal dues be paid within 12 months failing which the decree shall be made final and the plaintiff Bank shall be able to realize the dues by selling out the mortgaged property through execution case.

4. Against the aforesaid judgment and decree the petitioner filed Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 1287 of 2003 before the Hon'ble Appellate Division and after hearing, it was dismissed by judgment and Order dated 24-5-2007 affirming the judgment and decree of the High Court Division.

5. Thereafter, on 2-8-2007 the decree holder Bank filed Artha Jari Case No. 170 of 2007 before the Artha Rin Adalat No. 4, Dhaka (the Adalat) to execute the aforementioned decree impleading the petitioners as judgment-debtors. The petitioners on 11-10-2007 filed an application before the executing Court praying for rejecting the execution case on the ground that there being no final decree as per judgment of the Court, the execution case cannot proceed. The said application was rejected on 30-3-2008. On the other hand, the decree holder Bank also filed an application in the original suit (Annexure-G to the writ petition) on 19-2-2008 before the Adalat praying to draw up a final decree and another application was also filed to get back the original documents (Exhibits) and that both the applications are still pending and till now no final decree has been drawn up. In the circumstances, the petitioners again filed an application on 20-4-2008 praying to dismiss the Artha Jari Case on the ground that there is no final decree as per judgment of the High Court Division and, as such, the execution case is premature.

6. In the meantime, the Adalat had been proceeding with the execution case and fixed the case on 26-4-2008 for selling the mortgaged property in auction. On the day of auction, no bidder having been found in the auction process, the decree holder Bank made a prayer for issuing title certificate under section 33(7) of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003 (shortly, the Ain, 2003). In this backdrop, the petitioners have challenged entertainment of the execution case and continuation thereof, by filing writ petition before this Court under its constitutional jurisdiction, obtained the present Rule and interim Order of stay.

7. The Bank as the respondent No. 2 has been contesting the Rule by filing an affidavit-in-opposition controverting the statements as made in the writ petition. This respondent also contends that section 5 (4) of the Ain, 2003 provides that except the decree of foreclosure suit, the other decrees passed by the Artha Rin Adalat become final with the sale of mortgaged property. The present suit is not a foreclosure suit. It is a suit for recovery of the bank loan by selling the mortgaged property and, as such, no final decree is required as per section 5 (4) of the Ain, 2003. Therefore, the Rule does not have any merit and, as such, it is liable to be discharged.

8. Mr AKM Asiful Haque, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioners after placing the writ petition and all its annexures, submits that the High Court Division passed the judgment and decree in the preliminary form with a direction that on failure to make the payment within 12 months, the decree shall be made final to realize the decretal dues by selling the mortgaged property in execution case and the said judgment has been affirmed by the Appellate Division. But the decree holder Bank without having any final decree as per requirement of the aforesaid judgment and decree, put the decree into execution. Therefore, the execution case on the face of it premature and cannot proceed. He further submits that though the prevailing law is that all the Artha decrees, except the decree of foreclosure suit, do not require to be made final decree for execution but in this particular case the Court has specifically required final decree for execution. Therefore, the present execution case cannot proceed without final decree and thus, the execution case on the face of it premature for want of final decree. In view of the facts, the Artha jari case should be interfered by this Court under its constitutional jurisdiction.

9. In reply to the aforesaid submissions, Mr Md Imam Hasan, the learned Advocate, appearing for the respondent No. 2 submits that the judgment and decree was passed on 12-5-2003 and that on 1st May, 2003 the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003 introduced the provision that except the foreclosure suit in the case of simple Artha decree, no final decree is required and on the basis of the preliminary decree, the execution case will be proceeded and the preliminary decree would be final after selling the mortgaged property. In view of prevailing legal position, the decree holder Bank does not required any final decree to execute the preliminary decree of the Artha Rin Suit and, as such, the Adalat is proceeding rightly with the execution case having the sanction of law. He further submits that just 11 days before the Judgment, the law was enacted expressing provision that no final decree is required and that the latest legal position (as amended on 1-5-2003) having not been brought to the notice of the High Court Division, the preliminary decree was passed on 12-5-2003 requiring final decree. Thus, the decision of the High Court Division being per-incuriam, the executing Court is not bound to follow the same in proceeding with the execution case by the final decree. In this regard, the learned Advocate refers to the case of Municipal Corporation of Delhi vs Gurnam Kaur reported in AIR 1989 (SC) 38.

10. We have gone through the writ petition, the affidavit-in-opposition, relevant papers as annexed to the writ petition and also the legal provisions as well as the cited decision.

11. It appears that the execution case has been initiated to execute the judgment and decree dated 12-5-2003 (preliminary decree drawn up on 31-8-2003) passed by the High Court Division in First Appeal No. 432 of 1996 decreeing the Title Suit No. 106 of 1993 for Taka 3,57,46,721.78 under the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003. Relevant ordering portion of the said judgment runs as follows:—

"And it is further ordered and decreed that the plaintiff Bank is hereby entitled to get Taka 3,57,46,721.78 from the defendant together with 14% simple interest thereon per annum to be calculated from the date of filing of the suit till realization of the decretal amount with 12(twelve) months  failing which, the decree shall be made final and the plaintiff Bank shall be able to  realize the dues by selling out the mortgaged property through execution case."

12. Ultimately the aforesaid judgment and decree has been affirmed by the Hon'ble Appellate Division by the judgment and Order dated 24-5-2007 passed in Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 1287 of 2003.

13. On the basis of the aforesaid judgment and decree, the decree holder Bank has filed an application for drawing up final decree. But the said final decree has not yet been drawn up as it is evidenced from the Annexure-G(2) to the writ petition.

14. In view of the facts, the question now arises as whether the executing Court can entertain the execution case to execute a preliminary decree as per the judgment and preliminary decree of the Court and wherein no final decree has yet been drawn up.

15. The Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003 came into force on 1-5-2003 providing the provisions exempting to make final decree for execution of the Artha decree except the decree passed in foreclosure suit. In order to appreciate the legal position, the relevant provisions are quoted herein below:—

“৫। আদালতের একক এখতিয়ারঃ

(১) -----

(২) এই আইনের অধীন আর্থিক প্রতিষ্ঠান, স্থাবর সম্পত্তি জামানত স্বরুপ বন্ধক গ্রহণ পূর্বক প্রদত্ত ঋণের বিপরীতে উক্ত বন্ধকী স্থাবর সম্পত্তির বিক্রয় (Sale) বা নিষ্ক্রিয় সমাপ্তির (Forcelosure) উদ্দেশ্যে The Transfer of Property Act, 1882 (Act, No. IV) of 1882 এর Section 67 অধীন এবং The Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 (Act No. V of 1908) 43 Order XXXIV এর বিধান অনুযায়ী কোন বন্ধকী মামলা (Mortgage suit) দায়ের করিতে চাহিলে, উক্ত মামলাও এই আইনের অধীন প্রতিষ্ঠিত অর্থ ঋণ আদালতেই দায়ের করিতে হইবে; এবং এইরুপ ক্ষেত্রে The Code of Civil Procedure ১৯০৮ এর বিধান সমূহ আইনের বিধান সমূহের সহিত, যতদুর সম্ভব সমন্বয়ের মাধ্যমে প্রযোজ্য হইবে।

(৩) উপ-ধারা (২) এর অধীন আর্থিক প্রতিষ্ঠান কর্তৃক দায়েরকৃত মামলা নিষ্ক্রিয় সমাপ্তির (Forcelosure) উদ্দেশ্যে একটি বন্ধকী মামলা (Mortgage suit) হইলে, কেবলমাত্র সেইক্ষেত্রে আদালত কর্তৃক প্রদত্ত ডিক্রি প্রাথমিক ডিক্রি হইবে (Preliminary decree) এবং অন্যান্য সকল ক্ষেত্রে ঋণ অনাদায়ার্থে দায়েরকৃত মামলায় আদালত কর্তৃক প্রদত্ত ডিক্রি চুড়ান্ত ডিক্রি হইবে।

(৪) The Transfer of Property Act, 1882  অথবা বর্তমানে প্রচলিত অন্য কোন আইনে বিপরীত যাহা কিছুই থাকুক না কেন, উপ-ধারা (৩) এর অধীন বন্ধকী মামলা ব্যতিরেকে এই আইনের অধীন দায়েরকৃত কোন মামলায় আদালত কর্তৃক প্রদত্ত ডিক্রি বাদী আর্থিক প্রতিষ্ঠানের পক্ষে নিস্ক্রিয় সমাপ্তির (Foreclosure) প্রাথমিক ডিক্রি হিসাবে গণ্য হইবে এবং ঋনের বিপরীতে বাদীর অনুকুলে বন্ধকী স্থাবর সম্পত্তি ডিক্রির ধারাবাহিকতায়  নিলাম বিক্রয় হওয়া মাত্রই উক্ত প্রাথমিক ডিক্রি চুড়ান্ত হিসাবে গণ্য হইবে এবং বিক্রয় চুড়ান্ত ও ক্রয় বৈধ গণ্য হইবে এবং অতঃপর উক্ত সম্পত্তি পুনরুদ্ধার করিবার কোনরুপ অধিকার (Right to redeem) বিবাদী দায়ীকের থাকিবে না।

(৫) (১১) -----

16. On the basis of the aforesaid legal pro-vision, the question earlier arose as to whether final decree is required to execute the Artha Rin decree which was filed for realization of loan money by selling the mortgaged property. In this context law has already been settled by the High Court Division as well as our Apex Court deciding that except the decrees passed in mortgage suits for foreclosure, the decrees passed in other mortgage suits do not require to be made final for the purpose of starting the execution case. In this regard in the case of KM Mozahid Islam vs Bangladesh reported in VI ADC (2009) 865 their Lordships held as under:—

"It appears from the prayer portion, quoted above, that the 'respondent bank has prayed for personal decree in preliminary form and further prayed for sale of the mortgaged property in case of default of the part of the judgment debtor in satisfying the decree, to be passed. Thus the suit as framed and filed cannot be said to attract section- 5(3) of the Ain but the same attracts section 5(4) of the Air, and therefore a decree passed in preliminary form after sale of the mortgage property automatically becomes a final decree. Thus we do not find any substance in the submission of the learned Advocate that the decree, being passed in preliminary form, cannot be put into execution for realization of decreetal amount by sale of the mortgage property, before making the decree final, and hence the decree is bad in the eye of law."

17. Besides the aforesaid decision, in a good number of cases the High Court Division including this Bench also held that except mortgage the decree of foreclosure suit the other Artha decrees do no required any final decree though it is obtained for realization of loan money by selling the mortgaged property.

18. In view of aforesaid established principle that final decree is not required to execute the Artha decree, the question now arises whether in this particular case in our hand, the Adalat can proceed to execute the decree of the High Court Division passed in the form of preliminary decree.

19. It appears that in this case, the Adalat (executing Court) is proceeding the execute a particular judgment and decree. Therefore, the executing Court (Adalat) has to be remained confined within the periphery of this particular judgment and decree and that operating portion of the judgment and decree are as follows:—

"And it is further ordered and decreed that the plaintiff Bank is hereby entitled to get Taka 3,57,46,721.78 from the defendant together with 14% simple interest thereon per annum to be calculated from the date of filing of the suit till realization of the decretal amount with 12(twelve) months failing which, the decree shall be made  final and the plaintiff Bank shall be able to  realize the dues by selling out the  mortgaged property through execution Case."

<u>20. Though legal position is that Artha decree except foreclosure suits, does not require final decree for execution case but since the present judgment itself requires final decree before execution. Therefore, the executing Court must have final decree for execution of the decree and, as such, without final decree, the execution case appears to us premature. In view of the above, the Adalat cannot entertain any execution case to execute the aforesaid decree in the preliminary form requiring final decree and, as such, continuation of the said execution case is unlawful apparent on the face of record without having any legal sanction.</u>

21. We have gone through the cited case as reported in AIR 1989 (SC) 38. The above referred case is regarding application of precedent in another case. A particular decision was made by the Court with the consent of parties and being in lack of some facts as well as on law. Subsequently, while the ratio decidendi was referred to another case, their Lordships held that Court is not bound to follow the decision per-incuriam inasmuch as the only thing in a judge's decision binding as an authority upon a subsequent judge, is the principle upon which the case was decided.

22. But the case before us appears that the judgment itself has required a final decree and, as such, the executing Court cannot proceed to execute the said decree unless the decree is made final. The Adalat is, therefore, bound to draw up final decree as per requirement of the judgment of the High Court Division. As such, the cited decision is not applicable in the case before us in view of its different facts and circumstances.

23. In view of above discussions, we are led to held that since the very judgment requires final decree, without such final decree the executing Court cannot entertain any execution proceeding. Therefore, the Adalat is proceeding with a premature decree without having any legal sanction and, as such, the proceeding of the Artha Jari Case is liable to be interfered. Thus, we find merit in this Rule.

24. In the result, the Rule is made absolute. Entertainment of the Artha Jari Case No. 170 of 2007 and continuation thereof before the Artha Rin Adalat No. 4, Dhaka is hereby declared to be without lawful authority and is of no legal effect.

25. Since it is evident that the decree-holder Bank has already filed an application praying to draw up final decree and it is now pending before the Adalat, the decree holder bank is at liberty to file a fresh execution case after obtaining the final decree.

26. The ad-interim order of stay stands vacated.

Communicate the judgment and Order to the respondent No. 1 expeditiously.

End.

case_source: (From the judgment and decree dated 10-3-2004 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 2622 of 1995).
full_judgment:
Nazmun Ara Sultana J : This Civil Appeal, by leave, is directed against the judgment and decree dated 10-3-2004 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 2622 of 1995 making the Rule absolute.

2. The present appellants, as plaintiffs, instituted Other Class Suit No. 123 of 1985 in the Court of the learned Subordinate Judge, Jamalpur for declaration of their title in the suit land. Their case, in short, is that the suit land comprising 1.80 acres out of total 2.87 acres of RoR Khatian Nos. 23, 25 and 26 and CS Khatian No. 20 of Sheikh Shadi mouza, Ps-Melandha, District-Jamalpur along with other land belonged to Bebuillah Sheikh the predecessor of the plaintiffs and Nabu Sheikh, Vadu Sheikh and Gendi and CS khatian was accordingly published. That Babuillah Sheikh died leaving 2 sons Nabu Sheikh and Vadu Sheikh and daughter Gendi as his heirs. Thereafter, Gendi died leaving brothers Nabu Sheikh and Vadu Sheikh. Nabu Sheikh and Vedu Sheikh were in possession of entire 2.87 acres of land. Nabu Sheikh died leaving behind daughter plaintiff No. 1, son. Ayub Ali-predecessor of plaintiff Nos. 2 to 8 and another son named Najimuddin-predecessor of the plaintiff Nos. 9 to 14. Vadu Sheikh died leaving behind 3 daughters and 3 sons, the plaintiff Nos. 15 to 19 and Salimuddin who died leaving behind plaintiff Nos. 20 to 26 as his heirs. Thus the plaintiffs inherited the suit property and enjoyed the suit property continuously for more than 12 years. In suit plot Nos. 384 and 386 the plaintiffs have their homestead and have been residing therein with their families. The plaintiffs have been possessing other lands in ejmali through cultivation. That during RoR operation the suit property was wrongly recorded and only 1.07 acres of land out of total 2.87 acres of land was recorded in Khatian No. 24 in the name of the predecessor of the plaintiffs and the suit land comprising 1.80 acres of land was erroneously recorded in the name of the defendants and thereby a cloud being created the plaintiffs instituted the suit for declaration of their title.

3. The defendant Nos. 1, 2 and 8 contested the suit by filing written statement. The material case of these defendants is that the entire 2.87 acres of land of the suit plots was made khas by the owners as the previous tenants defaulted in payment of rent and thereafter the said land was settled afresh in the name of different persons and the predecessor of the plaintiffs got settlement of 1.07 acres of land out of the suit plots and creating a new holding they paid rents for the same. That out of remaining 1.80 acres of land Bhajan Ali took settlement of 0.60 acre and possessed the same peacefully and after the death of Bhajan Ali his 3 sons, named, Azam, Miar and Nizam Ali owned that property. That Azam Ali sold his share to Hossain AM Miaruddin died leaving heirs. The RS Khatian was duly prepared in their names. That Yakub Ali took settlement of 0.60 acre of land and the record of right was duly prepared in his name. Yakub Ali died leaving Abdul Gafur and others as his heirs. Abdul Gafur subsequently died leaving defendant No. 1 Nowsher Ali and others as his. Nowsher Ali purchased 0.7½ acre of land by registered kabala dated 1-3-1973 from Kaser. Nazer Ali sold his share to defendant No. 1 Nowsher Ali and others by registered kabala dated 25-3-1975. Hafizuddin and others also sold their share to defendant No. 1 Nowsher Ali and others. Haji Fakir sold 0.08 acre of land to Suruj Ali the defendant No. 2. That Hossain Ali Fakir took settlement of the remaining 0.60 acre of land and possessed the same. After the death of Hossain Ali Fakir his heirs Newaz and others possessed that land. That Ayuzuddin son of Hossain Ali sold some land to Jamaluddin. Ahej Ali and others sold some land to Sahar Fakir the defendant No. 8. Thus these defendants have acquired the suit land and have been possessing the same. That the plaintiffs have filed this suit on false claim and, as such, it is liable to be dismissed.

4. The trial court, on consideration of the evidence adduced by both the parties, dismissed the suit by the judgment and decree dated 31-7-1993 making observation to the effect that though the plaintiffs have proved their title in the suit land but they could not prove their possession in the suit land and that the suit is also barred by limitation. Against this judgment and decree of the trial court the plaintiffs preferred Other Appeal No. 53 of 1993 before the learned District Judge, Jamalpur who, by the judgment and order dated 29-3-1995, allowed that appeal and set aside the judgment and decree of the trial court and decreed the suit declaring plaintiffs title in the suit land. The appellate court found that the plaintiffs had both title and possession in the suit land and the suit was not barred by limitation. Against this judgment and decree of the appellate court below the contesting defendants preferred the above mentioned Civil Revision No. 2622 of 1995 before the High Court Division and obtained Rule. A Division Bench of the High Court Division, after hearing both the parties, made that Rule absolute by setting aside the judgment and decree of the appellate court below and restoring those of the trial court by the impugned judgment and order. The High Court Division made observations to the effect that the plaintiffs could not prove their possession in the entire suit land and that the suit was barred by limitation.

5. Being aggrieved by this judgment and order of the High Court Division the plaintiffs preferred Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 508 of 2004 before this Division. This Division granted leave to consider the submissions of the learned Advocate-on-Record for the plaintiff-leave-petitioners to the effect that in this suit the evidence adduced by the plaintiffs proved sufficiently that the plaintiffs came to know about the wrong recording of the suit land in the record-of-right on 17-10-1985 only when they went to pay rent and there being no evidence to the contrary, the High Court Division erred in law without discussing and considering the evidence of the PWs in holding that by the evidence it has not been substantiated on what date the plaintiffs went to pay rent; that the High Court Division without discussing and considering the evidence on record has wrongly and illegally found that the plaintiffs could not prove their possession in the suit property while the appellate court below has elaborately and exhaustively discussed and considered the evidence on record and found that the plaintiffs are in possession of the suit land.

6. Mr Subrata Sana, the learned Advocate for the appellants has made submissions before us to the effect that in this suit both the trial court and the appellate court below, considering the facts, circumstances and the evidence on record, found that the plaintiffs have title in the suit land; that the trial court though found that the plaintiffs could not prove their possession in the suit land, but the appellate court below, on proper appreciation of the evidence adduced by both the parties, rightly found that the plaintiffs have been able to prove their possession in the suit land; but the High Court Division most arbitrarily and abruptly, without making any discussion of any evidence at all and without controverting the findings and decision of the appellate court below and also the trial court made observations to the effect that the plaintiffs could not prove their title and also possession in the suit land. The learned Advocate for the appellants has argued that the High Court Division committed wrong and also great injustice in making the above observation without making any discussion at all and without reversing the clear findings and decision of the appellate court below as to title and possession of the plaintiffs in the suit land and the clear decision of the trial court also as to title of the plaintiffs in the suit land. The learned Advocate has argued also that in this suit it is rather an admitted fact that the plaintiffs predecessors were the original owners of the suit land and the suit land was duly recorded in the CS khatian in the name of the plaintiffs predecessors; that the contesting defendants though have alleged that the predecessors of the plaintiffs defaulted in payment of rent and, as such, the original landlords took back the suit land from them and subsequently they settled the same with different persons including the predecessors-in-interest of the plaintiffs and the predecessors-in-interest of the defendants, but this defence case has not been substantiated at all by any sort of evidence; that both the trial court and the appellate court below, therefore, rightly found plaintiffs title in the suit land, but the High Court Division, ignoring this fact that the defendants could not adduce any evidence whatsoever before court to prove their defence case, most unreasonably and unjustly opined that the plaintiffs could not prove their title also in the suit land. The learned Advocate for the plaintiff-appellants have made submissions to the effect also that this suit is not barred by limitation also as the plaintiffs have proved by sufficient evidence that they knew about the wrong recording of the suit land on 17-10-1985 only and thereafter they filed this suit within a short time; that the appellate court below, on thorough examination and consideration of the evidence adduced by both the parties rightly found that the plaintiffs filed the suit for declaration of their title within the statutory period of limitation and, as such, the suit is not barred by limitation.

7. Mr Awlad Ali, the learned Senior Advocate for the defendant-respondents has made submissions supporting the impugned judgment and order of the High Court Division. The learned Senior Advocate has argued that the High Court Division though did not make elaborate discussion in the impugned judgment, but it examined and considered the evidence on record thoroughly and found rightly that the plaintiffs failed to prove their title and possession in the suit land and the suit is also barred by limitation. The learned Senior Advocate has contended that the findings and decision of the High Court Division being correct this appeal is liable to be dismissed.

8. We have considered the submissions of the learned Counsel of both the sides and gone through the impugned judgment and order of the High Court Division, those of the appellate court below and the trial court and also the evidence on record.

9. In this suit it is not disputed, rather admitted that the suit land originally belonged to the predecessors of the plaintiffs. In the CS khatian also the suit land was recorded in the name of the predecessors of the plaintiffs. The plaintiffs have claimed that they have acquired the suit land by way of inheritance from their predecessors the recorded owners of the land and have been possessing the same peacefully for more than 12 years. The contesting defendants though have pleaded a case to the effect that since the original tenants of the suit land defaulted in payment of rent the landlords took the entire 2.87 acres of land of the suit plots under their khas possession and subsequently the landlords settled those lands afresh with different persons including the predecessors of the plaintiffs and also the predecessors of the defendants, but this case of the defendants has not been substantiated at all by any evidence. Both the trial court and the appellate court below on consideration of the facts and circumstances and the evidence on record disbelieved this case of the contesting defendants and found plaintiffs title in the suit land. The trial court in his judgment made specific observation to the effect that the contesting defendants could not prove their alleged title in the suit land rather the plaintiffs have got title in the suit land. Against this clear observations and findings of the trial court the contesting defendants did not prefer any appeal or cross appeal. However, considering the evidence on record and the facts and circumstances we also, in agreement with the trial court and also the appellate court below, find that in this suit it has been well proved that the plaintiffs have title in the suit land.

10. As regards possession the trial court though found that the plaintiffs could not prove their possession in the suit land, but the appellate court below, on thorough examination and consideration of the evidence adduced by both the parties, found that the plaintiffs proved their possession also in the suit land. The High Court Division without discussing any evidence of any of the parties at all and without adverting to the findings and decision of the appellate court below and reversing those, and without giving any reasoning even of its own most arbitrarily made observation to the effect that the plaintiffs could not prove their possession in the entire suit property. However, we have examined the evidence adduced by both the parties.

11. It appears that in this suit the plaintiffs have examined 4 witnesses while the defendants have examined 3 witnesses. The PW 1 is the plaintiff No. 2 himself. This witness has deposed fully corroborating the plaintiffs case and has asserted also that the plaintiffs are in possession of the entire suit land. The PW 2 has deposed supporting the plaintiffs possession in the suit land. The PW 3 also has deposed supporting the plaintiffs possession in the suit land and has denied the defendants possession in the suit land. The PW 4 also has deposed stating that the plaintiffs have been possessing the suit land and that the defendants do not possess the suit land. On the other hand, the witnesses of the defendants side, namely, the DWs 2 and 3 though in their examination-in-chief has stated that the defendants are in possession of the suit land, but in course of cross-examination the DW 2 has stated that at present the defendants do not possess the suit land and the DW 3 has stated that at present none of the parties possessed the suit land. The above evidence of both the contesting parties coupled with the facts that the plaintiffs are the heirs of the admitted original owners of the suit land and there is no evidence to prove that plaintiffs predecessors title in the suit land was extinguished prove sufficiently that the plaintiffs are in possession of the suit land. The appellate court below on thorough analysis and consideration of the evidence adduced by both the parties and the facts and circumstances rightly found that the plaintiffs have been possessing the suit land.

12. The trial court though found that this suit, being not filed within 6 years from the date of the plaintiffs knowledge about recording of the suit land in the name of the defendants, is barred by limitation, but the appellate court below, on careful examination of evidence on record, found that the plaintiffs have proved sufficiently that they could know about the wrong recording of the suit land in the names of the defendants on 17-10-1985 only and, as such, this suit filed within 6 years from 17-10-1985 is not barred by limitation. The appellate court below made observations to the effect also that there is no evidence at all on record to prove that the plaintiffs had knowledge about the wrong recording of the suit land in the name of the defendants before 17-10-1985 and in the circumstances there was no reason not to believe the plaintiffs assertion that they could know about wrong recording of the suit land only on 17-10-1985. We have also examined the evidence on record and found no reason to disagree with these findings and decision of the appellate court below the plaintiffs have title in the suit land and they have also proved their possession in the suit land. The plaintiffs have adduced evidence to prove that they could know about the wrong recording of the suit land on 17-10-1985 only. There is no evidence on record to prove that the plaintiffs had knowledge about the wrong recording of the suit land before 17-10-1985. In the circumstances the appellate court below rightly found this suit for declaration of title not barred by limitation.

<u>13. Before drawing the end we like to make some comments about the impugned judgment of the High Court Division. It has already been pointed out above that the High Court Division, without making any discussion of any evidence at all and without adverting to the findings and decision and the reasoning thereof made by the appellate court below, set aside the judgment and decree of the appellate court below, the last court of fact. The High Court Division did not bother even to make any reasoning as to why it set aside the judgment of the appellate court below. When the High Court Division, in exercising its revisional jurisdiction, concurs with the findings and decision made by the appellate court below it (High Court Division) may not make elaborate discussion of the evidence on record, but even then also it must give reasonings of its concurring with the findings and decision of the appellant court below. In the present case, the High Court Division set aside the judgment and decree of the appellate court below without making any discussion of the evidence on record and without giving any reasoning at all of doing so. We, with high dissatisfaction, deprecate writing of this sort of judgments by the High Court Division.</u>

14. However, from the above discussion it is evident that this appeal deserves to be allowed.

Hence it is Ordered .....

That the appeal be allowed with cost. The impugned judgment of the High Court Division be set aside and the judgment and decree of the appellate court below be upheld.

End.

full_judgment:
Sharif Uddin Chaklader J : This appeal by the defendants directed against judgment and decree dated 18-1-2007 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, first Court, Narayangonj decreeing Title Suit No. 80 of 1999.

2. Plaintiff-respondents instituted the aforesaid suit for declaration of 16 annas title of 'ka' schedule land and further declaration that the decree passed in Title Suit No. 20 of 1995 on 18-7-1996 by the learned Additional Subordinate Judge Narayangonj, to be declared as void, illegal, collusive and not binding upon the plaintiffs. With further declaration that kabala deed in favour of the defendants as mentioned in 'kha schedule to be declared as illegal, fraudulent not acted upon with the averments that the suit land was originally belonged to Ashutosh Chandra Bondhopaddhya and later on, the father of defendant No. 2, Kalu Mia, by a registered deed in 1950 purchased the suit land and thereafter, on amicable partition, defendant No. 2 got absolute title over the suit land. Defendant No. 2 having in need of money, gave out selling of the suit land, to which, plaintiffs agreed and by 12 saf kabalas plaintiffs purchased the suit land on 3-12-87, 6-12-87 and 9-12-87 and after purchase, plaintiffs mutated their names and opened separate khatians and gradually, constructed pucca and kanccha homesteads, giving rents to different tenants and by realizing rents, plaintiffs are enjoying the suit properties. In the first week of July, 1999, plaintiffs found process server of the Court loitering on the suit property. Plaintiff No. 2 came to learn from the process server that defendant No. 1 obtained a decree over the suit property in connivance with men of the Court and wanted to take delivery of the suit property. Plaintiff No. 2 went to Court and through the lawyer, came to know that defendant No. 1 filed Other Class Suit No. 20 of 1995 against defendant No. 2 for specific performance of a contract and obtained a decree by suppressing the real fact and by executing in Title Execution Case No. 4 of 1996, obtained saf kabala deed through court. Plaintiffs getting such knowledge filed an application under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure for staying the proceeding of Title Execution Case No. 4 of 1996 which was fixed for hearing on 28-7-1999. The plaintiffs obtained entire order sheets including the judgment and decree of Title Suit No. 20 of 1995 on 25-7-1999 and came to know that for entire suit land the price of the suit property was fixed at Taka 2,40,000 and after taking Taka 10,000 from defendant No. 1, defendant No. 2 executed bainama on 9-9-1985 and on the strength of the said baina defendant No. 1 filed Title Suit No. 246 of 1987 in the Court of Subordinate Judge, first Court, which was transferred to the Court of Additional Subordinate Judge, first Court and re-numbered as Title Suit No. 20 of 1995, in which defendant No. 2 filed written statement but did not contest the suit and in connivance with defendant No. 1, allowed the suit decreed ex-parte on 18-7-1996. In that suit, defendant No. 2 in written statement stating that the period mentioning in the bainama being expired, defendant No. 1 having not paying the balance consideration money, said baina was cancelled and defendant No. 2 sold the property to different persons. Plaintiffs being subsequent purchasers with valuable consideration without notice of the alleged bainapatra and having been in possession of the suit land from 3-12-1987 by constructing pucca, semipucca structure on the suit land but defendant No. 1 obtained decree in Title Suit No.20 of 1995 stating in the plaint that defendant No. 1 is in possession of the suit land from 9-9-1985 and obtained the aforesaid decree fraudulently.

3. Appellant as defendant No. 1 contested the suit by filing written statement wherein appellant disclosed that he being a simple school teacher, agreed to purchase the suit land at Taka 2,40,000 and out of that money he paid in cash Taka 10,000 to defendant No. 2 and baina was executed on 9-9-1985 with condition that kabala deed is to be executed and registered within 3 months and if defendant No. 2 did not act as per terms of the baina then defendant No.1 through Court can execute and register the kabala. Defendant No. 2 on 17-9-1985 took further Taka 12,000 as per terms of the bainapatra and defendant No.1 was prepared with remaining Taka 2,18,000 and through his witness, requested defendant No. 2 to execute and register the kabala but defendant No. 2 did not execute and register the kabala on this and that pretext. Defendant No. 2 while trying to sell the suit land to some other persons, defendant No. 1 instituted Criminal Case No. 30 (7)86 with Demra police station. The local people knew about the bainapatra and when defendant No. 2 was not agreeable despite requested of the plaintiffs to execute and register the kabala, on 27-6-1987 he instituted the suit.

4. In the suit, defendant No. 2 also filed written statement almost supporting the case of the plaintiffs.

5. In the suit plaintiffs examined 7 witnesses and for the defendants' 8 witnesses were examined.

Learned Judge decreed the suit.

6. In the body of the judgment the learned Judge found inter alia that it is admitted position that defendant No. 2 executed a bainama in favour of defendant No. 1 on 9-9-1985. Learned Judge also found that the deeds in favour of the plaintiffs are of 3-12-1987, 6-12-1987 and 9-12-1987. Learned Judge also found that bainapatra in point of time was earlier then the deeds in favour of plaintiff. Learned judge thereafter put a question on himself as to whether plaintiffs aware of the bainapatra and whether defendant No. 1 after the bainapatra got delivery of possession and answered that plaintiffs were in possession of the suit property after the kabala executed by defendant No. 2 in favour of the plaintiffs. Learned Judge further found that defendant No. 1 got possession of the suit land on executing decree passed in Title Suit No. 20 of 1995. Learned Judge, thereafter, found that although the bainapatra was executed in 9-9-1985 but possession was not delivered to defendant No. 1. Learned judge upon an application for mandatory injunction filed on 1-2-2000 directed defendant No. 1 to give delivery of possession of the suit land to the plaintiffs by order dated 6-2-2000. Learned Judge thereafter hold that by executing a bainapatra, no title was establish in favour of the bainapatra holder and although bainapatra was executed earlier but no title was passed in favour of defendant No. 1 and by saf kabala deed the title of the plaintiffs have been established over the suit property. Learned Judge also found that pursuant to the decree obtained in Title Suit No. 20 of 1995, the saf kabala deed was executed and, registered on 1-12-1997. Learned Judge also found that deeds were registered in 1997 but the suit land already transferred to the plaintiffs in 1987. Learned judge thereafter held that defendant No. 2 ought to implead plaintiffs in Title Suit No. 20 of 1995 and the plaintiffs although being necessary parties, they were not impleaded in that suit and further held that although in the bainama it was stipulated execution and registration of the deed within 3 months from the date of execution of bainama but that have not been done as such the bainama stand as void. Learned Judge thereafter hold that defendant No. 1 in this way, failed to prove that during the period of bainama, defendant No. 1 ever made 'Tagid' to defendant No. 2 for executing and registering the saf kabala deed. Thereafter, the learned judge held that defendant No.1 as plaintiff, failed to prove the bainamapatra and also execution payment of the consideration money. On the question of possession by defendant No. 1, learned judge held that defendant No.1 with some miscreants (shontrashilok) dismantle 13 premises of the plaintiff out of 17 premises and looted away the valuables. Thereafter, learned Judge decreed the suit.

7. Mr. Md. Shah Alam, learned Advocate appearing for the appellants assail the judgment particularly on the ground that Other Class Suit having been filed prior to the kabala of these plaintiffs and common vendor of the plaintiffs, defendant No. 1 contested the earlier suit by filing written statement the transaction made in favour of the plaintiffs is hit by section 52 of Transfer of Property Act. Learned Advocate submits that, during continuation of the suit if there be any change made by any parties by transfer, the purchaser will be bound by the result of the suit. Learned Advocate on refenence to the plaint, submits that, from the plaint it appears that plaintiff admitted that bainapatra was executed on 9-9-1985 and defendant No. 1 filed Title Suit No. 246 of 1987 on 19-6-1987 and the plaintiffs admitted that they have purchased the suit land in December, 1987 as such all transactions is hit by principal of lispendency. Learned Advocate relied on the decisions of KM Zahirul Haque vs	Shahida	Khanam, 12 BLC (AD) 65, the case of Jamaluddin vs Rabeya Begum, 32 DLR 63, the case of Muzaffor Ali vs Messrs Monwora Hospital, 19 BLD 484 = 51 DLR 341, the case of Hochenaddi Shaikh vs Esrnail Sikder, 9 DLR 294, the case of Debendra Chandra Saha, decree-holder vs Nabin alias Nalini Chandra Pal, 7 DLR 186.

8. Mr Abdul Wadud Bhuiyan, learned Advocate, appearing for the plaintiff-respondents, on the other hand, submits that, in the instant case the question calls for determination as to whose documents executed earlier. Learned Advocate further submits that, it is not denied that the deed of the plaintiffs were later in point of time than the bainama of the defendant No. 1 but the kabalas of the plaintiffs executed much earlier than the kabala of the defendant No. 1 which was executed in 1997 and on reference to section 47 of the Registration Act, submits that, section 47 of the Registration Act provides when there is conflict in between the parties as to their purchase from the same vendor the question of title to be acquired by the person whose deed was executed earlier and submits that since the deed of the plaintiffs being earlier in point of time before the kabala of the defendant No. 1 executed through Court and by this time the suit property transferred to the plaintiffs and after kabalas, plaintiffs mutated their names, paying rents and taxes and also constructed pucca and semi pucca structures on the suit land, as such deed in favour of the plaintiffs acted upon, as such the decree passed by the learned judge should not be interfere. Learned Advocate in support of his submission relied on the decision of Secretary, Board of Trustee, RAJLIK Karmachari Kalyan Trust vs Dhaka City Corporation and others, 2 MLR (AD) 101, the case of Abdur Rashid vs Abdul Bashir, 20 BLD (AD) 262 = 5 BLC (AD) 185, the case of Mir Abdul Ali vs Md Rafiqul Islam, 8 BLD (AD)149 = 40 DLR (AD) 75, the case of Haji Md Ishaque vs Rupali Bank, 43 DLR 621.

9. In this case the simple question calls for determination as to whether the instant suit is governed by section 47 of the Registration Act or by section 52 of the Transfer of Property Act. Let us quote both the sections.

<u>10. Section 47 of the Registration Act speaks time from which registered document operates- A registered document shall operate from the time from which it would have commenced to operate if no registration thereof had been required or made, and not from the time of its registration.</u>

11. Section 52 of the Transfer of Property Act speaks that during the pendency in any Court in Bangladesh of any suit or proceeding which is not collusive and in which any right to immovable property is directly and specifically in question, the property cannot be transferred or otherwise dealt with by any party to the suitor proceeding so as to affect the rights of any other party thereto under any decree or order which may be made therein, except under the authority of the Court and on such terms as it may impose.

12. Lis means a suit and pendents means pending and it imposes conditions,

(i) The existence of a continuous suit,

(ii) Transfer took place during its active prosecution.

(iii) Its a constructive notice to a purchaser that he will be bound by the decree of the suit.

<u>13. Having noted the character of the people of this region as they can do anything for self interest, law makers in section 52 of Transfer of Property Act protect the right of a transferee that pendente lite neither party to the litigation can alienate the property in dispute so as to affect his opponent. It operate in a suit where the rights to immovable property are involve and transaction is subject to the decree of the Court.</u>

14. Section 47 of the Registration Act as we see is that if there be any conflict in between two parties of the same property transferred by same vendor then the deed in favour of person executed earlier will prevail over the other deed, when the deed registered then it will take effect from the date when it was executed. In the case of Azizuddin vs Abu Taleb Sarder, 35 DLR 360, where the Court found the defendant's kabala was executed earlier than the plaintiffs kabala which though executed later was, however, registered before the defendant's kabala; it was held that execution of the defendant's Kabala being earlier in point of time will have precedence over the plaintiff's kabala.

15. Mr Wadud Bhuiyan, learned Advocate, on section 47 of the Registration Act relied on the case of Mir Abdul Ali vs Md Rafiqul Islam, 8 BLD (AD)149 = 40 DLR (AD) 75, where the question was when there be successive documents of transfer by self-same vendor, question as to which document is valid and it was decided that 'a document that has been registered relates back to the date of its execution. The question of title as between the two contestants claiming on the basis of successive documents executed by the self-same vendor must be determined with reference to the title to the later on the date of execution and not of registration'. Other decisions cited by the learned Advocate for the plaintiff respondent were of the same line.

16. The fact is that common vendor in the instant case executed the baina in 1985 and kabala in 1987; defendant No. 1 filed suit in 1987 which was decreed in 1997 and kabala was registered in 1997, as such, even we fall back on section 47 of the Registration Act then also the title passed to defendant No. 1 from the date of execution of the bainama i.e. from 1985. The decisions cited by the learned Advocate for the plaintiff-respondents also propounded same proposition of law that registration of the document goes back to the date of execution.

17. The question calls for determination as whether the plaintiffs' suit is maintainable on the ground of lis-pendency. It appears from the plaint that plaintiff purchased the suit property subsequently when the suit of defendant No. 1 was already filed and proceeded. The best case for the plaintiff is that plaintiffs kabalas being registered document and defendant No. 1 is armed with only a bainama through which title did not pass, but since the suit was decreed that title of the suit land was passed to defendant No. 1 from the date of execution of baina in 1985 i.e. before registration of kabala of the plaintiffs which were registered in 1987. In the instant suit the question is very much clear that when the suit was filed in 1987 plaintiffs even did not go near to the suit property as their kabalas were executed more than two years after institution of the suit.

<u>18. It is an admitted fact that when plaintiffs purchased the suit property in 1987 when the suit of this defendant appellant i.e. Title Suit of 1987 was pending as such, the transaction in favour of plaintiffs during continuation of the suit is hit by doctrine of lis pendency. Transact-ion of the plaintiffs is hit by section 52 of the Transfer of Property Act i.e. lis-pendency and the plaintiffs of the instant suit will be abide by the decree passed against their vendor in Suit No. 20 of 1995 and by virtue of the decree passed in Suit No. 20 of 1995, the suit land was transferred to defendant No. 1 from the date of execution of bainama i.e. from 1985 as such, when the suit land was transferred to the plaintiffs, plaintiffs did not acquire any title but only they purchased litigation on some paper transaction.</u>

19. The plaintiffs claimed that defendant No. 2 in his written statement disclose the fact that he has already transferred the suit land to someone. We have gone through the written statement but no where defendant No. 2 stated to whom he has sold the suit land as such we are of the view that this statement made by the defendant No. 2 is totally vague and on the basis of vague statement no one can be brought into the suit or impleaded in the suit.

20. We find substance in this appeal.

21. In the result, this appeal is allowed without any order as to costs.

22. The impugned judgment and decree dated 18-1-2007 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, Narayangonj in Title Suit No.80 of 1999 is set-aside. The suit is dismissed.

Send down the lower Court records at once.

End.
